    We evaluate learned game dynamics through player–geometry and player–NPC interactions, assess long-horizon rendering and world generation on seen and unseen maps, and measure end-to-end inference efficiency. We also demonstrate multiplayer composition and programmable gameplay without retraining. Together, these experiments show that PlayGen2 supports real-time interactive world simulation with transferable dynamics and an extensible state interface.

    Training data and compute. We train on approximately 500 hours of gameplay automatically collected exclusively on Freedoom2 MAP01 using a rule-based controller in ViZDoom [(Kempka et al., 2016)]. The dataset totals roughly 500 GB. The world-state model and rendering model contain 41.2 M and 29.1 M parameters, respectively; the latter excludes the fixed 55.3 M-parameter VAE. RGB frame resolution is 160×120. All models are trained from scratch. The total training budget is approximately three days on four NVIDIA A100 GPUs (288 GPU-hours).

    Evaluation setting. Seen-map evaluation uses Freedoom2 MAP01. Unseen-map evaluation uses seven levels from Scythe, a community-created Doom II map pack. Starting positions are fixed before evaluation, and the same starting configurations and controller settings are used across global and local initialization. For learned-world rollout, global initialization supplies the full static map, whereas local initialization supplies only the initial neighborhood and requires learned completion during exploration. Both initialization modes provide local entity histories only at the start of rollout; subsequent entity states and newly discovered entities are predicted by the model. We evaluate each map from multiple predefined starting positions using a rule-based stochastic exploration controller to select actions. A failure occurs when more than half of the player’s bounding box overlaps occupied geometry. The player respawns after a failure. We evaluate 64 exploration trajectories for each combination of map familiarity (seen/unseen) and map initialization (global/local). Each trajectory lasts 10 simulated minutes, yielding 256 trajectories in total. Visual-quality evaluation uses BF16 inference and eight renderer denoising steps by default. Each simulation step corresponds to three engine tics at 35 Hz, yielding 700 steps per simulated minute. The 1-, 5-, and 10-minute stages below refer to simulated time rather than wall-clock duration. Checkpoints and detailed protocols are provided in Appendix C.

    4.1 Learned Game Dynamics and Control

    We measure player–geometry interaction using contact error rate (CER), the fraction of resolved obstacle encounters and landings that end in severe penetration. CER aggregates resolved encounters across respawns up to each evaluation horizon. RGB action accuracy (ActAcc) [(Yang et al., 2024)] measures agreement between commanded actions and actions recognized from generated RGB, assessing control through both dynamics and rendering.

    Table 1 demonstrates sustained action-conditioned control over ten-minute rollouts, achieving ActAcc of 82.1–85.6% and cumulative CER of 5.2–6.8%. Comparable performance on seen and unseen maps shows that the model learns transferable player dynamics rather than memorizing interactions within the training map. Both CER and ActAcc remain relatively stable between five and ten minutes, indicating sustained control and physical interaction over long-horizon rollouts. Together, these results demonstrate the framework’s ability to maintain controllable, geometry-aware interaction over long horizons and across new environments.

    Monster–player interaction.

    In Doom, monsters pursue the player as part of their combat behavior. We evaluate randomly sampled player locations around an observed Zombieman initialization, keeping the player stationary during each rollout. Pursuit is considered successful when the monster reaches a horizontal body-surface distance less than 30 world units from the player. The model achieves a 55% pursuit success rate within 200 steps. Figure 3 illustrates successful model-generated approaches toward different player locations, demonstrating that our model learns game world dynamics that encompass player–NCP interactions and reasonable NPC behavior.

    Importantly, these interactions extend beyond the camera’s field of view. PlayGen2 updates NPC states throughout its active 3D simulation volume, regardless of whether they are currently visible. A monster can therefore continue pursuing the player and approach from behind even while the player is looking elsewhere. By decoupling entity dynamics from visual observation, our framework allows off-screen entities to remain active participants in gameplay: turning away changes what the player sees, not whether the surrounding world continues to evolve. This capability supports a more coherent and engaging interactive experience.

    4.2 Long-Horizon Rendering and World Generation

    We evaluate long-horizon visual quality under global and local initialization on seen and unseen maps. For each trajectory, we sample three 32-frame clips from a one-minute window near each evaluated horizon. All horizons refer to simulated time. Under global initialization, the explicit player state allows us to extract camera trajectories from rollouts driven by a rule-based stochastic exploration policy and replay them in the ViZDoom engine to obtain pose-aligned reference videos. Under local initialization, the model generates previously unknown geometry, so no unique aligned engine reference exists. We therefore report only FID and FVD for this setting, using a fixed Freedoom2 reference pool.

    We compare with PlayGen [(Yang et al., 2024)] on Freedoom2 MAP01, the training map shared by both systems. We convert the exploration trajectories into action sequences and use them to drive PlayGen. Notice that PlayGen do not have the capabilities to generalize on unseen maps. We report PlayGen results at one and five minutes; by five minutes, its generated videos exhibit substantial visual degradation.

    Seen-map comparison. The two systems achieve comparable visual quality at one minute. By five minutes, however, PlayGen’s quality deteriorates substantially, whereas PlayGen2 retains substantially more stable scores and performs better on all five metrics. Across the one-, five-, and ten- minute stages, PlayGen2’s LPIPS remains within 0.41–0.44. These results support the framework’s ability to sustain visual quality during long-horizon generation.

    Unseen maps. Figure 4 shows zero-shot rendering on unseen Scythe maps. The examples illustrate that PlayGen2 follows the supplied spatial structure while synthesizing appearance in its learned Freedoom2 style. Because depth and semantic conditions do not specify the native Scythe textures, reference-based metrics reflect both structural discrepancies and appearance differences; we therefore interpret them alongside qualitative results and their variation over time. PSNR remains within 16.1–16.6 dB and LPIPS within 0.63–0.66 across the sampled stages, showing limited variation over ten simulated minutes and supporting transfer to layouts absent from training.

    Generating local worlds. Starting from a local neighborhood, PlayGen2 incrementally generates geometry and introduces entities as the player explores. FID and FVD remain broadly stable across the evaluated horizons, supporting sustained visual quality as the generated world expands. Figure 5 shows the resulting spatial layouts, distinguishing initialized geometry from generated extensions and newly introduced entities. Despite training on a single map, the model generates plausible geometry and entity configurations from both seen- and unseen-map initializations. These results indicate that PlayGen2 learns transferable spatial priors for game-world structure: the learned regularities support world expansion beyond the specific training layout and can be applied to new spatial contexts without retraining.

    4.3 Extensible Gameplay

    PlayGen2’s explicit state interface enables participant synchronization and programmable rules on top of learned dynamics. We demonstrate multiplayer composition and programmable interaction using models trained exclusively on single-player gameplay, without updating their weights.

    Multiplayer composition. We compose single-player model instances by exchanging player states and representing the other participant as a Zombieman. Each player supplies independent actions and maintains a separate RGB history. Both players’ motion is predicted by learned action-conditioned transitions without runtime collision correction. Following the opponent-presence evaluation of MultiGen [(Po et al., 2026)] as closely as possible, we assess whether generated observations depict the opponent consistently with reference visibility. PlayGen2 achieves 96.3% accuracy, 90.5% precision, and 95.0% recall, with opponent visibility as the positive class (Table 3). Synchronized views and trajectories for approach, departure, and following are shown in Figure 6; setup details are provided in Appendix C.1. These results demonstrate that models trained for single-player interaction can be composed into a multiplayer experience through their shared state interface, without multiplayer-specific training.

    Programmable interaction. Figure 3 demonstrates rule-based health loss and death implemented through explicit state interventions, with feedback overlaid on generated observations. The state interface allows these rules to be specified and modified directly, rather than requiring the neural models to learn each rule from additional examples. The learned dynamics and renderer are reused, while selected gameplay events are governed by explicit code. This combination supports precise control over chosen mechanics without replacing the learned simulation, allowing the same trained system to accommodate new interaction rules.

    4.4 Interactive Efficiency

    The complete simulation–rendering pipeline is able to run locally on a MacBook Pro (M4 Pro). With 8 denoising steps, serial execution achieves 4.98 FPS at 200.6 ms mean per-frame backend latency.Separate profiling measures approximately 75/90/30 ms for world-state updates, latent rendering, and VAE decoding, respectively. Overlapping world updates and rendering on the same device raises throughput to 7.16 FPS (+44%), at 275.7 ms latency. These results demonstrate that our world-state modeling makes a complete learned 3D simulation and rendering loop computationally tractable at interactive rates on consumer hardware.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented PlayGen2, a playable world model that decouples learned 3D world-state evolution from neural rendering. By explicitly representing static geometry and dynamic entities, the framework integrates geometry completion, entity discovery, and action-conditioned dynamics within persistent world memory. Our Doom experiments demonstrate learned player–geometry and player–NPC interactions, sustained visual quality over long-horizon rollouts, and interactive execution on a consumer laptop. Beyond the training environment, the same framework supports zero-shot deployment on unseen maps, multiplayer composition, and programmable gameplay without retraining. Together, these results establish explicit 3D world state as a practical foundation for unifying learned simulation, neural rendering, and flexible interaction in efficient, extensible, and playable game worlds.

    Appendix A World-State Model Details

    This appendix specifies the representation, architecture, supervision, and memory operations underlying Section 3.2.

    A.1 Persistent World State

    We use the world state defined in Equation 1. Entity positions refer to their bases, and player orientation is encoded as (\sinθₜ,\cosθₜ). The object table includes moving entities and stationary interactable items. Identity-aligned slots and validity masks distinguish missing observations from observed stationary states.

    The network operates on an axis-aligned crop centered approximately on the current player position, without rotating the map into the viewing direction. The crop covers 800×800×200 world units with a voxel width of five units, giving a 40×160×160 volume in Z,Y,X order. Let Vₜ⁻ and Kₜ⁻ denote its occupancy and availability before scene completion. A zero in Kₜ⁻ denotes unknown geometry, not empty space. At inference, available voxels can come from initialization or earlier predictions.

    We retain four history frames and at most 24 active object slots. Historical positions share the current crop origin. For continuous attributes x=(x,y,z,h,r,vₓ,v_y,v_z), network inputs use the elementwise transform

    x̄=2x-l/u-l-1,

    		(5)

    where l=(-80,-80,-120,5,5,-15,-15,-15) and u=(900,900,300,128,32,15,15,15) are fixed normalization constants, not clipping bounds. World-space memory, transition reference positions, and displacement composition retain FP32 physical coordinates.

    A.2 Joint Geometry and History Encoding

    Volumetric geometry. The geometry encoder receives Kₜ⁻⊙Vₜ⁻, Kₜ⁻, and voxel-center height relative to the player divided by 100. Residual blocks combine horizontal 1×3×3 and vertical 3×1×1 convolutions, GroupNorm, and GELU. Table 4 specifies the feature pyramid and Transformer sizes. The coarsest volume is projected to width 512 and flattened into 500 tokens with 3D sinusoidal position encodings. Finer levels support reconstruction and entity-local geometry conditioning.

    Player and object histories. Player tokens combine normalized state, orientation, and an action embedding; object tokens combine normalized state and a class embedding. For incomplete histories, adjacent-frame position differences carry identity-aware validity:

    b_τⁱ=1[same object valid atτ-1,τ], d_τⁱ=b_τⁱ(p_τⁱ-p_τ-1ⁱ).

    		(6)

    A learned projection of [d_τⁱ/10,b_τⁱ] is added to the corresponding object token. A missing pair has b=0, whereas an observed stationary pair has b=1 and d=0. Single-frame histories therefore remain distinguishable from observed stationary histories.

    Temporal, slot, and token-type embeddings identify history tokens. The Shared Context Transformer jointly encodes geometry, player history, and masked object history into ℂₜ, excluding current-frame entrants and future states.

    A.3 Scene Discovery at a Committed Pose

    Discovery completes the scene at the committed player pose at t; transition then advances its entities to t+1. The crop origin thus remains independent of the same-step predicted pose. The Discovery Transformer processes Geometry Queries and Spatial Entity Queries jointly, with cross-attention to ℂₜ.

    Geometry completion. The Geometry Decoder reshapes the 500 Geometry Query outputs into a coarse volume and reconstructs occupancy using trilinear upsampling and encoder skip connections. Separate voxel heads predict occupancy and an auxiliary new-entity heatmap. Only unavailable voxels receive occupancy updates. The heatmap provides training supervision, not query selection.

    Spatial entity proposals. Training and inference share deterministic anchor rules (Table 5), using only available state. After clipping and deduplication, anchors occupy up to 128 query slots; unused slots are masked. For player displacement exceeding 0.5 units on any axis, 44 boundary samples favor motion-leading faces and 20 retain six-face safety coverage. Otherwise all 64 use six-face coverage, with horizontal faces weighted twice as strongly as top and bottom. Each Spatial Entity Query combines a learned embedding with anchor, family, and applicable source-slot embeddings.

    After the Discovery Transformer, Spatial Entity Queries attend to local features from the encoder’s 40×80×80 level and to a global memory of 10×20×20 encoder features through the New-entity Decoder. They predict objectness, foreground class, and continuous attributes. New-entity positions are bounded residuals relative to their anchors:

    p̂ₜʲ=aₜʲ+100\tanh(uₜʲ).

    		(7)

    Height and radius use scaled sigmoid outputs, and velocity uses scaled \tanh outputs. Objectness is predicted separately from foreground identity, separating existence prediction from semantic classification.

    Supervision uses a coordinate-only Hungarian assignment restricted to reachable anchor–target pairs, maximizing the number of distinct matched objects before minimizing normalized position cost. Reachability requires distance at most 100 world units and per-axis offsets within the output range. Additional nearby anchors regress to their nearest reachable target, while primary assignments preserve distinct target coverage; unreachable targets remain unmatched. At inference, proposals above the objectness threshold are ranked by objectness times foreground-class probability. Class-aware non-maximum suppression treats two proposals as duplicates when their vertical intervals overlap and their horizontal distance is at most \max(5,(rᵢ+rⱼ)/2). Filtering against existing same-class entities additionally requires positive vertical overlap of at least half the smaller height. Accepted entities enter free slots with one valid history frame.

    A.4 Geometry-Conditioned State Transitions

    The Transition Transformer attends to shared context concatenated with Current Entity Tokens, including newly committed entities, while reusing the original encoder features. Each non-player Entity Query is conditioned through an MLP on its current class and state, three history differences, and their validity bits.

    To supply finer geometry, we trilinearly sample a 5×5×5 neighborhood from the encoder’s 40×80×80 feature volume. For persistent objects, the samples span ±20 world units horizontally and extend from ten units below the object’s base to ten units above its top. Relative sample positions are embedded, and entity-local attention produces an additive query condition:

    q̄ₜⁱ=qⁱ+eₛₗₒₜⁱ+Fₛₜₐₜₑ(oₜⁱ,d_t-2:tⁱ,b_t-2:tⁱ),(8)
    q_t,condⁱ=q̄ₜⁱ+F_local(q̄ₜⁱ,ℙₜⁱ),

    where ℙₜⁱ contains sampled geometry features. Conditioning is applied once before the Transition Transformer. Both the new-entity and persistent-entity geometry paths backpropagate into the encoder; neither reads newly decoded occupancy. The player query accesses geometry and action history through the shared context.

    Separate heads predict object XYZ displacement, height/radius, velocity, and class; the player additionally predicts a normalized orientation vector. Positions follow Equation 2: the learned displacement is added to the current position, with no prescribed velocity integration. A background class permits object retirement. State transitions are deterministic given their inputs.

    A.5 Training Objectives and History Augmentation

    We train on reset-safe five-frame windows: four context frames and one next-state target. Static targets and newly discovered objects belong to the last context frame t, whereas player and persistent-object targets belong to t+1. The static input is the preceding crop reprojected to the origin at t; its overlap defines the known mask. Current-frame entrants are hidden from discovery and teacher-forced into the transition input with a single valid frame. Instance identities define persistent supervision, and crop exits are distinguished from actual disappearances. Training uses one-step supervision.

    Static geometry. Unknown-voxel completion combines focal and volumetric Dice losses, with a smaller reconstruction term on known voxels:

    L_static=10L_focalᵘⁿᵏⁿᵒʷⁿ+L_Diceᵘⁿᵏⁿᵒʷⁿ+0.1L_BCEᵏⁿᵒʷⁿ.

    		(9)

    Known and unknown terms have independent denominators. Dice is computed over each full 3D crop rather than independently per height slice, excluding crops with no unknown voxels. The focal loss uses α=0.25 and γ=2. A Gaussian focal objective supervises the auxiliary new-object heatmap.

    Player and persistent entities. The player objective is L_ego=5L_ego,geom+L_ego,vel, using mean L1 errors on (x,y,z,h,r) and velocity, respectively. Orientation has a separate L1 term L_angle on (\sinθ,\cosθ). Persistent entities use focal classification (γ=2) and L1 attribute regression, with separate classification and regression counts. Attribute errors sum over channels and average over valid entities. Their objective is

    Lₚₑᵣₛ=L_pers,cls+5L_pers,hr+L_pers,vel+Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ+Lᵢₜₑₘ.

    		(10)

    Non-item XYZ supervision uses the six phases in Table 6. Within each phase, we average summed per-axis Smooth L1 errors between predicted and target displacements, both divided by 10, with β=0.1. Let ℓ̄ₘₒᵥₑ average the nonempty continue, start, and unknown-moving phase means, and let ℓ̄_stay average the nonempty stay and unknown-stationary means. Then

    Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ=5ℓ̄ₘₒᵥₑ+ℓ̄_stay+2ℓₛₜₒₚ.

    		(11)

    Empty groups contribute zero; phase counts are aggregated across devices. Separately normalized phases balance motion against frequent stationary examples. Stationary interactable item classes are excluded from these groups; Lᵢₜₑₘ averages their summed XYZ L1 errors divided by 10.

    New entities and joint objective. New entities use sigmoid focal objectness (α=0.25, γ=2), foreground focal classification (γ=2) on positive anchors, and Smooth L1 regression on normalized attributes, weighted 5:1:1 for XYZ, height/radius, and velocity. Objectness weight increases linearly from 0.1 to 1 over the first 500 training steps. These terms form L_new and share a normalizer equal to the global positive-query count divided by device count, or one if there are no positives. GIoU is monitored only. The joint objective is

    Lₛₜₐₜₑ=5L_static+10Lₕₑₐₜ+20L_ego+10L_angle(12)
    +Lₚₑᵣₛ+L_new.

    Robustness to imperfect histories. We randomly permute object slots and truncate history prefixes with probability 0.3 per object, preserving the latest valid frame and allowing single-frame histories. Player and non-item positions receive independent uniform noise with horizontal bounds ±ρr and vertical bounds ±ρh, using ρ=0.002 and 0.02, respectively. For stationary items, 30% of sequences instead receive temporally correlated drift after history truncation. For m≥2 surviving observations, the kth valid position is perturbed by

    p̃ₖⁱ=pₖⁱ+k/m-1ηⁱ, k=0,…,m-1,

    		(13)

    where horizontal components of ηⁱ are uniform in [-1,1] and its vertical component is uniform in [-2,2] world units. The first surviving observation stays clean, and one-frame histories are not corrupted. Targets remain clean; conditioning differences are recomputed from the perturbed histories, while motion-phase labels use clean differences with the updated validity masks. Static inputs remain unperturbed.

    A.6 Rollout and Memory Management

    Given the current committed player pose, retained histories, and action aₜ, one simulator step proceeds as follows:

  • 1.

    Crop the global occupancy and availability caches at the current pose. Express the retained object and player histories in this crop’s coordinate frame and construct state-derived candidate anchors.

  • 2.

    Encode the pre-discovery histories and crop once. Retain the shared context tokens and the multiscale geometry features.

  • 3.

    Run the Discovery Transformer and New-entity Decoder. Run the Geometry Decoder when the crop contains unavailable voxels.

  • 4.

    Commit geometry at the current crop origin, preserving known voxels. Restore eligible dormant entities, then threshold and deduplicate discovered objects. Allocate clean slots and insert each accepted object into the current history frame.

  • 5.

    Concatenate Current Entity Tokens with the retained context and run the Transition Transformer without re-encoding completed occupancy.

  • 6.

    Convert predictions to world coordinates. Retire background-class entities, store out-of-volume entities as dormant, and append the next player and active-object states to history.

  • 7.

    Project available geometry and updated entities into depth and semantic conditions at the new viewpoint. Generated RGB updates only visual history; the next simulator step completes newly exposed map regions.

    • The map cache preserves both occupied and empty committed voxels on revisits. Dormant entities retain their last state outside the local volume and resume updates on re-entry; reallocated slots have their histories cleared. Skipping the Geometry Decoder leaves both entity branches active because they obtain spatial features from the encoder.

    Appendix B Renderer Details

    This appendix specifies world-state projection, renderer architecture, training stages, and cached inference described in Section 3.3.

    B.1 World-State Projection

    The deterministic operator Π converts occupancy and entity states into aligned 160×120 semantic and depth conditions. Camera rays use the player’s position and yaw, the configured pitch, and a 90^∘ horizontal field of view, following Doom’s 320/200 projection aspect ratio. Rays march through the local occupancy grid in 2.5-unit increments, stopping at the first occupied voxel, the crop boundary, or a 400-unit range limit. Surface hits provide camera-forward depth and a shared static-geometry label (255). Each non-player entity is represented by an axis-aligned box of size 2r×2r×h at its base position. Box faces are clipped at a one-unit near plane and rasterized from far to near. A face’s mean camera depth is checked against static depth at its projected polygon center before filling the polygon with that depth and the entity’s class ID. The same lightweight projection convention is used for data generation and learned-world rollout; surface textures are supplied by the neural renderer.

    For a projected surface with camera-forward depth Dₜ(u,v), the normalized depth condition is

    dₜ(u,v)=Q₈ (1-clip((Dₜ(u,v))/(400),0,1)), Q₈(q)=(⌊255q⌋)/(255).

    		(14)

    This encoding gives larger values to nearer surfaces and preserves the 8-bit quantization used in the training data. Pixels with no projected surface have semantic label sₜ=0 and depth value dₜ=0. The renderer receives separate validity masks mₜˢ=1[sₜ≠0] and mₜᵈ=1[dₜ>0] alongside these maps.

    B.2 Architecture

    The renderer predicts frame xₜ from four preceding RGB frames, target-view conditions cₜ=(sₜ,dₜ,mₜˢ,mₜᵈ), and action aₜ₋₁. Here sₜ and dₜ are semantic labels and normalized depth as defined above, with validity masks mₜˢ,mₜᵈ. A frozen, domain-trained VAE encodes each 120×160 image into a 4×30×40 latent using its posterior mean. Latents are standardized channel-wise before diffusion and unstandardized before decoding. The history and scene-condition encoders are separate from target denoising.

    RGB-history encoding. Each latent is divided into 2×2 patches, producing 300 tokens per frame and 1,200 for a complete four-frame history. Learned spatial and relative frame-position embeddings identify location and time. A two-block Transformer attends over valid history tokens to produce Hₜ; all history frames precede the target.

    Scene-condition encoding. Categorical semantic embeddings are concatenated with normalized depth and both validity masks. A convolutional encoder reduces them to latent resolution; patch projection and spatial/type embeddings produce scene-condition tokens Cₜ. Token validity follows the input masks. Keeping Cₜ separate from Hₜ gives each denoising block direct access to current geometry and semantics alongside historical appearance.

    Target denoiser. The noisy target uses the same latent patch projection, with spatial and target-type embeddings. Each of eight blocks applies target self-attention, cross-attention to Hₜ, cross-attention to Cₜ, and a feed-forward network, using pre-normalization and residual connections. Summed noise-index and action embeddings are projected in each block and added before query and feed-forward normalizations. A linear output head reconstructs the latent grid. Both Transformers use width 384, six attention heads, feed-forward width 1,536, and zero dropout.

    B.3 Training Stages and History Construction

    Denoising objective. Diffusion perturbs only the target latent; history and scene conditions are held fixed. For standardized target zₜ and ε∼ℕ(0,I),

    zₜ⁽ⁿ⁾=αₙzₜ+σₙε, vₜ⁽ⁿ⁾=αₙε-σₙzₜ,

    		(15)

    where αₙ²+σₙ²=1. We use 1,000 diffusion indices with linearly spaced variances from 10⁻⁴ to 0.02. The base objective is v-prediction MSE:

    L_diff=𝔼 [∥v_θ(zₜ⁽ⁿ⁾,Hₜ,Cₜ,aₜ₋₁,n)-vₜ⁽ⁿ⁾∥₂²],

    		(16)

    averaged over latent elements. Table 7 distinguishes the training stages. The final 90,000 updates use this MSE with uniformly sampled diffusion indices and a mixture of 50% ground-truth history, 40% generated history, and 10% history dropout. Ground-truth examples supply the four recorded frames preceding the target. The VAE stays frozen throughout.

    Generated RGB history. We cache short autoregressive rollouts from the frozen step-102,500 renderer. Each anchor contains four recorded initial frames followed by four generated frames, using recorded scene conditions and actions. We uniformly sample a depth k∈{1,2,3,4} and take the last four frames after k generated frames as history. The target is the next recorded frame, with its aligned scene conditions and preceding action. Thus histories contain one to four generated frames while targets stay clean. Anchors use non-overlapping nine-frame windows within reset-safe trajectory segments. The offline cache remains fixed during fine-tuning, so each update requires one target-denoising evaluation per example rather than an online rollout.

    RGB-history dropout. All RGB-history slots are marked invalid while scene conditions and action remain available. The history encoder supplies a content-free fallback. This trains condition-only synthesis and supports initialization without reference RGB frames.

    B.4 Efficient Sampling

    Each frame starts from Gaussian latent noise and uses eight denoising steps by default, with indices evenly spaced from 999 to 0 and rounded to integers. Updates combine the predicted clean latent and noise at the next index without injecting additional noise. The final clean prediction is unstandardized, decoded to RGB, and retained directly as a latent history entry, replacing the oldest frame without re-encoding the generated image.

    History and scene conditions are encoded once per frame. Their tokens and per-block cross-attention keys and values are cached across all denoising steps; only target-dependent computation is repeated. The cache is rebuilt for the next frame, keeping the history length and per-frame computation independent of total rollout duration.

    Appendix C Evaluation Details

    World-state and renderer checkpoints are at steps 200,000 and 192,500. Unseen levels are Scythe MAP01–05, MAP07, and MAP10; engine references use ViZDoom 1.3.0 and 90^∘ horizontal field of view. Other shared settings are given in Section 4.

    C.1 Interaction and Control

    Contact counting. CER is 100N_failed/N_resolved, counting successful and failed obstacle contacts and landings up to each horizon. Overlapping categories count once; unfinished or unassessable encounters are excluded. Counts persist across respawns, excluding teleportation. Contact tests use supplied geometry in Global and generated memory in Local.

    Monster pursuit. Trials reset one four-frame Zombieman history in the full map, remove other entities, and disable discovery. We sample 20 stationary player locations on a 20-unit grid, five per quadrant, 100–220 units from the monster (seed 1234), requiring support, empty body volume, and a sampled supported straight path. Success requires body-surface gap ≤30, feet-height difference ≤10, and vertical overlap ≥28 units, using initial body dimensions. All trials count toward the 200-step statistic. Figure 3A–D use 300 steps; E uses a separate wall-side initialization.

    Multiplayer and interventions. Examples use full-map initialization with other entities removed. Players exchange states, representing peers as Zombiemen, with independent actions and RGB histories and no collision correction. Opponent-presence scores follow the VLM protocol of [Po et al. (2026)], with visible as positive; MultiGen values are quoted from that paper. Programmed health loss and death modify explicit state with fixed weights; health feedback is overlaid on rendered observations.

    C.2 Visual Quality

    Frame and distribution metrics. PSNR, SSIM, and VGG LPIPS v0.1 use full 160×120 frames, including weapons, averaged within clips and equally across episodes. SSIM uses an 11×11 Gaussian window (σ=1.5), population covariance, and valid centers. FID uses Inception-v3 pool3 (2048-D); FVD uses TF-Hub Kinetics-400 I3D pre-softmax logits (400-D). Both sides use lossless RGB, resized identically to 299×299 for FID and 224×224 for FVD. Each 32-frame clip supplies eight FID frames at offsets 0,4,…,28 and one FVD sample. Distribution scores pool samples per setting and horizon, using FP32 features and FP64 statistics (sample covariance for FID; population covariance for FVD).

    References and recovery. Global frame metrics use pose-aligned engine references with native map textures. Local FID/FVD share an unpaired Freedoom2 reference pool. Recovery retains world memory but resets RGB history. Clips overlapping failure, recovery, or 32 post-recovery warmup steps are excluded from visual scores, but failures remain in CER. PlayGen receives actions rather than explicit states; its paired scores include trajectory divergence as well as appearance differences.

    C.3 Interactive Efficiency

    Both models share one M4 Pro device (MPS FP32), with one process and one Torch CPU thread per model. Pipelining overlaps world update t+1 with rendering t. Table 8 uses two 60-frame repeats, after 12 warmup frames and reset, with matched actions and noise. Throughput includes pipeline fill/drain and inter-process transport, excluding initialization, network, and display.

    Appendix D Design Comparisons

    We examine local geometry conditioning, volumetric map modeling, and renderer training. Comparisons use trained checkpoints with differing training budgets and settings rather than budget-matched retraining.

    D.1 Local Geometry Conditioning

    We compare 2D world-state models trained without and with encoder-side local-map conditioning, retaining each model’s trained inputs. Both use the same 28 player placements from three NPC histories: 16 obstructed and twelve clear initial directions. Each rollout keeps one Zombieman and a stationary player in the full reference map for at most 300 steps, without collision correction or ground-truth NPC feedback. Rollouts end at severe penetration, target proximity, entity loss, or timeout. Penetration requires more than half of 125 torso samples to overlap occupied voxels; proximity uses a 30-unit body-surface gap with vertical compatibility. Contact counting follows Appendix C.1.

    The local-map model halves penetration episodes and increases successful approaches from 4/28 to 15/28 (Table 9). Both variants move by more than one unit in approximately 77% of audited steps, so the improvement is not explained by stationary predictions. Figure 8 shows paired trajectories, including a remaining failure.

    D.2 Geometry Representation

    We compare the 2D encoder-local-map model with the 3D model at step 200,000 along eight fixed Freedoom2 engine trajectories, each lasting 700 transitions (60 seconds). Poses, actions, and initial local geometry are identical; predicted map updates are committed to memory and fed back without future reference geometry. Dynamic entities and learned player updates are excluded to isolate map generation from trajectory drift.

    The 3D model produces 79.5% fewer small isolated components (919 versus 188), with reductions on all eight paths and the same trend under alternative connectivity and size thresholds. Aggregate IoU and recall increase, with a modest decrease in precision (Table 10). Figure 9 compares generated geometry along matched paths.

    D.3 Renderer Training

    We report one-minute rendering quality on Freedoom2 MAP01 with condition-only initialization: no real RGB history is supplied, and subsequent RGB histories are generated autoregressively. The earlier checkpoint (step 102,500) is evaluated using fixed engine conditions, eight denoising steps, BF16, and full-frame metrics at 160×120. The final checkpoint (step 192,500) follows mixed-history training (Appendix B.3). Table 11 reproduces its Seen/Global scores from Table 2; the two rows come from separate evaluation runs.

item.title: 交互式视觉助手不能只看「离线回放」：Interactive Visual Gym 把「用户会被助手改变行为」这件事也模拟进去 ｜ Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds
item.description:
一句话：闭环里助手的回答会改变用户下一步动作，因而也改变任务结果——离线回放量不到这些效应。

要点：

  • 评估缺陷很本质：视觉交互模型要在用户执行实体任务的过程中给予协助，这就要求**闭环**评估——助手的回答会改变用户之后的行为，进而改变任务结果
  • 现有基准大多依赖离线回放，因此完全捕捉不到这些效应
  • Interactive Visual Gym 用「可执行任务环境 + 模拟用户」的联合仿真来做闭环评估与训练，并提供了三个模拟器

为什么值得看：任何「AI 在旁边看着你干活」的产品（装配、维修、游戏内教学）都需要闭环评测。把模拟用户放进环境，是一个可复用的评测框架——比拿录屏打分的离线基准更接近真实效果。

中文摘要：支持用户完成实体任务的视觉交互模型，必须在闭环中评估：助手的回答会改变用户接下来的行为，从而改变任务结果。而现有基准大多依赖离线回放，捕捉不到这种效应。Interactive Visual Gym 因此提出一个闭环评估与训练框架，通过「可执行任务环境 + 模拟用户」的联合仿真来生成反馈，并贡献了三个模拟器。对任何「AI 在旁边指导人干活」的产品——装配、维修、游戏内教学——这种把用户反应纳入回路的评测方式，比离线打分更接近真实效果。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-07

本期推送：2026-11-09

Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds

Abstract

Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.

1 Introduction

Building systems that collaborate effectively with people is a longstanding goal of interactive machine learning [(Amershi et al., 2014)]. Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled collaboration on digital tasks, including web research and software development, through dialogue, preference adaptation, and coordinated action [(Shao et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026)]. More recently, extending such collaboration to everyday physical tasks has drawn growing interest, motivating visual interaction models that observe a video stream of a user’s ongoing activities and provide guidance [(Cui et al., 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026; Yao et al., 2026)]. For example, an assistant monitoring a procedural physical task like cooking can help plan the next step, detect execution errors, and guide recovery if a mistake happens.

Developing and evaluating interactive agents requires closed-loop rollouts that capture how each interaction changes subsequent user behavior and environment state, enabling assessment of its contribution to task completion. For digital agents, existing websites and software provide readily available tasks and executable environments, which can be paired with simulated users to support such rollouts [(Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2026)]. Building an equivalent testbed for visual assistance is substantially more difficult. First, physical tasks and their environments are not readily available in a digital form; they must be reconstructed with visual observations, underlying world state, and an action space that supports human task execution. Second, visual assistance places substantially greater demands on user simulation. In most digital settings, the model executes actions while the user primarily clarifies goals and preferences. In physical activities, the user is the acting agent, and the model influences execution through communication. The simulated user must plan, act, make plausible mistakes, while interpreting guidance and deciding how to respond. These simulation challenges have limited visual interaction model training and evaluation to replaying recorded interactions and matching reference responses [(Liu et al., 2026; Kundu et al., 2026; Ran et al., 2026)], where the user’s actions and responses remain unchanged regardless of the assistant’s guidance.

We present Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation of visual interaction models through joint simulation of task environments and human users. Our framework has three components:

First, we recreate everyday tasks across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile interface use in executable visual environments. These environments render visual observations from the user’s perspective. They use scene graphs to represent world state and track task progress independently of variations in action execution. They expose a human-aligned semantic action space for simulated users to operate in, translating instructions such as “put the pan on the stove” into executable operations.

Second, we design a harness that turns a state-of-the-art VLM into simulated users that plan and act within these environments while interacting with the assistant and revising their actions in response to its guidance. The harness supports controlled insertion of common human out-of-plan events at specified task states, including repeating, forgetting, or incorrectly executing a step, changing plans, and asking questions. We further model diverse user personas through attributes such as skill level, trust in AI, and interruption preference. These attributes shape how users perform tasks and respond to guidance differently, enabling evaluation of the assistant’s adaptation to different users.

Third, simulation provides execution traces that support comprehensive evaluation of an assistant, covering task completion, error detection, and interaction quality. This captures how assistance affects task execution and user experience, which offline replay cannot assess.

As an initial instantiation of our framework, we construct IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 150 cooking, 75 household, and 90 mobile-interface interaction scenarios to evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models. In each episode, the assistant is tasked to support a simulated user with a sampled persona through task execution, and needs to deal with a set of scheduled out-of-plan events. The dynamic rollout allows us to measure task completion under assistance and assess individual responses against the underlying world state. The best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, averaged across the three environments, and also shows severe deficits in factual grounding and actionable guidance, revealing a substantial gap toward reliable interactive assistance.

Finally, we demonstrate that CookSim can support end-to-end reinforcement learning of multimodal assistants through a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment with Qwen3.5-4B [(Qwen Team, 2026a)] as the assistant and Gemini 3.7 Flash [(Google, 2026b)] as the simulated novice user. After 12 RL updates, the assistant’s mean in-time task success rate improves by 8.9 percentage points on held-out development-validation scenarios with a Gemini 3.7 Flash user, and by 3.3 percentage points in a separate evaluation with a Gemini 3.8 Flash user (Tab.5). Despite limited tasks and training updates, these results show that CookSim can supply a learning signal and induce policy improvements in interactive task performance.

2 Related Work

Streaming visual assistance. Recent interaction models continuously process multimodal streams and support low-latency, proactive, or full-duplex responses [(Cui et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Orantqing et al., 2026)]. Live guidance has also been studied through user-in-the-loop cooking assistance [(Verghese et al., 2024)] and workspace-conditioned visual instructions [(Wu et al., 2026)]. Complementary datasets and benchmarks study procedural guidance, mistake recovery, correct silence, and response timing in egocentric or general video streams [(Zhang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026; Kundu et al., 2026; Bhattacharyya et al., 2026; Chatterjee et al., 2026; Vasu et al., 2026)]. In these benchmarks a candidate model is typically scored against a prerecorded trajectory. Our framework instead evaluates response-contingent rollouts.

Interactive agent environments. Embodied benchmarks place agents in simulated worlds for navigation, manipulation, and collaboration [(Shridhar et al., 2020; Puig et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022; Padmakumar et al., 2022; Puig et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2025)], and recent multimodal gyms unify diverse visual tasks for evaluation and reinforcement learning [(Wang et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026)] or study which environment mixtures best train visual agents [(Zhu et al., 2026)]; in all of these, the evaluated model selects the actions itself. Digital interaction benchmarks instead pair tool-using agents with simulated users and verify outcomes from application state [(Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2026)], which τ-Voice extends to voice interaction [(Ray et al., 2026)]. BASIS trains and evaluates visual interaction models through simulated user interactions in Alexa Arena [(Zhang et al., 2025b)]. User simulation has long enabled scalable dialogue evaluation [(Schatzmann et al., 2005)], and language models now support persona-conditioned users [(Aher et al., 2023)], but simulated users can diverge systematically from people, requesting validation [(Seshadri et al., 2026)].

3 Method

Our framework combines executable physical task environments with simulated human users to evaluate visual interaction models. We first describe how these environments reconstruct everyday tasks, expose human-communicable actions, and track task progress. We then introduce the human-agent harness and its interaction with the assistant, followed by the evaluation metrics.

3.1 Executable Physical Task Environments

Simulating everyday tasks. We reconstruct procedural physical tasks in three domains (Fig.2):

Cooking. Inspired by Overcooked [(Ghost Town Games, 2016)], we build CookSim from scratch, with recipes specifying ingredient quantities, preparation requirements, and plating order where applicable. Users navigate kitchens with distributed ingredients and tools while accomplishing the cooking task. For example, preparing a cheeseburger requires cooking a patty and plating the bun, patty, and cheese in that order. The simulator is implemented in Three.js/WebGL and supports top-down and egocentric 3D rendering.

Household activities. We adapt VirtualHome [(Puig et al., 2018)] for everyday apartment tasks combining navigation and object manipulation. For example, cleaning up after a meal requires loading plates and a mug into the dishwasher, returning an apple to the fridge, and closing both appliances. The simulator uses VirtualHome’s Unity backend for egocentric 3D rendering, while providing a top-down trajectory map.

Mobile interface use. ScreenSim replicates the iPhone 17 Settings interface, with multi-step configuration tasks derived from Apple’s user guides [(Apple, 2026)]. For example, restricting an app’s access requires disabling its location permission, cross-app tracking, and background refresh while leaving other apps unchanged. The simulator is implemented in HTML/CSS rendered in Chromium and captures mobile-screen observations through Playwright.

Human-communicable action space. Existing physical-task simulators expose simulator-specific movement and interaction primitives, such as movement increments or object identifiers [(Li et al., 2022; Puig et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2022)]. People typically communicate at a more abstract semantic level, referring to objects and intended operations. We therefore build a semantic action space for each environment (Fig.2), with commands such as “go to the nearest pan” in CookSim, “place the book on the table” in VHSim, and “select Background App Refresh” in ScreenSim. During execution, an LLM-based grounding module resolves contextual references, such as “the pan on your left,” into object identifiers recognized by the simulator. The simulator then expands each high-level action into a sequence of low-level controls that update the world state and generate visual observations.

Progress tracking via scene-graph state. Each simulator represents world state as a scene graph with nodes encoding objects and attributes, such as a dishwasher’s open or closed state, and edges encoding containment and support relations. We decompose each task into sub-goals defined by conditions over partial graph state, such as the designated dishes being inside the dishwasher. Tracking these conditions measures task progress independently of different valid execution procedures.

3.2 User–Assistant Interaction

The visual interaction model under evaluation is tasked with guiding a simulated user through tasks in the environments described above. We implement the user as a VLM agent with access to structured world-state information, execution feedback, and conversation history. The VLM is prompted to role-play a human user to test the assistant’s interaction capabilities, planning and acting independently while responding to guidance according to its persona. A user-simulation harness conditions its behavior through persona instructions and temporarily takes control of its actions to enact scheduled out-of-plan events. Below, we describe the action and communication interfaces, account for assistant response delays, and detail these mechanisms for controlling user behavior.

Action interface: user–environment. The simulated user maintains an action queue that the engine executes at each simulation tick and can revise in response to environment changes or assistant suggestions. The engine updates the world state and renders the resulting observation:

sₜ₊₁=T(sₜ,aₜ), oₜ₊₁=R(sₜ₊₁),

(1)

where aₜ is the action executed from the user’s queue, T is the state-transition, and R is the renderer.

Communication interface: user–assistant. The assistant monitors sampled frames from the user’s observation stream alongside the conversation history. At an assistant invocation at tick t, it generates a response

mₜ=A(o_≤t,c_≤t),

(2)

where o_≤t denotes the sampled visual history and c_≤t is the conversation history. The response mₜ contains an utterance or silence in text format and an optional event-type flag (Tab.1(A)), which is enabled when the assistant detects a user execution error. On each user turn, the simulated user likewise produces an utterance or remains silent. Its conversational response types include asking for an explanation, questioning the correctness of guidance, requesting more guidance or fewer interruptions, accepting or rejecting a suggestion, and answering a question.

Accounting for assistant delay. Assistant processing delay can substantially affect interaction quality: by the time a response arrives, the user and environment may have progressed beyond the observed state, rendering the guidance outdated or invalid. Following the separation of simulation time and wall-clock time in τ-Voice [(Ray et al., 2026)], we assign each simulation tick a duration Δ based on approximate real-world action speeds. For example, VirtualHome is configured to move the user one meter per simulation tick. Assuming this distance takes 1.2 seconds to walk in the real world, we assign each tick a duration of Δ=1.2 seconds. We convert the measured assistant inference latency ℓₜ into a delay of dₜ=⌈ℓₜ/Δ⌉ simulation ticks. The response mₜ, generated from observations through tick t, is delivered at tick t+dₜ. During this interval, the engine continues executing the user’s queued actions and updating the world state.

Scheduled out-of-plan events. We introduce scheduled out-of-plan events in all three simulators that require the assistant to respond to execution errors, questions and intended plan change. For example, the event types in CookSim are shown in Tab.1(A): we simulate common cooking errors of incorrect preparation, omitted or improperly sequenced steps, and ill-timed actions [(Peddi et al., 2024)]; we generate temporal questions adapted from streaming-video benchmarks [(Niu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026)] and proactive requests for timely assistance [(Zhang et al., 2025a)]; we also introduce intended plan changes, where users may announce revised goals or a side task during execution. Each event is triggered by a specified condition on task progress.

When an event is triggered, the harness temporarily takes control of the user’s action queue to enforce its execution. It privately informs the user agent of the ongoing event and explains that the event is intended to test the assistant, instructing the user agent to adapt its conversation accordingly. For mistake events, the user agent judges whether the assistant has correctly identified the mistake and decides whether to accept its guidance. Once the guidance is accepted, the harness returns control of the action queue to the user agent.

Persona-conditioned users. Real-world users differ in how they perform tasks and respond to assistance. Drawing on HCI and related behavioral research, we operationalize this diversity through four representative axes: skill level [(Shneiderman, 2000)], trust in AI [(Lee & See, 2004)], execution speed [(Wickelgren, 1977)], and interruption preference [(McFarlane, 2002)] (Tab.1(B)). The harness instantiates each persona through axis-specific instructions in the user model’s context. For example, high-skill users are prompted to plan ahead independently, while low-skill users are prompted to ask assistant frequently to determine the next steps. Users who prefer minimal interruption are prompted to find unnecessary commentary disruptive, whereas those who benefit from step-by-step support prefer more frequent guidance. The execution speed and interruption preference are shared to assistant as part of announced user preference, while the skill level and trust in AI are treated as internal property of a user for assistants to infer and adapt.

3.3 Evaluation Metrics

Our simulation rollouts allow us to measure task completion under assistance and assess individual responses against the underlying world state. We evaluate the assistants with the following metrics:

In-time success.In-time success measures the proportion of episodes whose engine-verified goal is satisfied within a completion budget of 2(Tᵢ^ref+αᵢ), where Tᵢ^ref is the duration of an engine-generated, error-free reference rollout and αᵢ is the prescribed event allowance. Environment-specific budgets are detailed in AppendixD.

Error detection.Detection recall is the proportion of triggered errors correctly identified within their eligible detection windows, credited when the assistant raises a correct event flag verified by the engine or when the simulated user judges its diagnosis correct. For the latency ablation, we also report error prevention, the proportion of triggered errors prevented before the point of no return. Prevention requires both timely identification and guidance that persuades the user to change course.

Interaction quality. We evaluate each assistant response against the underlying world state, rather than against a reference response as in prior works. We define five dimensions of evaluation informed by dialogue evaluation [(Mehri & Eskenazi, 2020)] and HCI guidance on context-sensitive, user-controllable assistance [(Amershi et al., 2019)]: factual grounding, situational relevance, actionable guidance, user intent uptake, and guidance conciseness. We operationalize these dimensions as binary rubric items evaluated by two LLM judges [(Liu et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025)]. For each conversational round, each judge receives engine state, user preferences, conversation history, and subsequent user actions, returning evidence-supported pass, fail, or not-applicable judgments of each rubrics. A category passes only when all applicable items pass; each judge’s overall score averages applicable categories, gated by its factual-grounding judgment. We average the two judges’ round scores before aggregating across rounds and runs. Judge prompts and score aggregation are detailed in AppendixI.

Question answering and proactive requests. The engine pairs each generated question with a grading procedure that derives reference facts from world state and execution history. A semantic judge assigns correctness against these facts. For proactive requests, the engine derives an acceptable notification window from the relevant state transitions.

4 Experiments

We use our engine to instantiate IVG-Bench benchmark for evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models (Sec.4.1), and validate our evaluation paradigm through a human study (Sec.4.2). We further present a preliminary reinforcement learning experiment showing that our engine can support training visual interaction models and improve their interaction performance (Sec.4.3).

4.1 IVG-Bench: Benchmarking Visual Interaction Models in Interactive Visual Gym

IVG-Bench comprises 315 interaction scenarios: 150 in CookSim, 75 in VHSim, and 90 in ScreenSim. Each case specifies a task, a user persona, and scheduled out-of-plan events triggered by task-progress conditions. Below we detail the setting for evaluated visual interaction models and show evaluation results.

4.1.1 Visual Interaction Model Setting

Models. We evaluate four classes of assistants: (1) frontier API models: GPT-6 Astra [(OpenAI, 2026a)], GPT-6.1 Sol [(OpenAI, 2026c)], Gemini 3.8 Flash [(Google, 2026c)], and Gemini 4 Argon [(Kavukcuoglu, 2026)]; (2) real-time streaming API models: Gemini 3.8 Live [(Google, 2026d)] and GPT-Realtime 2.1 [(OpenAI, 2026b)]; (3) open-weight non-streaming VLMs: Qwen3.8-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026b)], Molmo2-8B [(Clark et al., 2026)], InternVideo3-8B [(Yan et al., 2026b)], Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking [(Kimi Team et al., 2025)], and Muse Glimmer [(Meta, 2026)]; and (4) open-weight streaming VLMs: MiniCPM-o 4.5 [(Cui et al., 2026)], Qwen3-Omni-30B [(Xu et al., 2025a)], Proact-VL [(Yan et al., 2026a)], and StreamingVLM [(Xu et al., 2025b)]. We use Gemini 3.7 Flash as the simulated user in CookSim and ScreenSim, and Gemini 3.1 Pro [(Google, 2026a)] in VHSim. We examine sensitivity to the user model in AppendixA.

Inference. Assistants observe the user’s ongoing activity through visual observations and conversation, without access to the scheduled events or the user’s private action plan. In CookSim and VHSim, we query assistants every two simulation ticks, including real-time API models in a polled setting. Streaming models retain context within their sessions. We adapt non-streaming models with a sliding window of the eight most recent observations and a recurrent, text-based Plan–Act memory. This follows the use of persistent procedural plans for visual assistance in [Kundu et al. (2026)]. Each open-weight model is served on an H100 GPU in CookSim and VHSim. ScreenSim settings are detailed in AppendixH.

Response timing. We use fixed response timing for the main comparison: two simulation ticks for CookSim and VHSim’s streaming interactions, and zero ticks for ScreenSim’s action–response interactions. We separately evaluate the effect of measured assistant latency in CookSim and VHSim. Each setting uses three independent rollouts per benchmark scenario.

4.1.2 Quantitative Results

We report task success, error detection, and interaction quality across the three environments in Tab.2 and Fig.3. Tabs.3 and 4 report question answering and the effect of assistant latency, respectively. We discuss the main findings below.

Even the strongest VLMs fall short of reliable visual assistance. Gemini 4 Argon achieves the highest task success, but completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, averaged across the three environments. Moreover, Gemini 4 Argon trails Astra, Sol, and Gemini Flash in interaction quality, with notable limitations in factual grounding and actionable guidance. Open-weight assistants generally fall short of proprietary models on both task success and interaction quality.

The strongest streaming models remain competitive in interaction quality but lag in task success. Gemini Live achieves high average interaction quality, yet completes fewer tasks than Astra and Gemini Flash. This pattern may reflect a trade-off between low-latency inference and high planning and reasoning ability.

Higher task success does not necessarily imply better interaction quality. Although the two measures are positively associated (Fig.3), task outcomes alone can hide weak assistance. For example, Muse Glimmer completes more tasks than Astra in CookSim while receiving much lower interaction-quality scores. Completing the task is therefore not sufficient evidence of high quality guidance.

Temporal question answering is surprisingly difficult during task-directed interaction. We present the result of temporal question answering from the measured-delay CookSim runs in Tab.3. Unlike questions about fixed videos, the questions are asked by human agent at specific moments during multi-turn interactions in which the assistant must also help the user complete the task, closely reflecting real world scenario. We find that open-weight models often lose track of the question or request during multi-turn conversations (Tab.3). Proprietary models generally perform better, with Gemini 4 Argon and Astra leading the pooled evaluation but still exhibit weakness in temporal action counting.

4.1.3 Effect of Assistant Latency

We assess the effect of assistant response latency in CookSim and VHSim by comparing rollouts with measured latency against the fixed two-tick setting (Tabs.4 and 4). We use the same tasks, personas, and scheduled events in both settings, each averaged across three independent runs.

Response latency substantially reduces in-time task success for frontier API models. Introducing measured latency lowers success for all four frontier API models in both environments. The accompanying decline in error prevention helps explain this loss (Tab.20): even when an assistant recognizes an impending mistake, its warning may arrive after the user has committed the action, incurring either task failure or additional steps to recover from errors.

Accounting for response latency changes model rankings. Gemini 4 Argon achieves the highest task success in CookSim under fixed response timing, while Muse Glimmer leads when measured latency is considered. In CookSim, Gemini 4 Argon’s success falls from 60.9% to 33.1%, while Muse Glimmer changes little. Measured latency also lowers interaction quality for the frontier API models in both environments, particularly in situational relevance and actionable guidance.

4.2 Validating Interactive Visual Gym via Human Study

To examine both evaluation validity and user-simulation fidelity, we conduct a human study in CookSim simulator. 45 participants interact with 3 anonymously labeled assistants and rank the interaction experience after completing for 3 rounds. Full study protocol provided in AppendixF.

Interaction quality reflects human preferences. To test the validity of our interaction-quality metric, we compare each assistant’s mean score with participants’ rankings. The metric agrees with human preferences in 78.5% of participant–assistant-pair comparisons, corresponding to a pooled Kendall’s τ of +0.57. This correspondence supports its use as a measure of the assistance experienced by users.

Simulated users reproduce most of human behaviors. We compare human and simulated episodes along three dimensions: communication behavior, persona-dependent variation, and action error types (Fig.5). We use binary rubrics to measure behavioral dimensions and compute the similarity between human and simulated users on each dimension (detailed in appendix). Simulated users reproduce human behavioral differences across most persona axes, with particularly close agreement for trust and interruption preferences. The engine also covers the error types observed in participants’ action behaviors, including incorrect preparation, omitted or repeated steps, and assembly-order errors. Action parallelism match less well, possibly because the human speed groups show almost no difference in parallel cooking. We also found a clear deviation between the communication hebavior between human agent and real human: although their utterance lengths are similar, simulated users speak to assistants much more often than human participants. One possible reason is that the simulated user is invoked very frequently to reconsider whether to speak, repeatedly making conversation salient.

4.3 Interactive Visual Gym as an RL environment

We train Qwen3.5-4B with GRPO on CookSim, using Gemini 3.7/3.8 Flash as a classic-novice user. We split CookSim’s 150 scenarios into 120 for training and 30 for validation. Each update uses 24 episodes: 6 scenarios with 4 episodes each. Because binary in-time success is sparse, we use the shaped reward r=I[success]+0.30 I[error prevented]-0.02\min(N_false flags,15)-0.05\min(T/200,1). Here, T counts interaction turns. Task success dominates (r≥0.65 for successes; r≤0.30 for completed failures); shaping encourages timely intervention and discourages false flags and excess turns (AppendixC).

Across three evaluation passes on CookSim’s held-out development-validation scenarios with a Gemini 3.7 Flash user, mean in-time task success rate rises from 33.3% to 42.2% after 12 updates, an increase of 8.9 percentage points (Tab.5). A separate experiment with a Gemini 3.8 Flash user improves mean in-time task success rate by 3.3 percentage points (64.4% to 67.8%) and mean interaction quality by 5.9 points (24.3% to 30.2%). Mean detection recall declines in both settings, possibly because the reward favors selective flagging that can miss uncertain errors, consistent with false flags falling from 517 to 391 across 90 episodes with a Gemini 3.8 Flash user. Fig.7 illustrates one case where the trained assistant gives timely guidance that prevents an error. These fixed-scenario results show that Interactive Visual Gym supplies a useful learning signal for interactive assistance, paving the foundation for future work to demonstrate generalization across tasks, user models, or domains.

5 Conclusion

We present Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of task environments and human users. Across three domains, we find substantial limitations in current VLM to serve as reliable assistants. We also validated our interaction paradigm with human study. Finally, a preliminary reinforcement-learning experiment shows that the environments can improve assistant performance.

AI use statement

We used generative AI tools, including coding agents, to assist with implementing our simulators and evaluation pipeline, generating synthetic benchmark cases, refining experiments, and interpreting results. We also used them for literature search, figure creation, code editing, and drafting and revising manuscript text. We reviewed AI-assisted outputs and take responsibility for the final code, data, figures, and claims.

Ethics statement

Our human study took place in a browser-based cooking simulator; participants did not perform physical cooking tasks. The study recorded action traces, text exchanges, and preferences, which we analyze and report in aggregate. Because free-text exchanges may contain personal information, any release of raw traces must follow the study’s consent and privacy procedures. Performance in our simulators should not be taken as evidence that an assistant is safe for real-world use.

Reproducibility statement

We describe environment and benchmark construction in AppendixG, assistant settings in AppendixH, user prompts in AppendixJ, and event placement and scoring in AppendicesE, D and I. The appendix also reports the human-study protocol (AppendixF), variation across independent runs (AppendixB), and the reinforcement-learning configuration (AppendixC).

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Sensitivity to the Simulated-User Model

We examine how the choice of base model for the simulated human agent affects evaluation results. We fix the visual interaction model to Gemini 3.7 Flash and vary the model controlling the simulated user in CookSim, evaluating on the same subset of 90 benchmark episodes (Tab.6).

We find that GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 3.7 Flash yield similar task-success rates when used to evaluate the same assistant, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro differ a bit. Local open-weight models yield much lower task-success rates, potentially reflecting smaller models’ difficulty following the complex instructions required to elicit the intended user behavior.

Appendix B Variation Across Independent Runs

We examine the variability of closed-loop evaluation by running each assistant three times with the same tasks, personas, and scheduled events. Tabs.7, 8 and 9 report in-time success, detection recall, and interaction quality for each run, together with their mean and population standard deviation (SD). We evaluate CookSim and VHSim under both fixed two-tick and measured assistant delay. All scores are percentages.

一句话：闭环里助手的回答会改变用户下一步动作，因而也改变任务结果——离线回放量不到这些效应。

要点：

  • 评估缺陷很本质：视觉交互模型要在用户执行实体任务的过程中给予协助，这就要求**闭环**评估——助手的回答会改变用户之后的行为，进而改变任务结果
  • 现有基准大多依赖离线回放，因此完全捕捉不到这些效应
  • Interactive Visual Gym 用「可执行任务环境 + 模拟用户」的联合仿真来做闭环评估与训练，并提供了三个模拟器

为什么值得看：任何「AI 在旁边看着你干活」的产品（装配、维修、游戏内教学）都需要闭环评测。把模拟用户放进环境，是一个可复用的评测框架——比拿录屏打分的离线基准更接近真实效果。

中文摘要：支持用户完成实体任务的视觉交互模型，必须在闭环中评估：助手的回答会改变用户接下来的行为，从而改变任务结果。而现有基准大多依赖离线回放，捕捉不到这种效应。Interactive Visual Gym 因此提出一个闭环评估与训练框架，通过「可执行任务环境 + 模拟用户」的联合仿真来生成反馈，并贡献了三个模拟器。对任何「AI 在旁边指导人干活」的产品——装配、维修、游戏内教学——这种把用户反应纳入回路的评测方式，比离线打分更接近真实效果。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-07

本期推送：2026-11-09

Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds

Abstract

Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.

1 Introduction

Building systems that collaborate effectively with people is a longstanding goal of interactive machine learning [(Amershi et al., 2014)]. Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled collaboration on digital tasks, including web research and software development, through dialogue, preference adaptation, and coordinated action [(Shao et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026)]. More recently, extending such collaboration to everyday physical tasks has drawn growing interest, motivating visual interaction models that observe a video stream of a user’s ongoing activities and provide guidance [(Cui et al., 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026; Yao et al., 2026)]. For example, an assistant monitoring a procedural physical task like cooking can help plan the next step, detect execution errors, and guide recovery if a mistake happens.

Developing and evaluating interactive agents requires closed-loop rollouts that capture how each interaction changes subsequent user behavior and environment state, enabling assessment of its contribution to task completion. For digital agents, existing websites and software provide readily available tasks and executable environments, which can be paired with simulated users to support such rollouts [(Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2026)]. Building an equivalent testbed for visual assistance is substantially more difficult. First, physical tasks and their environments are not readily available in a digital form; they must be reconstructed with visual observations, underlying world state, and an action space that supports human task execution. Second, visual assistance places substantially greater demands on user simulation. In most digital settings, the model executes actions while the user primarily clarifies goals and preferences. In physical activities, the user is the acting agent, and the model influences execution through communication. The simulated user must plan, act, make plausible mistakes, while interpreting guidance and deciding how to respond. These simulation challenges have limited visual interaction model training and evaluation to replaying recorded interactions and matching reference responses [(Liu et al., 2026; Kundu et al., 2026; Ran et al., 2026)], where the user’s actions and responses remain unchanged regardless of the assistant’s guidance.

We present Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation of visual interaction models through joint simulation of task environments and human users. Our framework has three components:

First, we recreate everyday tasks across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile interface use in executable visual environments. These environments render visual observations from the user’s perspective. They use scene graphs to represent world state and track task progress independently of variations in action execution. They expose a human-aligned semantic action space for simulated users to operate in, translating instructions such as “put the pan on the stove” into executable operations.

Second, we design a harness that turns a state-of-the-art VLM into simulated users that plan and act within these environments while interacting with the assistant and revising their actions in response to its guidance. The harness supports controlled insertion of common human out-of-plan events at specified task states, including repeating, forgetting, or incorrectly executing a step, changing plans, and asking questions. We further model diverse user personas through attributes such as skill level, trust in AI, and interruption preference. These attributes shape how users perform tasks and respond to guidance differently, enabling evaluation of the assistant’s adaptation to different users.

Third, simulation provides execution traces that support comprehensive evaluation of an assistant, covering task completion, error detection, and interaction quality. This captures how assistance affects task execution and user experience, which offline replay cannot assess.

As an initial instantiation of our framework, we construct IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 150 cooking, 75 household, and 90 mobile-interface interaction scenarios to evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models. In each episode, the assistant is tasked to support a simulated user with a sampled persona through task execution, and needs to deal with a set of scheduled out-of-plan events. The dynamic rollout allows us to measure task completion under assistance and assess individual responses against the underlying world state. The best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, averaged across the three environments, and also shows severe deficits in factual grounding and actionable guidance, revealing a substantial gap toward reliable interactive assistance.

Finally, we demonstrate that CookSim can support end-to-end reinforcement learning of multimodal assistants through a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment with Qwen3.5-4B [(Qwen Team, 2026a)] as the assistant and Gemini 3.7 Flash [(Google, 2026b)] as the simulated novice user. After 12 RL updates, the assistant’s mean in-time task success rate improves by 8.9 percentage points on held-out development-validation scenarios with a Gemini 3.7 Flash user, and by 3.3 percentage points in a separate evaluation with a Gemini 3.8 Flash user (Tab.5). Despite limited tasks and training updates, these results show that CookSim can supply a learning signal and induce policy improvements in interactive task performance.

2 Related Work

Streaming visual assistance. Recent interaction models continuously process multimodal streams and support low-latency, proactive, or full-duplex responses [(Cui et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Orantqing et al., 2026)]. Live guidance has also been studied through user-in-the-loop cooking assistance [(Verghese et al., 2024)] and workspace-conditioned visual instructions [(Wu et al., 2026)]. Complementary datasets and benchmarks study procedural guidance, mistake recovery, correct silence, and response timing in egocentric or general video streams [(Zhang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026; Kundu et al., 2026; Bhattacharyya et al., 2026; Chatterjee et al., 2026; Vasu et al., 2026)]. In these benchmarks a candidate model is typically scored against a prerecorded trajectory. Our framework instead evaluates response-contingent rollouts.

Interactive agent environments.
