Relative to camera-only SolarWM, it improves PSNR by 2.82 dB on EgoStandard-200 and 1.66 dB on EgoLife-300, while reducing LPIPS from 0.494 to 0.345 and from 0.584 to 0.488, respectively. On HOT3D-45, it achieves an LPIPS of 0.488 and a DINOv2 similarity of 0.769. These results show improved agreement with reference observations across both in-domain and out-of-domain scenes. Figure 5 further illustrates the visual results across diverse scenes, where the same camera and hand controls are reused with different initial images and scene descriptions.

    Our multi-step causal model also achieves lower LPIPS and higher DINOv2 similarity than SolarWM on all three datasets, while its PSNR improves or remains comparable. The four-step distilled model further improves PSNR and SSIM over the multi-step causal model across all three datasets, with mixed changes in LPIPS, DINOv2 similarity, and KID. These results characterize the visual-quality trade-offs introduced by causal adaptation and few-step distillation.

    We next evaluate hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response using TouchéBench to examine how these models translate visual generation quality into controllable interaction.

    4.3 Evaluation on TouchéBench

    Table 2 reports results on the four dimensions of TouchéBench. Our bidirectional teacher achieves the highest hand-following PCK@0.2 of 65.8%, compared with 61.2% for Hand2World and 59.1% for JCV, while our multi-step and four-step causal models obtain 57.9% and 54.0%, respectively. Hand2World achieves the lowest localization error on matched detections at 28.2 pixels. For camera–hand coordination, our teacher achieves 100.0% Camera and 60.0% Interaction pass rates, compared with 50.0% and 15.0% for JCV, and 40.0% and 15.0% for Hand2World. Our causal models retain this advantage, with the multi-step model scoring 70.0% and 40.0%, and the four-step model scoring 60.0% and 35.0%. On online interaction, the multi-step causal model achieves the highest overall pass rate of 75.0% and hard-criterion pass rate of 55.6%, exceeding the teacher’s 71.5% and 45.8%, respectively. The four-step model obtains 68.8% overall, remaining above JCV’s 51.4% and Hand2World’s 33.3%. For object response, JCV achieves the highest mask IoU of 38.7%, while our multi-step causal model achieves the lowest target-center offset of 48.8 pixels. These results highlight the distinction between image-space alignment and interaction success: favorable keypoint or object-overlap scores can coexist with low action-execution and final-state pass rates. The qualitative case study 6 illustrates this distinction through examples of camera movement and object behavior, while the action-branch examples 7 show different continuations from a shared context. Together, the quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate stronger joint-control and action-dependent interaction performance for our framework, with reduced hand-following and camera–hand coordination scores after causal adaptation and few-step distillation.

    4.4 Case Study

    Figure 5 illustrates how a shared camera–hand control sequence produces scene-dependent interactions. Starting from the osmanthus-tree example, we reuse the controls with four different scene initializations. The hand settles on the tabletop in the cafe scene, moves out of view after reaching through free space in the gallery, and grasps a package at the store shelf. These examples show that the generated hand behavior adapts to the surrounding scene while retaining the input motion pattern. In the shelf comparison, JCV produces substantial viewpoint changes toward the ceiling, while Hand2World generates hand motion in front of a largely unchanged shelf; our model instead produces a reach-and-lift interaction. Figure 6 further examines the distinction between spatial agreement and object interaction. In the reference, the hand moves the bottle relative to the cup. JCV retains the bottle near its initial position through much of the sequence, whereas our teacher and causal model generate more pronounced hand-associated object movement. Retaining an object near its initial location can preserve overlap with reference masks over parts of the sequence, illustrating why mask IoU should be interpreted alongside action execution and object-state changes. Finally, Figure 7 evaluates action-dependent continuations from a shared approximately two-second context. Different hand inputs ask the model to rotate a box, lift it above another box, or slide it along the tabletop. Our teacher and causal model produce distinct changes in box orientation, height, and position across these branches, while the baselines show less consistent separation of the intended outcomes. Together, these cases illustrate joint camera–hand control, scene-dependent contact behavior, and distinct object responses to actions introduced after a shared context.

    4.5 Ablation Studies and Analysis

    Hand-weighted loss.

    Tables 3, 5, and 4 examine the effect of hand-weighted training on video quality and interaction. Hand weighting improves keypoint accuracy for both the teacher and causal models across all three PCK thresholds. For the teacher, PCK@0.2 increases from 58.7% to 65.8%, while localization error decreases from 60.0 to 48.2 pixels. The causal model improves from 55.0% to 57.9% PCK, with localization error decreasing from 55.0 to 46.8 pixels. These improvements also extend to online interaction: Q3 Overall increases from 65.3% to 71.5% for the teacher and from 72.2% to 75.0% for the causal model. For camera–hand coordination, the teacher’s Interaction score increases from 40.0% to 60.0%, while its Camera score remains at 100.0%. The causal model exhibits a trade-off, with Camera decreasing from 90.0% to 70.0% and Interaction from 45.0% to 40.0%. Object-mask IoU improves for both model types. Changes in global video quality are dataset-dependent: all five metrics improve for the teacher on EgoStandard and for the causal model on EgoLife, while the remaining evaluation sets show mixed changes. Overall, hand-weighted supervision strengthens hand following and online interaction, with a coordination trade-off in the causal model.

    Causal adaptation and few-step distillation.

    We examine the generation stages through the teacher, multi-step causal, and four-step causal results in Tables 1 and 2. Moving from the bidirectional teacher to the causal model reduces reference-based video quality and hand-following accuracy, with PCK@0.2 decreasing from 65.8% to 57.9%. Q2 Camera and Interaction also decrease from 100.0% and 60.0% to 70.0% and 40.0%, respectively. On Q3, the causal model achieves higher Overall and Hard pass rates, increasing from 71.5% and 45.8% to 75.0% and 55.6% under the method-specific context initialization used in our evaluation. This contrast shows that stronger reference reconstruction and keypoint alignment do not directly imply better action-dependent continuations. Four-step distillation improves PSNR and SSIM over the multi-step causal model on all three video-quality test sets, while changes in LPIPS, DINOv2 similarity, and KID are mixed. Hand-following PCK decreases to 54.0%, Q2 Camera and Interaction decrease to 60.0% and 35.0%, and Q3 Overall decreases to 68.8%. Object-response measurements remain close, with mask IoU changing from 34.9% to 35.0% and target-center offset from 48.8 to 49.3 pixels. These results characterize the transition to four-step causal generation: object-response fidelity remains similar under the reported spatial metrics, while hand following, joint control, and online interaction show larger performance reductions.

    5 Conclusion and Future Work

    We presented TouchéWorld, a video world modeling framework that integrates continuous hand interaction with camera-guided exploration. We constructed joint camera–hand training data through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment, and combined spatial skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation enable chunk-level online generation with updated camera and hand controls. We further introduced TouchéBench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Experiments demonstrate scene-dependent interaction across diverse environments and action-dependent continuations from shared contexts, while revealing distinct trade-offs among visual quality, hand following, and interaction performance.

    Our qualitative results also reveal early signs of gesture-mediated interaction with people in generated scenes. This opens a direction for extending interactive world models beyond object manipulation toward human interaction. Future work will explore how generated people perceive and respond to user gestures, enabling richer exchanges between users and the inhabitants of generative worlds.

    6 Acknowledgements

    This work is partially supported by a public grant overseen by the French National Research Agency(ANR) as part of the program Investissements d’Avenir (ANR-10-LABX-0083).

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：相机导航之外，连续手部动作是更细的交互通道；难点是两类控制要按时间对齐。

要点：

  • 现状：视频世界模型让用户通过相机导航探索生成环境；但连续的手部运动才是与人和物体交互的细粒度通道
  • TouchéWorld 把**手势驱动的交互**接进相机可控的视频世界模型：给定初始图与场景描述提示，按时间对齐的相机与手部控制生成视频
  • 作者构建了配套的数据与控制方案，使「一边走一边动手」在生成世界里成立

为什么值得看：「可玩」的本质是能动手。多数世界模型只有相机这一个自由度，等于把交互降级成观看。把连续手部控制接进来，是从「能逛」走向「能操作」的必要一步。

中文摘要：近期的视频世界模型允许用户通过相机导航来探索生成环境，但真正与人和物体交互的细粒度通道是连续的手部运动。TouchéWorld 因此把「手势驱动交互」整合进相机可控的视频世界模型：给定一张初始图像和场景描述提示，模型在**时间对齐的相机控制与手部控制**条件下生成视频。作者为此构建了配套的数据与控制方案，让「一边走一边动手」在生成世界里成立。对交互式世界模型来说，这补上了除相机之外的第二个自由度——从「能逛」走向「能操作」。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-07

本期推送：2026-11-09

Abstract

Recent video world models allow users to explore generated environments through camera navigation. Continuous hand motion provides a fine-grained action channel for interacting with the people and objects encountered during exploration. We present TouchéWorld, a framework that integrates gesture-driven interaction into a camera-controlled video world model. Given an initial image and a scene-description prompt, the model generates video conditioned on temporally aligned camera and hand controls. We construct joint camera–hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment. Building on a pretrained camera-controlled world model, we combine spatial hand-skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation support chunk-level online generation, allowing users to update their controls based on generated visual feedback. We further introduce TouchéBench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Together, these components establish a framework for studying continuous exploration and hand-driven interaction within generative worlds.

1 Introduction

Video world models are turning generated visual content into environments that users can explore. Advances in camera-conditioned generation [47, 23, 15] and streaming inference [54, 53] allow users to move through scenes, choose their viewpoints, and explore worlds as they unfold [50, 54, 53, 19]. Exploration, however, naturally invites participation. Users may wish not only to observe what they encounter, but also to act on it. Consider walking through a generated courtyard, approaching a sweet-scented osmanthus tree, reaching out to touch its branches, and then continuing along the path. Supporting this process requires camera-guided navigation and hand-driven interaction to work together, with the generated world responding to user actions as exploration continues.

Continuous hand motion provides a natural interface for such participation. Camera control determines how users observe the world, while hand position, orientation, and articulation provide a fine-grained action channel for influencing its contents. Users can express actions such as reaching, touching, pushing, and withdrawing, and adjust their subsequent behavior based on generated visual feedback. We organize this process as online interaction: the system receives user controls while producing visual output and incorporates updated controls into subsequent video chunks, allowing users to decide their next action through ongoing observation.

Recent work provides important foundations through hand–object dynamics generation, joint hand and camera control, and streaming interaction [21, 41, 39]. The supported range of scenes and interactions nevertheless remains limited, particularly when manipulation is embedded within continuous navigation and exploration. We focus on the continuity across these activities: a user navigates toward an object, reaches out to manipulate it, withdraws their hand, and resumes exploration. Across these transitions, viewpoint control, hand motion, and scene responses must remain coordinated, while subsequent generation carries forward the state established by earlier actions. This calls for jointly considering the data, generation process, and evaluation of continuous camera–hand interaction.

Three challenges arise. First, joint control requires reliable supervision that separates viewpoint changes from action-induced scene dynamics. Camera motion, hand articulation, and their visual consequences must be accurately annotated and temporally aligned, despite incomplete or inconsistent estimates in egocentric videos. Second, online generation requires causal processing of both controls and visual history: each generated chunk must respond to available camera and hand inputs without relying on future actions. Third, interaction quality extends beyond visual similarity. A generated hand may follow its controls while the object remains unresponsive, and camera motion may produce apparent hand–object alignment without the intended manipulation. Evaluation must therefore distinguish hand following, joint control, and action-dependent scene responses.

To this end, we present a framework that integrates continuous hand interaction into a camera-controlled video world model. We first construct joint camera–hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos, completing missing annotations, filtering camera and hand estimates through consistency checks. Building on a pretrained camera-controlled model, we combine spatial hand-skeleton conditioning with numerical motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. We further impose consistent causal constraints on hand conditioning and visual generation, and apply few-step distillation to accelerate chunk-wise synthesis. The resulting model incorporates updated camera and hand controls into subsequent chunks, connecting exploration and manipulation within a shared generated history.

We further introduce TouchéBench to evaluate four aspects of interactive world generation: hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Reference-based evaluation on HOI4D [25] measures hand-control accuracy and object-response fidelity, while purpose-recorded scenarios assess joint camera–hand control and action-dependent continuations from shared contexts. Alongside TouchéBench, we evaluate video quality on unseen scenes from EgoStandard [24] and EgoLife [44], and on the out-of-domain HOT3D dataset [2]. Comparisons with external methods and across our bidirectional teacher, causal model, and four-step distilled model characterize visual quality and interaction performance across generation stages. Ablation studies further examine the effects of hand-weighted training on hand following and interaction outcomes.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    Joint camera–hand training data. We construct a data pipeline that completes missing camera and hand annotations, filters estimates through consistency checks, and aligns video and control signals to provide joint supervision for camera-guided exploration and hand-driven interaction.

  • •

    A framework for online camera–hand interaction. We extend a camera-controlled video world model with spatial skeleton and numerical motion conditioning. Parameter-efficient adaptation, causal training, and few-step distillation enable chunk-level online generation with continuously updated camera and hand controls.

  • •

    TouchéBench and experimental evaluation. We introduce a benchmark covering hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Comparisons and ablation studies evaluate these capabilities alongside video quality and examine the effects of causal adaptation, few-step distillation, and hand-weighted training.

    • 2 Related work

    2.1 Action-Conditioned Video World Models

    Action-conditioned video world models enable generated environments to respond to user control and evolve continuously by incorporating action signals into the video generation process. While early works primarily utilized discrete keystrokes or latent actions as control signals [30, 51, 15], recent research has introduced continuous camera trajectories to support more flexible navigation and viewpoint changes [35, 18, 50, 52, 10, 6, 34, 32]. To link camera motion with spatial changes in the generated imagery, existing methods have explored various geometric representations and conditioning mechanisms. For instance, LingBot-World 2.0 [10] employs Plücker embeddings to encode pixel-level observation rays and injects camera conditions via adaptive layer normalization; SolarWM [18] utilizes fused-PRoPE [23] to integrate projection geometry transformations, derived from camera intrinsics and extrinsics into self-attention computations; and EchoWM [50] adopts relative UCPE [47] to encode geometric relationships between local ray coordinate systems, thereby supporting continuous trajectory control.

    Beyond viewpoint navigation, recent work explores control [4, 12, 13, 36] interfaces for character behavior, scene events, and object dynamics. GameGen-X [6] and Hunyuan-GameCraft-2 [33] combine instruction-based control with game interaction, enabling users to specify actions and changes to scene contents. LongLive enables interactive streaming video generation and introduces KV-recache to refresh cached states when text prompts change [45]. H3-World [7] explores language-based action control on MiniMax-H3 [26] by converting character and camera actions into temporally aligned textual instructions [7]. Complementary approaches introduce spatial control signals: MotionStream [31] supports interactive motion guidance, while Force Prompting [11] and StreamForce [37] condition generation on physical forces, with StreamForce extending force control to causal streaming generation. Code World Model explores an alternative formulation in which a coding agent maintains executable world states and compiles them into proxy videos that condition visual generation [8]. These studies broaden the ways users can influence generated worlds. Our work investigates continuous hand motion as an action interface, jointly with camera control, to connect exploration and manipulation within an ongoing generation process.

    2.2 Hand-Conditioned Video Generation and Interaction Evaluation

    Hand-conditioned video generation models how hand motion influences scene contents. InterDyn [1] conditions video generation on driving-motion cues, including hand-mask sequences, to synthesize the resulting interaction dynamics. Dexterous World Models [21] combines hand-mesh renderings with static-scene videos rendered along a specified camera trajectory to model action-induced scene changes. Recent egocentric approaches further investigate joint hand and viewpoint control: Generated Reality [41] conditions generation on tracked head and hand poses and supports autoregressive interaction. HandsOnWorld [9] learns from unconstrained monocular videos and introduces camera-disentangled hand control. Hand2World [39] and JCV [48] primarily study hand–object interaction in tabletop manipulation settings. While these settings capture local interactions, they provide limited coverage of the transitions between navigation and manipulation. Related interaction-generation methods also investigate structural supervision: SCAR jointly generates videos and structure- and contact-aware representations to improve hand–object interaction synthesis [43]. Building on these developments, we focus on connecting camera-guided exploration and hand-driven manipulation within a continuous generation process, supported by joint camera–hand data construction and causal control.

    Interaction evaluation examines both control fidelity and the consequences of actions. Existing methods assess visual quality, hand-motion agreement, and generated interaction behavior under their respective conditioning settings [1, 21, 41, 39]. Complementing control-conditioned evaluation, Ego2Act evaluates goal-directed egocentric manipulation from an initial image and a high-level goal, assessing task completion and physical plausibility [20]. Continuous camera–hand interaction additionally calls for evaluating how newly introduced controls affect subsequent generation and how hand actions operate alongside navigation. TouchéBench brings these aspects together through hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online intervention response, and object response. Paired trajectory evaluation and action interventions from shared contexts relate control accuracy to the resulting interaction outcomes.

    3 Method

    We present a video world modeling framework that integrates continuous hand interaction with camera-guided exploration. Building on a camera-controlled image-to-video model, we introduce complementary skeleton and motion conditions, followed by causal adaptation and few-step distillation. Figure 2 illustrates joint data construction, while Figure 3 summarizes conditioning, training, and online interaction.

    3.1 Problem Formulation

    Given an initial image I₀ and a scene-description prompt p, we generate a continuous video conditioned on camera controls ℂ and hand controls H. Camera controls specify the viewing trajectory, while hand controls specify hand poses and motion at the corresponding video time positions. Together, they allow users to navigate the generated environment and interact with its contents.

    We generate video chunks X₁,…,X_K sequentially:

    p_θ(X_1:K|I₀,p,ℂ,H)(1)
    =∏ₖ₌₁^Kp_θ (Xₖ|I₀,p,X_

    where ℂ_≤k and H_≤k denote the controls available when generating chunk k. Within each chunk, hand-control latents are temporally aligned with the corresponding video latent positions.

    The system receives user controls while producing visual output and incorporates updated controls into subsequent chunks. This chunk-level online interaction allows users to adjust camera movement and hand actions based on generated visual feedback, connecting exploration and interaction within a shared video history.

    3.2 Data Construction

    As shown in Figure 2, we construct aligned video–camera–hand data from heterogeneous egocentric videos. We retain valid existing annotations and complete missing camera and hand annotations through separate estimation and validation branches.

    For videos without camera annotations, we estimate camera poses using ViPE [17] and depth using MoGe2 [38]. We reproject source frames into target views using the estimated geometry and compare them with the observed target frames. Reprojection consistency and trajectory-quality checks are used to filter unreliable camera estimates.

    For videos without hand annotations, we independently estimate hand poses using MINT [55] and HandFlow [42] and reject samples with inconsistent predictions. The retained annotations are converted into skeleton renderings and numerical hand features for joint conditioning.

    We temporally align video frames, camera poses, and hand annotations, updating camera intrinsics and image-space hand coordinates consistently with resizing and cropping. Camera trajectories are expressed relative to the initial frame. Alongside interaction clips, we include clips with hands entering an initially hand-free view and static clips with and without hands, covering both interaction and periods without hand motion.

    We plan to release the constructed dataset to support further research on joint camera–hand control in video world models.

    3.3 Joint Camera–Hand Conditioning

    Camera conditioning. We build on the LTX-2.5 [14] image-to-video backbone with a SolarWM camera adapter. Camera intrinsics and relative extrinsics are incorporated into self-attention through PRoPE. We retain this camera-conditioning pathway while introducing two complementary branches for hand control.

    Hand conditioning. The spatial branch encodes rendered skeleton videos S with the video VAE [22] and projects their latents into the video-token space. The motion branch encodes numerical hand features H, consisting of wrist translation, joint geometry, and a validity mask, using a temporal encoder Eₘ with linear projections and a residual temporal convolution. Given noisy video latents z_τ, we form the Transformer input as

    U=W_zP(z_τ)+WₛP (E_VAE(S))+B (Eₘ(H)),(2)

    where P denotes patchification, W_z and Wₛ are the video and skeleton projections, and B broadcasts each motion embedding across the spatial tokens at the corresponding latent time position. The two branches provide spatially localized skeleton features and temporally contextualized motion features.

    Joint adaptation. We freeze the pretrained backbone and camera LoRA[16], and jointly optimize an additional hand LoRA with the two hand-conditioning branches. The skeleton projection and the motion encoder’s output projection are bias-free and zero-initialized, so the added conditioning residual is initially zero.

    To emphasize hand reconstruction while retaining scene-wide supervision, we use a weighted denoising loss:

    Lⱼₒᵢₙₜ=𝔼 [(∑ᵢwᵢ∥ŷᵢ-yᵢ∥₂²)/(∑ᵢwᵢ)], wᵢ=mᵢ(1+λ_handrᵢ),

    		(3)

    where ŷᵢ and yᵢ are the prediction and denoising target for video token i, respectively. The binary mask rᵢ identifies hand-region tokens, mᵢ excludes the initial conditioning latent, and λ_hand controls the additional hand weight. Setting λ_hand=0 recovers uniform weighting over valid tokens.

    3.4 Causal Adaptation and Asymmetric DMD

    We obtain a streaming generator in two stages: teacher-forced causal adaptation, followed by asymmetric Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [46] from a bidirectional teacher to obtain a few-step causal generator.

    Teacher-forced causal adaptation. We initialize from the bidirectional joint-control teacher, freeze the backbone, camera and hand LoRAs, and both hand-conditioning branches, and train only an additional causal-adaptation LoRA. We adopt bidirectional attention within each chunk and causal attention across chunks. Each chunk is jointly denoised with access to its own tokens and the available preceding chunks. During teacher-forced training, preceding video chunks are supplied from ground-truth sequences. We also use left-padded temporal convolutions in the motion encoder and restrict skeleton conditions to the available temporal range to prevent information leakage from future chunks.

    Asymmetric DMD with self-forcing. We initialize the few-step student from the causally adapted model and distill it using the frozen bidirectional joint-control teacher. During distillation, the student performs self-forcing [19] rollouts, conditioning each chunk on its own generated history:

    ẑ⁽ᵏ⁾=G_θ (ξ⁽ᵏ⁾;ẑ^(

    		(4)

    where G_θ denotes the complete few-step sampling procedure, ξ⁽ᵏ⁾ denotes its sampling noise, and c_≤k contains the initial image, scene-description prompt, and camera–hand controls available when generating chunk k.

    We apply Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) to align the student and teacher distributions through a noise-averaged reverse KL objective. Given the generated sequence ẑ, we construct ẑ_τ=α_τẑ+σ_τε, where ε∼ℕ(0,I). A trainable fake-score network s_ψ estimates the student distribution score, while the frozen teacher provides s_T. Their difference yields the generator update:

    ∇_θL_DMD≈(5)
    𝔼[w(τ)J_θ^⊤·(s_ψ(ẑ_τ,τ;c)-s_T(ẑ_τ,τ;c))],

    where J_θ=∂ẑ/∂θ, c denotes the conditioning information for the full distillation sequence, and w(τ) incorporates the noise weighting and the perturbation factor α_τ. Here, s_ψ and s_T denote the student-distribution and teacher-distribution scores, respectively, expressed in a common score parameterization.

    Online inference.

    The distilled student generates video sequentially using four denoising steps per chunk. Each chunk conditions on the initial frame, a bounded history of generated chunks, and the available camera and hand controls. Committed outputs remain unchanged. The interface continues to receive updated controls during generation and incorporates them into subsequent chunks, allowing users to adjust their actions based on visual feedback.

    3.5 TouchéBench

    We introduce TouchéBench to evaluate four aspects of camera–hand-controlled world generation: hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response (Fig. 4). The benchmark combines reference-based evaluation on 200 held-out HOI4D clips with purpose-recorded scenarios for joint camera–hand control and action-dependent continuations. Hand-motion following and object response are evaluated on the same HOI4D clips and generated outputs, allowing control accuracy and object-response fidelity to be assessed together.

    Q1: Hand-motion following.

    We condition generation on the hand trajectories associated with each HOI4D clip and estimate hand keypoints from the generated frames. Following temporal alignment and hand correspondence matching, we compare detected joints û_t,j with reference joints u_t,j in a common normalized image coordinate system. We report the percentage of correct keypoints:

    PCK_δ=(1)/(|V|)∑_(t,j)∈V1 [d_t,j=1 ∧ ∥û_t,j-u_t,j∥₂≤δ],

    		(6)

    where V contains valid reference joints, d_t,j indicates a matched detection, and δ is the normalized distance threshold. We report PCK at δ=0.2, counting missing detections as incorrect. Joint localization error on matched detections and detection coverage are reported as supplementary measures. Scores are computed per clip and averaged across clips; the initial conditioning frame is excluded.

    Q2: Camera–hand coordination.

    We evaluate joint camera–hand control on ten purpose-recorded clips combining camera movement with hand interaction. Each clip uses first-frame image-to-video initialization and the camera and hand inputs supported by each method; JCV receives hand conditioning without camera control. GPT-6 Astra [28], accessed through Codex [27], assesses each continuation using six binary checklist questions covering visual consistency, viewpoint attainment, interaction execution, and the final object state. We report Camera as the viewpoint-attainment pass rate and Interaction as the average pass rate of interaction-execution and final-state judgments. Scores are averaged equally across clips.

    Q3: Online interaction.

    We evaluate action-dependent continuations using eight purpose-recorded scenarios, each containing three alternative hand-action branches following a shared approximately two-second context. The scene-description prompt remains unchanged across branches and does not specify the target action. Each branch supplies its corresponding hand controls to test whether the generated continuation realizes the intended interaction and distinguishes it from alternative outcomes. GPT-6 Astra [28], accessed through Codex [27], assesses the 24 continuations using six binary checklist questions per continuation, yielding 144 judgments. Three basic criteria assess visual and scene consistency, while three hard criteria assess action execution (A), the intended final state (S), and exclusion of alternative outcomes (X). We report the mean pass rates for Basic, Hard, and Overall.

    Q4: Object response.

    Using the same HOI4D-200 evaluation set, we compare target-object responses in generated and reference videos. We obtain temporally corresponding object masks with SAM3 [5] and evaluate mask overlap and centroid displacement:

    IoUₜ=(|M̂ₜ∩Mₜ|)/(|M̂ₜ∪Mₜ|),(7)
    E_center,t=∥c(M̂ₜ)-c(Mₜ)∥₂,

    where M̂ₜ and Mₜ denote generated and reference object masks, respectively, and c(·) denotes the mask centroid in image coordinates. We report mask IoU and centroid displacement in pixels. Frame-level measurements are averaged within each clip and then equally across clips, excluding the initial conditioning frame. Target-tracking coverage is reported separately.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    We train our model on 40,958 egocentric video clips, comprising 24,000 EgoLife [44] clips, 15,918 EgoStandard clips, and 1,040 auxiliary clips. The auxiliary set includes hand-emergence clips, in which hands are removed from the initial frame and appear in subsequent chunks, as well as static clips with and without hands. We evaluate on EgoStandard-200 [24], EgoLife-300 [44], and HOT3D-45 [2]. All three test sets contain scenes unseen during training. EgoStandard and EgoLife evaluate generalization to unseen scenes within the training domains, while HOT3D provides an out-of-domain evaluation. For HOT3D, we follow the original 81-frame configuration.

    Baselines.

    Few existing methods closely match our joint camera–hand control setting. We compare against the following models:

  • 1.

    LTX-2.5 I2V and the camera-only SolarWM model, which serve as baselines for video generation quality.

  • 2.

    JCV [48] and Hand2World [39], two related hand-conditioned video generation models with publicly available weights. We use their released weights without additional training or fine-tuning, adapting the input representation, resolution, and evaluation interface to our test protocol. Each method receives the inputs supported by its original implementation. In particular, JCV does not expose a camera-control interface and therefore receives hand conditioning only. For Hand2World, we project 3D MANO meshes to construct the hand-conditioning input used by its original pipeline. We use the same evaluation examples and scoring implementation across methods, with method-specific context initialization and temporal alignment described below.

    • We report our bidirectional teacher, the multi-step causal model obtained through teacher-forced adaptation, and the four-step causal model obtained through self-forcing DMD to examine video quality and interaction performance across training stages.

    Evaluation protocol.

    We evaluate video quality using PSNR, SSIM [40], LPIPS [49], DINOv2 [29] similarity, and KID [3], excluding the initial conditioning frame. The four paired metrics are averaged within each clip and then equally across clips, while KID measures distributional similarity over sampled frames. All methods are evaluated using a shared scoring implementation. We additionally assess hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response using TouchéBench.

    4.2 Video Generation Quality

    Table 1 compares video generation quality across two in-domain test sets with unseen scenes and the out-of-domain HOT3D-45 benchmark. Our bidirectional teacher achieves strong results across all three datasets. Relative to camera-only SolarWM, it improves PSNR by 2.82 dB on EgoStandard-200 and 1.66 dB on EgoLife-300, while reducing LPIPS from 0.494 to 0.345 and from 0.584 to 0.488, respectively. On HOT3D-45, it achieves an LPIPS of 0.488 and a DINOv2 similarity of 0.769. These results show improved agreement with reference observations across both in-domain and out-of-domain scenes. Figure 5 further illustrates the visual results across diverse scenes, where the same camera and hand controls are reused with different initial images and scene descriptions.

    Our multi-step causal model also achieves lower LPIPS and higher DINOv2 similarity than SolarWM on all three datasets, while its PSNR improves or remains comparable. The four-step distilled model further improves PSNR and SSIM over the multi-step causal model across all three datasets, with mixed changes in LPIPS, DINOv2 similarity, and KID. These results characterize the visual-quality trade-offs introduced by causal adaptation and few-step distillation.

    We next evaluate hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response using TouchéBench to examine how these models translate visual generation quality into controllable interaction.

    4.3 Evaluation on TouchéBench

    Table 2 reports results on the four dimensions of TouchéBench. Our bidirectional teacher achieves the highest hand-following PCK@0.2 of 65.8%, compared with 61.2% for Hand2World and 59.1% for JCV, while our multi-step and four-step causal models obtain 57.9% and 54.0%, respectively. Hand2World achieves the lowest localization error on matched detections at 28.2 pixels. For camera–hand coordination, our teacher achieves 100.0% Camera and 60.0% Interaction pass rates, compared with 50.0% and 15.0% for JCV, and 40.0% and 15.0% for Hand2World. Our causal models retain this advantage, with the multi-step model scoring 70.0% and 40.0%, and the four-step model scoring 60.0% and 35.0%. On online interaction, the multi-step causal model achieves the highest overall pass rate of 75.0% and hard-criterion pass rate of 55.6%, exceeding the teacher’s 71.5% and 45.8%, respectively. The four-step model obtains 68.8% overall, remaining above JCV’s 51.4% and Hand2World’s 33.3%. For object response, JCV achieves the highest mask IoU of 38.7%, while our multi-step causal model achieves the lowest target-center offset of 48.8 pixels. These results highlight the distinction between image-space alignment and interaction success: favorable keypoint or object-overlap scores can coexist with low action-execution and final-state pass rates. The qualitative case study 6 illustrates this distinction through examples of camera movement and object behavior, while the action-branch examples 7 show different continuations from a shared context. Together, the quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate stronger joint-control and action-dependent interaction performance for our framework, with reduced hand-following and camera–hand coordination scores after causal adaptation and few-step distillation.

    4.4 Case Study

    Figure 5 illustrates how a shared camera–hand control sequence produces scene-dependent interactions. Starting from the osmanthus-tree example, we reuse the controls with four different scene initializations. The hand settles on the tabletop in the cafe scene, moves out of view after reaching through free space in the gallery, and grasps a package at the store shelf. These examples show that the generated hand behavior adapts to the surrounding scene while retaining the input motion pattern. In the shelf comparison, JCV produces substantial viewpoint changes toward the ceiling, while Hand2World generates hand motion in front of a largely unchanged shelf; our model instead produces a reach-and-lift interaction. Figure 6 further examines the distinction between spatial agreement and object interaction. In the reference, the hand moves the bottle relative to the cup. JCV retains the bottle near its initial position through much of the sequence, whereas our teacher and causal model generate more pronounced hand-associated object movement. Retaining an object near its initial location can preserve overlap with reference masks over parts of the sequence, illustrating why mask IoU should be interpreted alongside action execution and object-state changes. Finally, Figure 7 evaluates action-dependent continuations from a shared approximately two-second context. Different hand inputs ask the model to rotate a box, lift it above another box, or slide it along the tabletop. Our teacher and causal model produce distinct changes in box orientation, height, and position across these branches, while the baselines show less consistent separation of the intended outcomes. Together, these cases illustrate joint camera–hand control, scene-dependent contact behavior, and distinct object responses to actions introduced after a shared context.

    4.5 Ablation Studies and Analysis

    Hand-weighted loss.

    Tables 3, 5, and 4 examine the effect of hand-weighted training on video quality and interaction. Hand weighting improves keypoint accuracy for both the teacher and causal models across all three PCK thresholds. For the teacher, PCK@0.2 increases from 58.7% to 65.8%, while localization error decreases from 60.0 to 48.2 pixels. The causal model improves from 55.0% to 57.9% PCK, with localization error decreasing from 55.0 to 46.8 pixels. These improvements also extend to online interaction: Q3 Overall increases from 65.3% to 71.5% for the teacher and from 72.2% to 75.0% for the causal model. For camera–hand coordination, the teacher’s Interaction score increases from 40.0% to 60.0%, while its Camera score remains at 100.0%. The causal model exhibits a trade-off, with Camera decreasing from 90.0% to 70.0% and Interaction from 45.0% to 40.0%. Object-mask IoU improves for both model types. Changes in global video quality are dataset-dependent: all five metrics improve for the teacher on EgoStandard and for the causal model on EgoLife, while the remaining evaluation sets show mixed changes. Overall, hand-weighted supervision strengthens hand following and online interaction, with a coordination trade-off in the causal model.

    Causal adaptation and few-step distillation.

    We examine the generation stages through the teacher, multi-step causal, and four-step causal results in Tables 1 and 2. Moving from the bidirectional teacher to the causal model reduces reference-based video quality and hand-following accuracy, with PCK@0.2 decreasing from 65.8% to 57.9%. Q2 Camera and Interaction also decrease from 100.0% and 60.0% to 70.0% and 40.0%, respectively. On Q3, the causal model achieves higher Overall and Hard pass rates, increasing from 71.5% and 45.8% to 75.0% and 55.6% under the method-specific context initialization used in our evaluation. This contrast shows that stronger reference reconstruction and keypoint alignment do not directly imply better action-dependent continuations. Four-step distillation improves PSNR and SSIM over the multi-step causal model on all three video-quality test sets, while changes in LPIPS, DINOv2 similarity, and KID are mixed. Hand-following PCK decreases to 54.0%, Q2 Camera and Interaction decrease to 60.0% and 35.0%, and Q3 Overall decreases to 68.8%. Object-response measurements remain close, with mask IoU changing from 34.9% to 35.0% and target-center offset from 48.8 to 49.3 pixels. These results characterize the transition to four-step causal generation: object-response fidelity remains similar under the reported spatial metrics, while hand following, joint control, and online interaction show larger performance reductions.

    5 Conclusion and Future Work

    We presented TouchéWorld, a video world modeling framework that integrates continuous hand interaction with camera-guided exploration. We constructed joint camera–hand training data through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment, and combined spatial skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation enable chunk-level online generation with updated camera and hand controls. We further introduced TouchéBench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Experiments demonstrate scene-dependent interaction across diverse environments and action-dependent continuations from shared contexts, while revealing distinct trade-offs among visual quality, hand following, and interaction performance.

    Our qualitative results also reveal early signs of gesture-mediated interaction with people in generated scenes. This opens a direction for extending interactive world models beyond object manipulation toward human interaction. Future work will explore how generated people perceive and respond to user gestures, enabling richer exchanges between users and the inhabitants of generative worlds.

    6 Acknowledgements

    This work is partially supported by a public grant overseen by the French National Research Agency(ANR) as part of the program Investissements d’Avenir (ANR-10-LABX-0083).

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 低分辨率纹理别再手动换：一个通用 MLP 插进采样阶段，渲染时按需超分，不用逐资产训练 ｜ Patch-Based Generalized Neural Texture Upscaling
item.description:
一句话：训练一个通用 MLP 就够：集成到纹理采样阶段，渲染时把低分纹理实时放大，不改资产管线。

要点：

  • 做法极轻：一个通用 MLP 在大量纹理 patch 上训练，直接集成进**纹理采样阶段**，渲染时实时把低分辨率纹理放大
  • 因为模型是「通用」而不是对特定内容过拟合，所以**不需要逐资产训练**——同一个模型能用于任意已有场景
  • 前提是不改纹理数据、也不改资产管线：只需存更低分辨率的纹理，靠采样时补细节来省显存与带宽

为什么值得看：显存与带宽是移动端/大世界的硬约束，而纹理是最大头。把超分放进采样阶段（而不是渲染后的图像超分），意味着省下的是真实显存占用，且对现有资产零侵入——这类「不换管线只加一层」的方案最容易落地。

中文摘要：这篇提出一种轻量的神经纹理超分方法：用一个通用 MLP 在多样化的纹理 patch 集合上训练，然后集成到纹理采样阶段，在渲染时按需把低分辨率纹理放大。由于模型是通用而非针对特定内容过拟合，因此不需要逐资产训练——同一个模型可直接用于任意已有场景，既不改纹理数据，也不改资产管线。实际收益来自「只存低分辨率纹理、采样时补细节」，省下的是显存与带宽；相比渲染完成后的图像超分，这种前移到采样阶段的做法规避了资产改造成本，更适合移动端与大世界项目。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-08

本期推送：2026-11-09

Patch-Based Generalized Neural Texture Upscaling

Abstract.

We propose a lightweight neural texture upscaling method. A single generalized MLP is trained on a diverse collection of texture patches and integrated into the texture sampling stage, upscaling low-resolution textures on-the-fly at rendering time. Because the model is generalized rather than overfit to specific content, no per-asset training is required - the same model applies to any existing scene without modifying texture data or the asset pipeline. Storing lower-resolution base textures reduces disk footprint, upscaling at sampling time eliminates the need to store high-resolution textures in VRAM, and sharing a single set of model weights across all textures ensures non-divergent GPU execution. We evaluate our method across multiple texture classes, demonstrating consistent improvement over analytic upscaling methods in perceptual quality.

1. Introduction

Textures and texture mappings are fundamental techniques for representing surface detail that cannot be captured by geometry alone. As display resolutions continue to increase, rendered images must achieve correspondingly higher resolutions, driving demand for higher-resolution textures. However, this comes at significant cost: higher-resolution textures consume more disk space and VRAM when rendering on a GPU. Greater disk space translates directly to larger download sizes for games and applications, while increased VRAM consumption raises hardware requirements for end users.

One class of approaches to this problem is offline neural image upscaling. Methods such as [(Dong et al., 2014; Long et al., 2025b)] produce high-quality upscaled images using deep neural networks (NNs) trained on large image datasets. These models are generalized: they require no training on the target content and can therefore be applied to existing assets without modifying the content creation pipeline. However, they are not designed to run at rendering time because of the computational cost and missing capability of random access, which is the typical use case for runtime. The option to use them is to perform upscaling as a preprocessing step before rendering begins. This means that the upscaled high-resolution textures must then be stored and loaded into VRAM at runtime. Consequently, while these methods can improve texture quality and reduce download size when applied to games, they offer no reduction in disk footprint or VRAM pressure.

Neural Texture Compression (NTC) [(Vaidyanathan et al., 2023)] takes a fundamentally different approach by representing each texture set as a compact neural network decoded on-the-fly at texture sampling time. This achieves high compression ratios, particularly when compressing correlated texture sets used in physically based rendering (PBR) such as diffuse, normal, ARM (AO, Roughness, Metallic), where correlation across channels can be exploited. Since decompression occurs at sampling time, NTC reduces both disk footprint and VRAM simultaneously. However, NTC presents practical challenges for adoption. First, because the neural network is overfit to each texture set, compression must be re-executed per asset, adding overhead to the content creation pipeline. Second, since each texture set is encoded as a separate network with different weights, concurrent sampling of multiple texture sets within a single GPU wavefront causes execution divergence — unfavorable for the matrix cores that are the key to GPU inference performance, and particularly problematic during non-primary material execution where many texture sets may be active simultaneously [(Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 2021; NVIDIA Corporation, 2017)].

Neural Texture Block Compression (NTBC) [(Fujieda and Harada, 2024)] combines neural network-based encoding with standard GPU-hardware block-compression formats [(Akenine-Möller et al., 2018)]. A neural network is used to produce block-compressed representations, while standard hardware texture units handle decoding — avoiding runtime neural inference cost and the divergence issues of NTC. However, because the output must conform to block compression constraints, the quality gains over conventional block compression are inherently bounded. Similar to NTC, NTBC must be applied per asset during content creation, adding pipeline overhead and precluding application to existing unmodified content.

We propose a lightweight neural texture upscaling method designed for ease of integration. We train a single generalized Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) on a diverse collection of texture patches from publicly available texture datasets. At rendering time, this model is integrated into the texture sampling stage: the renderer fetches a low-resolution texture, and the MLP upscales it on-the-fly. Because the model is generalized rather than overfit to specific content, no per-asset training is required: the same model can be applied to any texture set in any scene, making it directly compatible with existing games and rendering pipelines without modifying texture data or the asset creation workflow. Storing lower-resolution base textures reduces disk footprint, and since upscaling occurs at sampling time, high-resolution textures need never reside in VRAM. Furthermore, because all textures share a single set of model weights, GPU execution remains non-divergent regardless of how many texture sets are active simultaneously. While the compression ratio does not match NTC, we believe these practical advantages, such as generality, pipeline compatibility, and uniform GPU execution, make the proposed method compelling for real-time rendering applications such as games.

2. Related Work

Texture compression has been a fundamental component of real-time rendering pipelines. Block compression (BC) formats come in a wide variety depending on the number of channels and quality [(Akenine-Möller et al., 2018)]. As the name suggests, they are block-compressed, so they are suited for random access. However, the fixed-block structure imposes a ceiling on the compression ratio and quality, which some neural network-based methods managed to break as discussed later in this section. When a texture is viewed at close range, we need to magnify the texture content. There are a few analytic filters we can use to reconstruct signals higher than the original texture resolution. Bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos are the popular choices for the interpolation. Bilinear interpolation uses the four nearest neighboring texels, while bicubic and Lanczos operate on a larger neighborhood, enabling higher-quality reconstruction. They are also called resampling or upsampling. We call them upsampling in the rest of this paper, as they can be viewed as upsampling operations on texture data. Although these analytic methods are computationally inexpensive, they are fundamentally limited in reconstruction quality because they cannot recover details that are absent in the low-resolution textures.

A learning-based method or a neural network overcomes this limitation. The trend has shifted from CNN-based upscaling methods such as SRCNN [(Dong et al., 2014)] to transformer-based upscaling methods such as SwinIR [(Liang et al., 2021)] and, most recently, PFT [(Long et al., 2025b)]. These methods are general-purpose image upscalers that learn the image characteristics to reconstruct missing finer details. However, these methods are not designed to run in real time like real-time analytic upscaling methods. As they are computationally expensive and operate on the full image, they are not suitable to be executed at texture sampling in real-time rendering.

Another class of research is to apply learned upsampling specifically to PBR texture content. MATUP [(Gauthier et al., 2024)] repurposes pre-trained RGB image upsamplers to super-resolve SVBRDF maps by optimizing a local MLP filter per material, with a radiance-domain loss to ensure physically consistent upscaling. PBR-SR [(Chen et al., 2025)] similarly leverages pre-trained 2D image super-resolution priors and refines PBR textures through iterative differentiable rendering against multi-view constraints. Both methods produce high-quality results but require per-asset optimization, making them unsuitable for integration into real-time rendering pipelines. Our method, in contrast, is a fully generalized model trained across a diverse set of PBR textures, requiring no per-asset processing. This allows it to be applied at texture-sampling time without any content creation overhead, directly replacing the conventional analytic upsampling step in the rendering pipeline.

Neural Texture Compression (NTC) is specifically targeted to be executed in this context [(Vaidyanathan et al., 2023)]. Instead of using larger models such as CNNs, NTC uses a small MLP with an input encoder, which makes it possible to do local per-texel evaluation at sampling time, which CNN and transformer-based models cannot do. Another fundamental difference is that NTC is not a generalized model, but a set of PBR textures must be overfit into a single neural network. Although it achieves impressive compression, especially with the latest input encoding research [(Perez et al., 2026)], using NTC adds an overhead to content creation. Since the MLP execution is local, one can run a small inference for each texture sampling operation. However, the matrix cores on today’s GPUs are designed to use a group of threads for matrix computation, which is a different programming pattern from SIMT execution [(Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 2021; NVIDIA Corporation, 2017)]. This makes it difficult to execute NTC efficiently on the GPU when there are divergences in the execution, which is usually the case [(Belcour and Benyoub, 2025)]. Neural Texture Block Compression (NTBC) is a variant of NTC, which executes neural networks to create BC-format textures [(Fujieda and Harada, 2024)]. NTBC is designed that way so that it is easier to adopt to a game production. As the neural network produces BC blocks which can be parsed and decompressed using the hardware decoder, NTBC can be executed to decompress textures into BC textures on load. NTBC also requires overfitting, so it adds overhead to the content creation pipeline.

Our method is designed to reduce these adoption barriers. First, our method is generalized, so no need to add a processing step in the content creation pipeline. The execution divergence is eliminated as our model is generalized, so we can execute the same model for different textures. It is even possible to integrate our method into existing games by replacing the texture sampler with the neural upscaler, enabling higher-quality rendering without modifying texture assets. This makes our method stand in a unique position compared to all the existing works.

3. Method

A key design choice of our model is locality: rather than upscaling the entire texture at once, the model upscales a small patch at texture-sampling time. Conventional texture upscaling approaches either store full high-resolution textures in GPU memory or preprocess the textures offline before rendering. Instead, our method generates high-resolution texels on demand during a texture fetch, eliminating the memory overhead of storing a full-resolution copy. Critically, operating on small patches keeps the parameter count and arithmetic cost low enough for the model to be executed directly as a GPU shader. This patch-based execution is what makes our method easier to deploy.

Given a low-resolution input patch of n×n texels, the model outputs 2n×2n texels at twice the resolution, where we call n the patch size. However, upscaling a patch without surrounding context produces block artifacts at patch boundaries, because the model cannot observe the texture pattern beyond the patch edges. To address this, we extend the input patch by m texels on each side. The network therefore receives a (n+2m)×(n+2m)×c tensor as input and produces 2n×2n×c texels as output, where c is the number of channels. The m-texel margin is consumed as context and discarded from the output. In our experiments, we use n=1, m=1, and c=3 for RGB textures. We chose n=1 to minimize the number of texels fetched per sample while still producing a relatively small 2×2 output patch with a 3×3 input patch. In order to reduce the computational cost, we want to use as small an n as possible. For the texels close to the texture border where the padding texels do not exist, we mirror the texture values at the boundary, assuming that textures are smooth at the boundary.

We took an approach to upscale the texels using an analytic method first, as it is a good approximation although it is missing the high-frequency signal. Therefore, the network first upsamples the input patch to the output resolution using the analytic bilinear upscaling, which efficiently recovers the low-frequency content of the texture. The model then predicts the residual using an MLP, and the final output is the sum of the bilinear-upscaled texels and the residual. This residual formulation is effective because the bilinear baseline already provides a reasonable approximation: the MLP only needs to learn the high-frequency detail that bilinear interpolation fails to recover, which simplifies the learning problem and accelerates convergence. The input to the MLP is a flattened (n+2m)²×c-dimensional vector. The network consists of a linear projection to a hidden dimension of d, followed by L residual blocks. Each residual block applies two linear layers with a ReLU activation between them, adds the result to its input as a skip connection, and passes the sum through a final ReLU activation. After the residual connection, the values are clamped not to exceed 1. The output layer then projects back to the target dimension of 2n×2n×c. The network architecture is illustrated in Fig. 2.

The model is trained end-to-end using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10⁻³. We use an L1 loss between the predicted and ground-truth high-resolution patches, which we found to produce sharper texture reconstructions than MSE. Optionally, a cosine annealing scheduler is applied to decay the learning rate to 10⁻⁶ over the course of training.

4. Results

4.1. Dataset and Training Configuration

The model configuration we used for the experiments other than ablation studies is d=256 hidden dimension, with residual connections on, L=4 residual blocks, n=1, and m=1, so it produces 2×2 texel patches. We prepared a few datasets for the experiments as shown in Table 1. One is taken from the Poly Haven website [(Poly Haven, 2026)], and others are textures from rendering scenes (Hangar, Victorian, Museum). When the Poly Haven dataset is used for testing, the entire dataset is partitioned so that training data does not see the test data. Textures for these datasets are down-sampled to up to 2048×2048 resolution.

We focused on studying upscaling three classes of textures, diffuse, normal, and ARM textures, using the same model architecture. Since these textures show different characteristics, it is natural to train three different models for each dataset. However, if we can unify the models into a single one, it makes its deployment easier than the per-class-model approach. Therefore, we first explored the possibility of preparing the unified models to reduce the total number of models. Fig. 3 shows the study in which we use Hangar and Museum datasets as test data and compare models trained on different combinations of the Poly Haven training dataset. Here, we used LPIPS (the lower, the better) as the metric in the graphs. For the Hangar dataset, diffuse and normal textures showed the best metric when using the trained model with the same-category training dataset. Diffuse textures in the Museum dataset follow the same pattern, but normal textures did not perform well when the model is trained only with normal textures. In general, using the diffuse + normal + ARM textures for training shows a good balance for both scenes, although they are not the best for each texture class. Therefore, we use a single model trained with the diffuse + normal + ARM textures in the Poly Haven training dataset for all the experiments in this paper.

4.2. Comparison with Baseline Methods

We evaluated the quality of upscaling with our method by comparing different existing methods. We used three major analytic methods (bilinear, bicubic, Lanczos) and PFT, a state-of-the-art machine learning-based high-quality offline upscaler taken from the authors’ implementation [(Long et al., 2025a; Long et al., 2025b)]. Because the complexity of PFT is completely different from our method, we expect PFT to be used as the best-case performance for our model. We measured the metrics for each texture in the test dataset. Table 2 shows average metrics per texture class for each dataset. Although there are no huge differences in PSNR or SSIM, our method and PFT make relatively large differences in LPIPS. As the upscaled textures are not guaranteed to be pixel-accurate, per-pixel distance metrics such as PSNR are not well-suited to evaluate our method. To prove it, we confirmed that the LPIPS perceptual metric follows naturally with our visual evaluation, rather than per-pixel metrics. We found many cases where blurred textures score higher PSNR values than sharp textures, which we visually find higher quality. This is because PSNR only considers the error in each pixel rather than perceptual correctness. Therefore, we use LPIPS as the main metric for further discussion in this paper.

Along with the per-class average metrics, we also measured per-texture metrics for the test datasets used in Table 2. Fig. 4, 5, 6, and 7 show the LPIPS metrics for upscaled textures using the proposed method, analytic upscaling methods (bilinear, bicubic, Lanczos), and PFT. We can see that our method achieves better metrics compared to most of the textures upscaled using analytic methods. Our method even matched PFT for some textures from the Hangar normal, Victorian normal, and Museum diffuse datasets, even though the model complexity is totally different. Visual comparison also matches the LPIPS metrics, as illustrated in Fig. 8, 9, and 10. All the analytic methods produce smoother results, while our method and PFT produce sharper images, which is especially obvious from Fig. 9. The same pattern is observed in normal textures, which often have sharp edges and detailed features as shown in Fig. 10. Lanczos upscaling method, known for sharper reconstruction, also does not make a huge difference to bicubic in the experiments. However, our method reconstructs sharper edges as PFT. At the same time, careful inspection of these visual results clarifies the limitation of our method. It is obvious, especially from Fig. 8 (c) and Fig. 10, that fine detail, less than pixel scale, which does not exist in the source textures, does not appear in any of the upscaled images, even with PFT. This is a limitation of upscaling methods like ours, which do not store any other information than a low-resolution texture. We also evaluated our method by rendering scenes with a different set of textures using our renderer written in HIP [(AMD, 2023)]. One example is shown in Fig. 1, where our method produces fewer errors, resulting in a low FLIP score as shown in Table 3. The difference is obvious in the glossy reflection. We can even see the difference coming from diffuse textures in Fig. 1. The numbers in Table 3 are from different cameras, and the teaser is rendered using the first camera. Other views are shown in Fig. 11. The difference is bigger for views where the camera is close to objects, where we can see textures clearly.

Although we have not explored it in this research, we could omit the MLP execution completely and just sample the low-resolution texture at the vertices where high quality is not required, e.g., vertices after a diffuse reflection. This is possible with our method, as the input to the NN is the texels, while NTC cannot do so because the latent grid needs to be decoded before use.

4.3. Generalization vs. Overfitting

The results we have seen are obtained using generalized models: a single model is trained and applied to different test textures. Under some situations, we may want to overfit a model to the texture set as NTC does. It requires more training, but it should improve the quality. There are many options, but a reasonable option is to train a model for each class using the textures it needs to upscale. We compared the results with an over-fitted model to the ones with a generalized model in Table 4. Although the improvement with an over-fitted model is consistent except in a few cases, such as Museum normal, where the generalized model performed better, over-fitting adds overhead for the content creation pipeline. Whether to use overfitting or a generalized model depends on the situation of the development. Thus, developers can choose the appropriate approach case by case.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：训练一个通用 MLP 就够：集成到纹理采样阶段，渲染时把低分纹理实时放大，不改资产管线。

要点：

  • 做法极轻：一个通用 MLP 在大量纹理 patch 上训练，直接集成进**纹理采样阶段**，渲染时实时把低分辨率纹理放大
  • 因为模型是「通用」而不是对特定内容过拟合，所以**不需要逐资产训练**——同一个模型能用于任意已有场景
  • 前提是不改纹理数据、也不改资产管线：只需存更低分辨率的纹理，靠采样时补细节来省显存与带宽

为什么值得看：显存与带宽是移动端/大世界的硬约束，而纹理是最大头。把超分放进采样阶段（而不是渲染后的图像超分），意味着省下的是真实显存占用，且对现有资产零侵入——这类「不换管线只加一层」的方案最容易落地。

中文摘要：这篇提出一种轻量的神经纹理超分方法：用一个通用 MLP 在多样化的纹理 patch 集合上训练，然后集成到纹理采样阶段，在渲染时按需把低分辨率纹理放大。由于模型是通用而非针对特定内容过拟合，因此不需要逐资产训练——同一个模型可直接用于任意已有场景，既不改纹理数据，也不改资产管线。实际收益来自「只存低分辨率纹理、采样时补细节」，省下的是显存与带宽；相比渲染完成后的图像超分，这种前移到采样阶段的做法规避了资产改造成本，更适合移动端与大世界项目。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-08

本期推送：2026-11-09

Patch-Based Generalized Neural Texture Upscaling

Abstract.

We propose a lightweight neural texture upscaling method. A single generalized MLP is trained on a diverse collection of texture patches and integrated into the texture sampling stage, upscaling low-resolution textures on-the-fly at rendering time. Because the model is generalized rather than overfit to specific content, no per-asset training is required - the same model applies to any existing scene without modifying texture data or the asset pipeline. Storing lower-resolution base textures reduces disk footprint, upscaling at sampling time eliminates the need to store high-resolution textures in VRAM, and sharing a single set of model weights across all textures ensures non-divergent GPU execution. We evaluate our method across multiple texture classes, demonstrating consistent improvement over analytic upscaling methods in perceptual quality.

1. Introduction

Textures and texture mappings are fundamental techniques for representing surface detail that cannot be captured by geometry alone. As display resolutions continue to increase, rendered images must achieve correspondingly higher resolutions, driving demand for higher-resolution textures. However, this comes at significant cost: higher-resolution textures consume more disk space and VRAM when rendering on a GPU. Greater disk space translates directly to larger download sizes for games and applications, while increased VRAM consumption raises hardware requirements for end users.

One class of approaches to this problem is offline neural image upscaling. Methods such as [(Dong et al., 2014; Long et al., 2025b)] produce high-quality upscaled images using deep neural networks (NNs) trained on large image datasets. These models are generalized: they require no training on the target content and can therefore be applied to existing assets without modifying the content creation pipeline. However, they are not designed to run at rendering time because of the computational cost and missing capability of random access, which is the typical use case for runtime. The option to use them is to perform upscaling as a preprocessing step before rendering begins. This means that the upscaled high-resolution textures must then be stored and loaded into VRAM at runtime. Consequently, while these methods can improve texture quality and reduce download size when applied to games, they offer no reduction in disk footprint or VRAM pressure.

Neural Texture Compression (NTC) [(Vaidyanathan et al., 2023)] takes a fundamentally different approach by representing each texture set as a compact neural network decoded on-the-fly at texture sampling time. This achieves high compression ratios, particularly when compressing correlated texture sets used in physically based rendering (PBR) such as diffuse, normal, ARM (AO, Roughness, Metallic), where correlation across channels can be exploited. Since decompression occurs at sampling time, NTC reduces both disk footprint and VRAM simultaneously. However, NTC presents practical challenges for adoption. First, because the neural network is overfit to each texture set, compression must be re-executed per asset, adding overhead to the content creation pipeline. Second, since each texture set is encoded as a separate network with different weights, concurrent sampling of multiple texture sets within a single GPU wavefront causes execution divergence — unfavorable for the matrix cores that are the key to GPU inference performance, and particularly problematic during non-primary material execution where many texture sets may be active simultaneously [(Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 2021; NVIDIA Corporation, 2017)].

Neural Texture Block Compression (NTBC) [(Fujieda and Harada, 2024)] combines neural network-based encoding with standard GPU-hardware block-compression formats [(Akenine-Möller et al., 2018)]. A neural network is used to produce block-compressed representations, while standard hardware texture units handle decoding — avoiding runtime neural inference cost and the divergence issues of NTC. However, because the output must conform to block compression constraints, the quality gains over conventional block compression are inherently bounded. Similar to NTC, NTBC must be applied per asset during content creation, adding pipeline overhead and precluding application to existing unmodified content.

We propose a lightweight neural texture upscaling method designed for ease of integration. We train a single generalized Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) on a diverse collection of texture patches from publicly available texture datasets. At rendering time, this model is integrated into the texture sampling stage: the renderer fetches a low-resolution texture, and the MLP upscales it on-the-fly. Because the model is generalized rather than overfit to specific content, no per-asset training is required: the same model can be applied to any texture set in any scene, making it directly compatible with existing games and rendering pipelines without modifying texture data or the asset creation workflow. Storing lower-resolution base textures reduces disk footprint, and since upscaling occurs at sampling time, high-resolution textures need never reside in VRAM. Furthermore, because all textures share a single set of model weights, GPU execution remains non-divergent regardless of how many texture sets are active simultaneously. While the compression ratio does not match NTC, we believe these practical advantages, such as generality, pipeline compatibility, and uniform GPU execution, make the proposed method compelling for real-time rendering applications such as games.

2. Related Work

Texture compression has been a fundamental component of real-time rendering pipelines. Block compression (BC) formats come in a wide variety depending on the number of channels and quality [(Akenine-Möller et al., 2018)]. As the name suggests, they are block-compressed, so they are suited for random access. However, the fixed-block structure imposes a ceiling on the compression ratio and quality, which some neural network-based methods managed to break as discussed later in this section. When a texture is viewed at close range, we need to magnify the texture content. There are a few analytic filters we can use to reconstruct signals higher than the original texture resolution. Bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos are the popular choices for the interpolation. Bilinear interpolation uses the four nearest neighboring texels, while bicubic and Lanczos operate on a larger neighborhood, enabling higher-quality reconstruction. They are also called resampling or upsampling. We call them upsampling in the rest of this paper, as they can be viewed as upsampling operations on texture data. Although these analytic methods are computationally inexpensive, they are fundamentally limited in reconstruction quality because they cannot recover details that are absent in the low-resolution textures.

A learning-based method or a neural network overcomes this limitation. The trend has shifted from CNN-based upscaling methods such as SRCNN [(Dong et al., 2014)] to transformer-based upscaling methods such as SwinIR [(Liang et al., 2021)] and, most recently, PFT [(Long et al., 2025b)]. These methods are general-purpose image upscalers that learn the image characteristics to reconstruct missing finer details. However, these methods are not designed to run in real time like real-time analytic upscaling methods. As they are computationally expensive and operate on the full image, they are not suitable to be executed at texture sampling in real-time rendering.

Another class of research is to apply learned upsampling specifically to PBR texture content. MATUP [(Gauthier et al., 2024)] repurposes pre-trained RGB image upsamplers to super-resolve SVBRDF maps by optimizing a local MLP filter per material, with a radiance-domain loss to ensure physically consistent upscaling. PBR-SR [(Chen et al., 2025)] similarly leverages pre-trained 2D image super-resolution priors and refines PBR textures through iterative differentiable rendering against multi-view constraints. Both methods produce high-quality results but require per-asset optimization, making them unsuitable for integration into real-time rendering pipelines. Our method, in contrast, is a fully generalized model trained across a diverse set of PBR textures, requiring no per-asset processing. This allows it to be applied at texture-sampling time without any content creation overhead, directly replacing the conventional analytic upsampling step in the rendering pipeline.

Neural Texture Compression (NTC) is specifically targeted to be executed in this context [(Vaidyanathan et al., 2023)]. Instead of using larger models such as CNNs, NTC uses a small MLP with an input encoder, which makes it possible to do local per-texel evaluation at sampling time, which CNN and transformer-based models cannot do. As the neural network produces BC blocks which can be parsed and decompressed using the hardware decoder, NTBC can be executed to decompress textures into BC textures on load. NTBC also requires overfitting, so it adds overhead to the content creation pipeline.

Our method is designed to reduce these adoption barriers. First, our method is generalized, so no need to add a processing step in the content creation pipeline. The execution divergence is eliminated as our model is generalized, so we can execute the same model for different textures. item.title: 动作没录完也能实时补：REACT 做骨架运动信号的实时补全 ｜ REACT: Towards Real-Time Completion of Skeletal Motion Signals
item.description:
一句话：目标是在线补全骨架运动信号，而不是事后重建整段动作。

要点：

  • 任务定位：给定不完整的骨架运动信号，实时补全出可用的动作——这与「离线重建一段动作」是两种约束
  • 「实时」意味着补全必须在流式输入下持续进行，而不是等整段数据到齐再优化
  • 面向的是骨架信号本身（关节轨迹），因此结果可直接驱动现有动画系统，而不是先出网格再绑骨

为什么值得看：动捕会丢帧、网络会抖、输入本身可能不连续。能在信号层实时补全，等于给动画系统加了一道「抗抖动」缓冲，比在最终姿态上做平滑更接近根因。
