When this signal is high, we increase the weight of the median filter since it may reflect the velocity spikes of an artifact. In contrast, when Eₙ is low, we give more weight to the other, more flexible filters. We add these second priors (denoted b_filt) and a dynamical term generated by a small trained convolution layer g_θ to the previous logits and obtain z_gate=z_coarse+b_filt+g_θ(Eₙ), which is then fed to a softmax to compute normalized probabilities. Note that here, “static” refers to the explicitly designed structure and priors of the gate and a small learned dynamic correction is nevertheless retained.

3 Experiments

In this section, we present additional experiments and ablations.

3.1 Evaluated models

3.1.1 Variants

We define here all the variants defined by our newly presented design choices. We already introduced REACT-learned variants, and we thus define REACT-static ones, which use the static gate.

In addition to the -2S4 models, we want to observe the effect of partitioning a S4 layer between both heads, as described in Section 2.1. In addition, we can also observe the effect of loosely biasing the branches towards distinct spectral modes in the initial steps of the training. Thus, -lfd_hfp indicates an initial bias towards low frequencies (lf) for the Data (d) branch and high frequencies (hf) for the Phys (p) branch. By contrast, -lfp_hfd emphasizes an initial bias towards low frequencies for the Phys branch and high frequencies for the Data branch.

3.1.2 Observations buffer

To measure the effect of the observations buffer on the completion task, we articulate the training / inference of our problem under two distinct configurations. Each defines its own inputs and, as such, a set of models that can be compared fairly.

3.1.3 Configuration 1: Two-buffer input

That is precisely the configuration used in the main paper. Here, models receive both the prediction buffer and the raw-input buffer (, noisy and possibly missing measurements) and we describe them slightly more.

This configuration is used to train three GRU baselines, two distilled students and a rolling prediction model. We start by describing the GRUs.

(i) GRU-ctx is a 3-layer GRU with hidden size FJ, preceded by a linear projection that maps the concatenated buffers to the GRU input size,

(ii) GRU-ctx-large follows the same structure but uses a 5-layer GRU with hidden size 512,

(iii) GRU-ctx-large-noproj removes the input projection and feeds the (higher-dimensional) concatenated buffers directly to a 5-layer GRU with hidden size 512.

We report two distilled students with the same two-buffer input format and input linear projection: VQVAE-ctx-student (VQVAE backbone) and GRU-ctx-student (same backbone as GRU-ctx).

3.1.4 Configuration 2: One-buffer input

In this configuration, models receive only the prediction buffer and the current incomplete frame. We evaluate models, without input projection, including:

(i) GRU, a 3-layer GRU with hidden dimension FJ,

(ii) GRU-large, a 5-layer GRU with hidden dimension 512,

(iii) two students GRU-student and VQVAE-student.

This configuration is closer to a pure prediction setup and we expect it to reduce processing at runtime as well as memory footprint.

Strictly speaking the two configurations differ in formulation (, inputs dynamical filtering prediction-centric completion). As such, comparing them may also provide practical insights into the trade-off between robustness and simplicity in our completion task.

3.2 Metrics

In this section, we exhaustively present and define the metrics used to quantify the performance of our trained models the completion task challenges. We hierarchize our criteria into two categories: the primary metrics (our main objectives) and more complementary scores, highly dependent on context, to provide a deeper analysis.

3.2.1 Primary metrics

The metrics disclosed in this section are standard in the motion reconstruction literature. When applicable, they are scaled to obtain figures making sense in the International System of Units, using our skeleton’s normalized offsets. We robustly approximate a factor by using the distance between the head and toes of a standing skeleton over several frames and scaling it to reach 170 cm.

Among our reported metrics, we include scores on the position, such as the MPJPE (in world coordinates) defined as follows:

MPJPE=1/J∑ⱼ₌₀^J-1\lVertpⱼᵗ-p̂ⱼᵗ\rVert₂

(3)

, with p̂ⱼᵗ and pⱼᵗ the predicted and ground-truth joint positions. We also use the Procrustes-aligned MPJPE (P-MPJPE), which removes the optimal global similarity transformation before computing the positional error via a Singular Value Decomposition (SVD).

We also address joint rotation errors through the geodesic distance:

D_geo(R,R̂)=\arccos ((tr(RR̂^⊤)-1)/(2))

(4)

between R̂ and R, respectively the predicted and ground-truth rotations, applied on both local (MPJLAE) and global rotations (MPJAE). We emphasize their interest here since, although implicitly encoding rotational information, position-only metrics cannot reliably assess errors over all rotational Degrees of Freedom (DoFs). Indeed, such metrics are computed by collapsing sets of joint rotations into identical positional configurations and thus cannot disambiguate errors along axes that do not affect them. For instance, a rotation around a bone axis does not change the child joint position in space, even though creating artifacts during automatic skinning (, Linear Blend Skinning). As another example, position-only metrics often fail to reliably measure errors on distal joints kucherenko_mocap_2025, which may ultimately lead to models producing extreme failure scenarios (, >90° wrist bending).

To further measure the reliability of our system as a filter in an interactive setting, we use the metrics introduced by Barquero  barquero_auj_2024 to measure discrepancies during the update regime: the Peak Jerk (PJ) and the Area Under the Jerk (AUJ) such that:

PJ=\max_\substack1≤i≤K 1≤τ≤Lᵤᵣ\lVertjᵢ(τ)\rVert₁,

(5)

AUJ=∑_τ=1^Lᵤᵣ\max_1≤i≤K\lVertjᵢ(τ)-j_avg\rVert₁,

(6)

with Lᵤᵣ the length of the measured update regime (≈1 s), K the number of joints, jᵢ(τ) the jerk of the iᵗʰ joint at time τ and j_avg the average joint-wise maximum jerk across the dataset (0.3844 in our case).

Motion dynamics discrepancies are penalized by MPJPVE and MPJAVE. They represent the Mean Per Joints Velocity Error (even though sometimes denoted MPJVE in the literature, we call it MPJPVE to prevent any confusion with the next metric) and the Angular Velocity (or MPJAVE for Mean Per Joints Angular Velocity Error). They are defined as follow:

MPJPVE=1/J∑ⱼ₌₀^J-1\lVertvⱼᵗ-v̂ⱼᵗ\rVert₂,

(7)

MPJAVE=(1)/(Δt·J)∑ⱼ₌₀^J-1|D_geo(Rⱼᵗ,Rⱼᵗ⁺¹)-D_geo(R̂ⱼᵗ,R̂ⱼᵗ⁺¹)|,

(8)

with vⱼᵗ=(pⱼᵗ⁺¹-pⱼᵗ)/(Δt), D_geo as defined previously and Δt=1/60 in our case. Time derivative metrics tend to be unstable, with high inter-animation variance and may become arbitrarily large if a model sometimes produces velocity vectors of opposite direction ground-truth. For these reasons, we consider them of intermediary importance between primary and complementary metrics.

3.2.2 Complementary metrics

In addition to the per-frame (and per-event, for the PJ/AUJ) metrics, we introduce per-sequence scores. They aim to measure a similarity between the model’s output structure and the ground-truth’s. Specifically, we try to estimate whether the trained completion models preserve the spatiotemporal organization of the ground-truth motion by analysing their residual. For instance, an over-smoothing model may achieve low MPJPE and AUJ, while failing to reproduce high-frequency components. An extreme example of such a phenomenon would be a model outputting a static, average pose for most joints, while providing a robust rotation of proximal joints (, hips and trunk).

Temporal Power Spectral Entropy (TPSE) This metric corresponds to the entropy of the power spectral density distribution, and is computed on the temporal axis. Let p,p̂∈ℝ^T_psd×J×3 be the ground-truth and predicted joint positions respectively, and define the residual (or error signal) r=p-p̂. We flatten it over joints to obtain r_f∈ℝ^T_psd×3J. We compute its power spectral density PSD(r_f) (, via Welch’s method) and define the normalized spectral distribution pᵢ=(PSD(r_f)ᵢ)/(∑ⱼPSD(r_f)ⱼ). The temporal spectral entropy is then:

TPSE=(-∑ᵢpᵢ\log₂(pᵢ))/(Hₘₐₓ), Hₘₐₓ=\log₂(K),

(9)

where K is the number of frequency bins so that Hₘₐₓ is the maximum entropy of our spectrum. In other words, the TPSE aims to assess if the error signal still includes a temporal structure, , a non-uniform distribution of the signal power between low- and high-frequencies.

Residual Compression Size (RCS) This metric aims to measure a complementary notion of residual complexity. As its name suggests, we use existing algorithms to compress the quantized residual and compare the resulting size, , let r_q be the quantized version of r_f as defined previously. Then RCS=C(r_q) with , C=gzip. Such a compression process is already designed to capture relevant patterns, and we leverage it to loosely indicate the residual complexity (, a smooth and low-variance residual would have a lower compressed complexity than a highly irregular and noisy one). Note that this criterion is vulnerable to the inherent complexity of the motion (, a T-Pose would be much easier to compress than dancing), which implies high inter-motion and thus high intra-model variance.

Limitations In practice, we only compute both criteria described previously on short sequences (≈15-20 frames). This choice is motivated by the presence of real capturing noise in the ground-truth of the dataset, which could have invalidated our results. As such, we choose to compute the signal-complexity metrics on short sliding windows, which means most of the low-frequency content is missing (thereby mitigating the compressing capacities of gzip). Furthermore, absence of structure in the residual does not directly imply a good model, nor does structure necessarily tie to failure, in other words TPSE and RCS do not have a universally preferable direction, which motivates their use as complementary metrics.

3.3 Quantitative results

3.3.1 Complexity

We summarize the results of our experimented models’ complexity evaluation in Table 2. Despite the higher inference cost, our variants exceed the 30 fps threshold, which may be suitable for some interactive applications. However, they are currently not fast enough to support 60 or 90 Hz in particular under increased hardware constraints (, smaller GPUs). We observe that the one- and two-S4 variants exhibit similar runtime costs, suggesting that a substantial fraction of REACT’s latency originates outside the backbone itself. In short, a reasonable hypothesis is that the higher inference latency is caused by our non-fused custom operations, which lead to multiple CUDA kernels calls. As expected, we observe that the models in the second configuration are consistently faster than their equivalent in the first configuration (, GRUGRU-ctx), as they do not need to maintain an additional input buffer.

3.3.2 Completion

The main evaluation focuses on the signal completion, , its reconstruction. We first introduce some details before presenting the results.

During testing, we use constraints on the samples similar to the data augmentation seen during training to prevent, to some extent, the performance degradation caused by a distribution shift. The main difference between both settings is the necessary insertion of a clear switch between masking and de-masking. Such edge can be either rising (0 to 1 switch) or falling (1 to 0 switch). They are, indeed, necessary to precisely define the beginning of the update regime sequence (duration of ≈1 s) and thus to compute the AUJ and PJ.

Moreover, we compute the metrics on small predicted sequences to reduce the number of comparisons with noisy ground-truth (detected by a threshold on inter-frame jerk).

Our completion evaluations are separated into two broad categories. First, (as usually done in the literature) we keep all hyperparameters constant to compare the variants against the baselines of both input configurations. Second, we observe the impact of modifying the mask hyperparameters, and more specifically the models’ robustness to the maximal number of masked joints.

Comprehensive metrics evaluation We exhaustively detail the quantitative results related to the main evaluation (, constant hyper-parameters and metrics reported as mean±std) between configurations and baselines, which are presented in Tables 3 and 4.

First, the REACT variants consistently outperform the evaluated baselines on pose-level reconstruction metrics, with the largest improvements observed on rotational errors. On update-regime metrics, RPM remains particularly competitive and achieves the best score on several criteria, while the strongest REACT variants remain comparatively close. These results highlight the same reconstruction–stability trade-off discussed in the main paper.

Second, fusion ordering affects performance, although no ordering dominates every criterion. Within the two-S4 family, the Ref-last configuration performs best on most rotational and update-regime metrics, whereas the Data-last configuration achieves the lowest positional error. For the partitioned-S4 variants, we do not observe a clear advantage of either initial spectral assignment, suggesting that this initialization bias may be attenuated during training. The consistently better results of the 2S4 variants further suggest that partitioning a single S4 layer may constrain the available modelling capacity.

Third, distillation substantially improves the students’ rotational accuracy while preserving their low latency and memory footprint. However, these gains do not extend to positional accuracy or update-regime stability, which remain below those of the structured teacher. This suggests that some benefits of the structured teacher may be difficult to reproduce through output-level distillation alone. As such, increasingly constrained architectures could be explored and compared, to provide a more comprehensive analysis of the benefits and limitations, and reach a better trade-off between latency and performance.

Fourth, for GRU baselines, access to the raw-observation history generally improves frame-based reconstruction metrics but degrades update-regime stability. This suggests that recent observations provide useful reconstruction cues, while unreliable observation history can also destabilize regime transitions in architectures without explicit reliability handling. The effect of removing the input projection further indicates that the way both buffers are combined is itself an important design choice.

Fifth, completion without the observation buffer remains competitive. Although one-buffer models generally lose some reconstruction accuracy, they can produce more stable updates, possibly because they are less exposed to corrupted observation history. Choosing between both formulations may therefore depend on the expected reliability of the input signals and on the targeted reconstruction–stability trade-off.

Mask severity robustness As previously introduced, this specific evaluation quantifies the robustness to the mismatch between maximum masking range during training and testing. For each architecture, we train four checkpoints with M_\maxᵗʳᵃⁱⁿ∈{25,50,75,100}% while keeping M_\min=0% and evaluate them under four regimes M_\maxᵗᵉˢᵗ∈{25,50,75,100}%. This yields 16 values per model and for each metric. We further reduce the number of objective criteria to 2 (for an interpretable comparison): the MPJPE, and AUJ_\max=\max(AUJ_S→T,AUJ_T→S) (both are metrics where lower is better). Although incomplete, these metrics provide an overview of the evolution of both the pose reconstruction and the update regime dynamics. Note that during testing, we remove the joint mask from some subsequences to compute the update regime metrics. The results of our evaluation are detailed in Figure 3.

As hinted in the previous evaluation, GRU-based architectures provide relevant positional error at the cost of a jerky motion during transitions. Furthermore, their performance on positional metrics consistently degrades with an increase in mask severity. The additional buffer between GRU and GRU-ctx may improve the robustness to the mask severity, although it remains limited. The similar patterns exhibited by GRU-ctx-student, trained by distillation, may suggest that the masking range impact depends at least partly on the underlying architecture.

RPM prioritizes motion smoothness and is consistent on the related metric with a virtually constant AUJₘₐₓ no matter the mask severity. However, its positional error suffers from possible under-correction and seem to increase when trained with more occluded signals.

Finally, our variants provide both a good trade-off between motion smoothness and low positional error, as well as a reduced vulnerability to the training mask severity. The similar sensitivity patterns across REACT variants suggest that their shared system structure may contribute more strongly than the specific fusion ordering or other minor modifications to this behaviour.

item.title: CFG 要跑两遍太贵：Decompose the Distillation 把「条件/无条件」拆开蒸馏，单次前向也能调引导 ｜ Decompose the Distillation: Interpretable Single-Pass Guidance for Diffusion Models
item.description:
一句话：单次前向的替代方案大多把 CFG 两个分量揉成一团；先拆开再蒸，既能省一半算力又可解释。

要点：

  • 成本根源：classifier-free guidance 每一步都要同时算条件与无条件两支，N 步采样就是 2N 次前向
  • 现有单次前向替代方案大多把 CFG 的两个分量塌缩成一个不透明的「引导预测」，失去了引导强度可调与可解释性
  • 这篇把蒸馏拆开：分别蒸馏 CFG 的两个成分，从而在单次前向里保留「引导强度」这个旋钮

为什么值得看：生成式内容进实时管线时，采样步数与每次前向的成本直接决定可行性。把 CFG 蒸馏成单次前向又保留强度可调，等于同时拿回速度与可控性——对做实时生成式渲染的团队是直接收益。

中文摘要：Classifier-Free Guidance（CFG）是条件扩散生成里最常用的推理期引导规则，它暴露一个可调的引导强度，代价是每一步采样都要同时评估条件与无条件两支，N 步轨迹即 2N 次前向。已有的单次前向替代方案能压低成本，但大多把 CFG 的两个分量塌缩成一个不透明的「引导预测」，于是既失去强度可调性，也难以解释。这篇提出「拆开再蒸」：分别蒸馏 CFG 的两个成分，使单次前向也能保留引导强度这个旋钮。对要进实时管线的生成式渲染，速度与可控性同时被拿回。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-08

本期推送：2026-11-09

Decompose the Distillation: Interpretable Single-Pass Guidance for Diffusion Models

Abstract

Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is a widely used inference-time guidance rule for conditional image generation with diffusion models, which exposes a guidance scale that adjusts conditioning strength after training. This flexibility requires conditional and unconditional model evaluations at every sampling step, so an N-step trajectory takes 2N forward passes. Single-pass alternatives reduce such cost, yet most collapse CFG’s two components into one opaque guided prediction, losing the separable base flow and guidance direction that support per-step control and diagnostics, even when the scale remains adjustable. This work introduces CtrlFlow, a single-pass guidance method that preserves CFG’s separable base-flow and guidance-direction interface. To preserve both components at one-pass cost, CtrlFlow attaches two lightweight LoRA adapters to a frozen backbone, each adding 2.5% parameters, and predicts the base flow and guidance direction from one pass of the shared frozen backbone. Because the guidance scale multiplies the guidance direction only after the forward pass, one evaluation yields the guided velocity at any scale, so a single trained checkpoint remains adjustable at inference without retraining. Preserving two outputs introduces a training mismatch: inference amplifies guidance-direction errors by the chosen scale, while naive component-wise losses weight both outputs equally. To align training with this composed inference-time error, CtrlFlow uses a unified multi-scale distillation loss. Residual guidance errors can still persist at extreme scales, where even small guidance-direction errors are amplified by the guidance scale. To reduce this inference-time error, CtrlFlow applies scale-adaptive modulation to damp velocity-field errors and time-grid warping to concentrate solver evaluations where the trajectory changes most rapidly. On ImageNet 256×256 with the DiT-XL/2 backbone, CtrlFlow matches CFG within a pre-specified tolerance in 24 of 25 (N,s) configurations, against 20 of 25 for a matched scale-conditioned opaque student, and achieves a measured 1.93× wall-clock speedup at N=25.

1 Introduction

In conditional image generation with diffusion models [(Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Rombach et al., 2022)], each sample should both look like a plausible natural image and match the conditioning signal, such as the requested class in class-conditional generation [(Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Peebles and Xie, 2023)]. Achieving both goals simultaneously is challenging: stronger guidance improves condition matching, whereas overly strong guidance can introduce visible artifacts [(Sadat et al., 2025a)] and make the model produce similar outputs instead of diverse valid images for the same condition [(Karras et al., 2024; Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024)]. Inference-time guidance methods [(Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Ho and Salimans, 2021)] address this trade-off by letting practitioners control the strength of the conditioning signal during sampling. Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [(Ho and Salimans, 2021)], the most widely adopted such method and a foundation for many later variants, implements this control with a scalar guidance scale s that can be tuned after training. Because CFG compares two predictions from the same network at every sampling step, practitioners obtain per-sample, per-step control over the quality-alignment trade-off without retraining. This flexibility carries a cost: every guided step requires two network evaluations rather than one, so an N-step trajectory takes 2N forward passes and wall-clock latency nearly doubles [(Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Rombach et al., 2022)].

Several recent works attacked this 2N overhead. Across these attempts, speed is typically gained by giving up some facet of CFG’s interface, leaving practitioners to choose between latency and control. One route distills guidance into a single-pass student that takes the scale as a network input, as in AGD [(Jensen and Sadat, 2025)], which trains an adapter on a frozen backbone, and Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [(Chen et al., 2025a)], which fine-tunes the whole model. Both halve the forward passes and keep the scale adjustable, but each pass commits to one scale and returns an opaque guided velocity with no separable base flow or guidance direction. Model Guidance [(Tang et al., 2025)] and Entropy Rectifying Guidance [(Ifriqi et al., 2025)] take a different route, building guidance directly into the model. Both methods run in a single pass, yet both collapse the base/guidance split and surrender the post-hoc scale knob that motivated CFG. A complementary pattern keeps two passes and improves the guidance step instead. CFG-Zero* [(Fan et al., 2025)] and APG [(Sadat et al., 2025a)] sharpen the guided update, while retaining the conditional and unconditional evaluations. Autoguidance [(Karras et al., 2024)] makes the second evaluation cheaper by replacing the unconditional model with a smaller trained network. None of these two-pass refinements reduces the 2N evaluation count. For the goal of CFG-like control at lower latency, these trade-offs reduce to three axes. Single-pass compute measures whether each step uses one network evaluation or two. The criterion of explicit access to v₀ and g concerns whether the method’s inference interface keeps base flow and guidance direction separately available for control or diagnosis. The remaining axis, post-hoc s, captures whether the method exposes a guidance-scale knob that is not tied to a single training scale and can be varied at inference without retraining. Table 1 organizes existing methods along these axes. Scale-conditioned students such as AGD and GFT already combine single-pass compute with post-hoc s, so the missing piece is the interface: to our knowledge, no prior single-pass method keeps v₀ and g separately available.

Motivated by this missing intersection, we observe that CFG’s two-prediction structure exposes an interpretable interface between a base flow v₀ and a guidance direction g, which should be preserved rather than collapsed into a single opaque prediction. The base flow captures how the model moves toward the data manifold without conditioning, while the guidance direction encodes how the conditioning signal redirects that flow. Existing single-pass efficient methods compress this interface into a single opaque output. To preserve it at one-pass cost, CtrlFlow attaches two lightweight LoRA adapters [(Hu et al., 2022)], each adding 2.5% parameters, to a frozen backbone and computes both components in a single forward pass. As a result, the guidance scale s multiplies the guidance direction after the forward pass, so s remains adjustable at inference and no retraining is needed. Unlike a scale input, this lets one evaluation yield the guided velocity at every s. In addition to post-hoc scale control, the preserved interface opens a diagnostic channel unavailable to opaque single-pass methods. Norm maps reveal where guidance acts spatially, while alignment maps reveal whether guidance reinforces or opposes the base flow, and this geometric signal later enables the alignment-based correction in Section 3.4.

Preserving the decomposition is not free, however, because distilling this interface exposes three challenges that require explicit handling.

(i) Training-pressure mismatch. Supervising the two components independently creates a mismatch between training pressure and inference-time error importance within the fixed adapter budget. Inference weights guidance errors by s, but a naive component-wise loss treats both components equally, so the guidance adapter receives weaker gradient signal than its inference-time importance warrants. A unified distillation objective sidesteps this mismatch by supervising only the composed output, which aligns gradient pressure with the composed inference-time error (Section 3.3).

(ii) Error amplification. At high guidance scales with low step counts, small prediction errors in the guidance direction are magnified by s, producing visible artifacts. Scale-adaptive modulation addresses this amplification by targeting three sources of error (Section 3.4). Temporal windowing narrows the guidance-active interval as s grows, while scale dampening reduces the guidance magnitude above a tuned threshold. Alignment-based correction then uses the geometric agreement between base flow and guidance direction, a signal that no opaque single-pass student exposes.

(iii) Dead zones. In our diagnostics, certain (N,s) configurations show large FID degradation that is better explained by temporal under-resolution of the solver than by a globally inaccurate learned velocity field. A scale-dependent time-warp controller redistributes the existing N evaluations near critical trajectory regions without adding forward passes (Section 3.5). With this warp, all observed dead-zone failures except the extreme (2,8) setting are resolved (Appendix D.13), leaving 24 of 25 configurations within tolerance.

We evaluate on ImageNet 256×256 with the DiT-XL/2 backbone [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)]. Under the FID tolerance defined in Section 4, these mechanisms recover CFG-match quality while retaining one-pass sampling. CtrlFlow matches CFG quality across all five tested step counts at s=1 and across four of five at s=8. At N=25, wall-clock time falls from 843 ms per image to 437 ms, a 1.93× speedup. Beyond the training range of s≤8, CtrlFlow remains competitive: it outperforms CFG at s=10 (FID 28.41 versus 31.24) and trails CFG by 3.1 FID at the more extreme s=12 setting in our DiT-XL/2 protocol. Against a scale-conditioned opaque student with the same capacity, teacher, and curriculum (AGD-MultiScale), CtrlFlow is on par at (25,2) and 0.96 to 4.14 FID lower at the harder tested configurations, matches CFG in 24 of 25 configurations against 20 of 25, and keeps top-1 class accuracy within 2 points of CFG.

Our contributions are organized around preserving and exploiting this interface.

•Interpretable single-pass guidance interface. CtrlFlow exposes both v₀ and g in one forward pass with 5% parameter overhead, while keeping the guidance scale s adjustable at inference without retraining. The dual-adapter architecture and unified distillation objective that enable this interface are described in Sections 3.2 and 3.3.

•Decomposition-enabled stabilization. CtrlFlow combines temporal windowing and scale dampening with an alignment-based correction that only the preserved split makes possible, reducing error amplification across the tested range of s. At (4,8), these modulations lower FID from 73.41 to 63.42 before time warping is applied (Section 3.4, Table 3). These mechanisms also help opaque students, but with every transferable mechanism given to a matched opaque student, CtrlFlow remains 1.3 to 2.1 FID lower (Section 4.3).

•Dead-zone removal. Scale-dependent time-grid warping resolves all observed dead-zone failures except (2,8), leaving 24 of 25 configurations within tolerance without additional forward passes (Section 3.5).

•CFG-match quality at one-pass cost. Across the 25-point (N,s) grid on DiT-XL/2, CtrlFlow matches CFG quality in 24 of 25 cases, against 20 of 25 for the matched scale-conditioned opaque student, and the measured N=25 latency shows a 1.93× wall-clock speedup over CFG (Section 4, Table 2). On DiT-L/4, CtrlFlow stays within 0.19 FID of CFG at (25,2) and outperforms CFG at the tested high-scale settings, and a Stable Diffusion 2.1 pilot adds text conditioning (Section 4.5).

2 Background and Related Works

CFG and its Interface. Because CtrlFlow uses a DiT velocity-prediction backbone [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], we write diffusion sampling in the flow-matching form [(Lipman et al., 2023)], where a learned velocity field transports noise to data along an ODE. Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [(Ho and Salimans, 2021)] steers conditional generation by interpolating unconditional and conditional predictions,

v_cfg=v_uncond+s·(v_cond-v_uncond),

(1)

where s controls guidance strength. Equivalently, CFG computes v₀+s g, where v₀\triangleqv_uncond is the base flow and g\triangleqv_cond-v_uncond is the guidance direction. This decomposition reveals an interpretable interface between unconditional generation and conditioning adjustment, but CFG obtains both components through two evaluations per step, doubling the forward-pass count.

Efficient Guidance. Existing efficiency methods mostly split between lowering the number of evaluations and preserving CFG’s separate outputs. Single-pass methods such as Plug-and-Play Distillation [(Hsiao et al., 2024)], AGD [(Jensen and Sadat, 2025)], Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [(Chen et al., 2025a)], Model Guidance [(Tang et al., 2025)], and ERG [(Ifriqi et al., 2025)] reduce per-step cost by avoiding a separate unconditional evaluation, often through a compressed guide or training-time guidance surrogate. AGD and GFT take the guidance strength as a network input, so one checkpoint covers many scales, but each pass still returns one opaque guided velocity at one scale. Two-pass refinements such as APG [(Sadat et al., 2025a)], CFG-Zero* [(Fan et al., 2025)], Autoguidance [(Karras et al., 2024)], Dynamic Negative Guidance [(Koulischer et al., 2024)], and ICG [(Sadat et al., 2025b)] preserve or improve CFG quality, but they retain the 2N evaluation cost. Thus, prior work either preserves the CFG interface at two-pass cost or reduces the pass count by exposing only a single opaque guided output.

Schedules and Training Pressure. This interface gap also affects distillation and sampling design. Distillation methods [(Salimans and Ho, 2022; Meng et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2024)] collapse the two components into a single composed output, removing the separate guidance direction that CtrlFlow needs for post-hoc control and diagnostics. Guidance-window and solver-schedule methods [(Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024; Malarz et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2022; Sabour et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024)] instead modify when or where guidance is applied, but they do not adapt an exposed guidance direction across scales. Once a student is asked to output both v₀ and g, it also faces a training-pressure mismatch: a naive dual loss treats the two adapter errors equally even though inference amplifies guidance errors by s. CtrlFlow responds by preserving the v₀/g interface in one pass, aligning distillation with the composed inference-time error, and using scale-aware modulation and time-grid warping to adapt that interface across guidance scales.

Section 3 defines the decomposition formally, implements it with dual adapters, trains it with unified distillation, and introduces the inference-time mechanisms that stabilize it across scales and step counts. Appendix A provides an extended discussion of all related work.

3 Methodology

CtrlFlow distills CFG into a single-pass student that preserves separate base-flow and guidance-direction outputs rather than emitting one opaque guided velocity. Figure 1 summarizes this design. The section first formalizes this output interface and implements it with dual adapters (Sections 3.1 and 3.2). Because the resulting two-output student can still misallocate its limited adapter capacity (the training-pressure mismatch from Section 1), we train it with unified multi-scale distillation (Section 3.3). Finally, two inference-time mechanisms stabilize sampling: scale-adaptive modulation, whose alignment gate reuses the preserved interface, damps high-scale guidance errors, and time-grid warping adapts the solver schedule to the guidance regime (Sections 3.4 and 3.5).

3.1 Velocity Decomposition

As shown in Section 2, CFG can be written as v₀+s g, where v₀ is the base flow and g is the guidance direction. We now formalize this split as the output interface that the compressed student must preserve. Given a noisy sample xₜ, conditioning signal c, and timestep t, the two teacher-side fields are

v₀(xₜ,t)\triangleqv_θ(xₜ,∅,t),(2)
g(xₜ,c,t)\triangleqv_θ(xₜ,c,t)-v_θ(xₜ,∅,t),(3)

so the teacher’s guided velocity at any scale s is

v=v₀+s·g,

(4)

with the linear dependence on s explicit. Although this decomposition is algebraically identical to standard CFG, treating the pair (v₀,g) as the student’s required output interface is what enables the mechanisms that follow: the guidance scale s can be applied after the forward pass, the norm ∥g∥ can be inspected spatially, and the alignment between v₀ and g can drive inference-time gating. In the compressed student, v̂₀ and ĝ (hatted to distinguish student predictions from teacher-defined fields) are learned estimates of these teacher fields produced from a single shared forward pass that receives (xₜ,c,t). The unconditional teacher evaluation that defines v₀ is used only for supervision and is not repeated at inference. Below, hats appear when emphasizing training-time predictions. After training, we write the deployed student outputs as v₀ and g when no confusion with teacher fields arises.

Interpretable Diagnostics. Because the student preserves both fields as separate outputs, the decomposition exposes two quantities unavailable to single-output methods. The norm ∥g∥ measures the magnitude of the conditioning-induced adjustment at each spatial location and timestep: large values indicate strong redirection, while small values mark effectively unconditional regions. The alignment a\triangleq\cos(v₀,g) quantifies compatibility between the base flow and the conditioning adjustment. When a≈1, conditioning reinforces the base flow, and when a<0, conditioning opposes it, producing a diagnostic signal for potential artifacts. Section 3.4 uses a as an inference-time modulation signal, and Section 4.4 visualizes both quantities on generated samples. These diagnostics are only useful if compression keeps both fields accessible, which the next subsection implements with two explicit adapter branches.

3.2 Dual-Adapter Architecture

Implementing the decomposition requires an architecture that produces both v₀ and g in a single forward pass with minimal parameter overhead.

We freeze the pretrained diffusion backbone and attach two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters [(Hu et al., 2022)], one for each component. Each adapter computes a low-rank residual from the backbone’s hidden representations,

r=BA h_base,

(5)

where A∈ℝ^r×d and B∈ℝ^d×r with rank r≪d. The two branches do not keep separate hidden states. The frozen backbone computes one hidden-state stream per step, both adapters read it at the attention projections, and each branch accumulates its low-rank residuals into its own velocity-shaped output instead of writing them back, so backbone computation runs once per step and NFE=N is exact. The guided velocity is then assembled as v=v₀+s·g per Equation 4. Because s multiplies gafter the forward pass, it remains adjustable at inference without retraining. The full interface is thus preserved with only 2.5% additional parameters per adapter (5% total, rank r=64).

The architecture makes the two fields available, but does not determine how training pressure is distributed across them. A component-wise loss can underweight guidance errors that inference amplifies by s, while composed-output training at a single scale leaves the split underdetermined. Section 3.3 addresses both risks with a unified multi-scale distillation objective.

3.3 Unified Distillation

Training-Pressure Mismatch. The dual-adapter architecture exposes both v₀ and g, but a naive component-wise objective would optimize the wrong error. If the two outputs are supervised independently, base-flow and guidance residuals receive equal loss weight even though inference uses the composed velocity v̂₀+s·ĝ. A residual error in ĝ is therefore magnified by s at sampling time, whereas a residual error in v̂₀ enters with unit weight. Because the backbone is frozen and each adapter has fixed rank, this mismatch determines which residuals receive training pressure within a fixed budget. At large s, equal component weighting under-prioritizes the guidance errors most likely to produce artifacts. Appendix B.1 formalizes this capacity-allocation analysis.

Unified Distillation Objective. To align training with the deployed interface, CtrlFlow supervises the composed output rather than the two components independently. For each training tuple (xₜ,c,t,s), a frozen CFG teacher provides the two-pass target v_cfgᵗᵉᵃᶜʰᵉʳ, and the student minimizes

L=𝔼[∥v̂₀+s·ĝ-v_cfgᵗᵉᵃᶜʰᵉʳ∥²].

(6)

This objective gives both adapters the same composed residual while the guidance branch inherits the chain-rule factor s. As a result, high-scale examples place stronger pressure on ĝ: Appendix B.1 shows that the guidance adapter’s squared gradient norm carries a factor s² relative to the base adapter, and verifies empirically the Jacobian-comparability condition behind this factor. The loss therefore allocates capacity according to inference-time error importance without a manually tuned component balance.

Identifiability and Curriculum. Composed-output supervision also creates a uniqueness question: at a single guidance scale, many (v₀,g) pairs can produce the same sum. Scale variation resolves this degeneracy. Under realizability, Appendix B.1 proves that training on at least two distinct values of s for the same input (xₜ,c,t) uniquely recovers the teacher decomposition (Proposition 1), a condition met by sampling s independently of the input. We use this observation as the organizing principle for a three-phase curriculum: Phase 1 first stabilizes the composed prediction at fixed s, Phase 2 expands to s∼U[1,s_\max] to identify the split, and Phase 3 samples the (N,s) solver regimes used at inference. This schedule introduces scale and discretization difficulty only after the composed prediction is stable, which avoids the convergence instability seen when Phase 1 is skipped and the single-scale overfitting seen when Phase 2 is skipped (Appendix D.10).

Remaining Gap. Unified distillation aligns training pressure with the composed inference-time error, but it does not remove the amplification caused by high guidance scales. At extreme values of s, residual errors in ĝ are multiplied during inference and can produce visible artifacts. Error amplification of this kind is an inference-time phenomenon, and the next subsection provides an inference-time solution.

3.4 Scale-Adaptive Guidance Modulation

As previewed at the close of Section 3.3, the guided velocity v₀+s·g multiplies prediction errors in g by the scale factor s at inference time. In the high-scale, low-step regime (s>4, N≤4), even small guidance errors can produce visible artifacts after amplification by s. We address this inference-time error with three lightweight multipliers that target where errors matter, how strongly they are scaled, and whether guidance agrees geometrically with the base flow. The effective guidance weight becomes s·w(t)·α(s)·φ(a), yielding the modulated velocity

vₒᵤₜ(t)=v₀+s·w(t)·α(s)·φ(a)·g.

(7)

Writing γ\triangleqw(t) α(s) φ(a)∈(0,1], modulation shrinks the amplified guidance error from s ε_g to sγ ε_g but also moves the output away from the CFG velocity by s(1-γ) g, a trade-off that Appendix B.2 states exactly.

Temporal Modulation w(t). Prior work [(Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024)] observed that guidance is most useful in a mid-timestep interval, whereas endpoint guidance can harm quality or add little benefit. We encode this pattern with a smooth window over t whose width narrows as s grows. Low scales therefore retain broad guidance, while high scales suppress endpoint guidance where amplification is most severe. Appendix C gives the exact Gaussian form and hyperparameters. This scale-adaptive schedule extends fixed-interval guidance [(Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024)] and beta-distribution schedules [(Malarz et al., 2025)].

Scale Dampening α(s). Even after temporal windowing narrows where guidance is active, high guidance scales still enlarge residual guidance-direction errors. To counteract this global scale growth, a monotonically decreasing function α(s) reduces the effective guidance magnitude as s increases. The function engages only above a threshold sₜₕᵣₑₛₕ, so dampening leaves low-s generation unchanged. Appendix C specifies the functional form.

Alignment Gating φ(a). The explicit decomposition into v₀ and g reveals per-step geometric relationships unavailable to single-output methods. The alignment a=\cos(v₀,g) from Section 3.1 measures whether conditioning reinforces or opposes the base flow. We attenuate guidance only when a<0, where guidance opposes the base flow and is more prone to artifacts, and leave well-aligned steps at full strength. Because CtrlFlow makes a available at every step, this correction requires no additional forward passes. APG [(Sadat et al., 2025a)] performs a related projection, but it requires two passes and decomposes relative to v_cond rather than the base flow. Appendix C gives our exact gate. Only φ(a) requires the split, since any method with a scale knob can mimic w(t) and α(s) (Section 4.3).

Two-Regime Design. This bias is intentional. At or below sₜₕᵣₑₛₕ, α(s) and the warp of Section 3.5 are inactive and the window is broad, so CtrlFlow tracks CFG closely (within 0.10 FID at (25,2)). Above it, CFG’s own dynamics degrade and CtrlFlow departs from them deliberately: applying windowing and dampening to exact two-pass CFG, which has no prediction error, lowers its FID from 53.84 to 46.02 at (4,8) (Appendix D.12).

Velocity-field modulation alone, however, does not address every failure case. At extreme (N,s) corners, the solver’s uniform time grid undersamples the part of the trajectory where the guided velocity changes most rapidly. Section 3.5 addresses this discretization-side failure by redistributing the fixed evaluations.

3.5 Reducing Dead Zones via Time-Grid Warping

Dead Zones. Certain (N,s) configurations produce sharply degraded generation quality even after velocity-field modulation. The baseline DPM-Solver schedule distributes timesteps uniformly across [0,1], whereas the guided trajectory changes most rapidly in a narrower mid-timestep region. When the fixed grid spends too many evaluations near smoother endpoints and too few in this high-curvature region, the resulting failure is better explained as temporal under-resolution than as another velocity-field error. We call these configurations dead zones.

Scale-Dependent Time Warping. To address dead zones without adding evaluations or retraining, CtrlFlow redistributes the existing N solver calls. A monotone schedule map τ transforms the uniform solver indices {i/N}ᵢ₌₀^N into non-uniform timesteps {tᵢ=τ(i/N)}ᵢ₌₀^N. Its dilation weight ω(t) is chosen to be small in the mid-timestep region and larger near trajectory endpoints, so the solver takes finer steps where guidance-induced curvature is highest and coarser steps where the trajectory is smoother. The warp magnitude increases only above the same high-scale threshold used by the dampening function in Section 3.4, and at lower guidance scales the schedule remains uniform. Appendices B.3 and C give the exact construction, monotonicity proof, and hyperparameter values.

Properties. Because the warping operates at the ODE solver level, orthogonal to the velocity-field modulations in Section 3.4, it requires no additional forward passes and can be precomputed once per (N,s) configuration with negligible cost. Because τ only moves the solver’s timesteps, warping adds no bias to the velocity field (Appendix B.3) and applies to any sampler. Together, modulation and warping stabilize what velocity is computed and where the solver evaluates it, while preserving the one-pass inference interface.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Backbone, Dataset, and Protocol. We evaluate CtrlFlow on class-conditional ImageNet 256×256 using DiT-XL/2 [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)] as the backbone. The frozen CFG teacher runs N_teacher=250 steps with DPM-Solver [(Lu et al., 2022)]. We generate 50K images per configuration following the ADM evaluation suite [(Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021)] across N∈{2,4,8,16,25} and s∈{1.0,2.0,4.0,6.0,8.0}, yielding 25 configurations. Each configuration is evaluated over three independent 50K-image seed lists, and table entries report mean FID-50K. We also report Precision, Recall [(Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019)], class adherence (top-1 accuracy of a frozen ResNet-50 [(He et al., 2015)] on the conditioning class), and CFG-Match Accuracy, defined as the percentage of configurations satisfying FID_CtrlFlow≤FID_CFG+δ, where δ=\max(2.0, 0.10×FID_CFG). Configurations where CtrlFlow improves over CFG are counted as matches. The absolute floor of 2.0 handles low-FID regimes where sub-unit differences are not visually meaningful, while the 10% relative term scales the tolerance in harder regimes. The criterion is one-sided by design, since modulation deliberately departs from CFG at high s (Section 3.4).

Baselines. We compare against seven methods spanning two-pass refinements and single-pass compression. (1) CFG[(Ho and Salimans, 2021)] (two-pass oracle), (2) CFG + Interval[(Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024)] (two-pass, mid-timestep guidance), (3) CFG-Zero*[(Fan et al., 2025)] (training-free, two-pass), (4) APG[(Sadat et al., 2025a)] (orthogonal projection, two-pass), (5) Autoguidance[(Karras et al., 2024)] (two-pass, smaller unconditional model), (6) AGD-MultiScale, the primary single-pass baseline, an opaque adapter following AGD [(Jensen and Sadat, 2025)] that receives s as an input, trained with s∼U[1,8] at matched capacity (rank 128, 34M parameters) and with the same teacher, curriculum, and optimizer as CtrlFlow, and (7) AGD (fixed s=2), a smaller (14M) variant trained at one scale. Two-pass baselines run official implementations with default hyperparameters, and we train both AGD variants since no DiT-XL/2 AGD checkpoint is public (Appendix E.1). Appendix D.16 also compares against the released GFT checkpoint.

Training Details. Both LoRA adapters use rank r=64 (5% total overhead), and training follows the three-phase curriculum from Section 3.3. The full run takes 48 GPU-hours on 8×A100. Appendices E.3 and C give optimizer settings, phase lengths, LoRA placement, teacher construction, solver settings, and validation protocol. Modulation and warping hyperparameters are tuned on 5K-image validation samples, while all reported FID values use independent 50K-image generations. These are the five configurations of Table 2, and the other 20 grid configurations were never used for selection.

4.2 Main Results

CtrlFlow uses a single forward pass (NFE=N), while CFG and the two-pass baselines require NFE=2N. Table 2 reports FID-50K at five representative (N,s) configurations spanning easy to extreme regimes.

At s=2, where the fixed-scale AGD variant is trained, the tested single-pass methods stay close to CFG, so the easy regime is not the main separator. CtrlFlow falls within 0.10 FID at N=25 and within 0.23 at N=4. The stronger tests are scale generalization and high-scale control. The fixed-scale variant degrades once s leaves its training scale (25.81 at (8,4), 82.17 at (4,8)), and its Recall of 0.14 at (25,8), against 0.32 for CFG and 0.35 for CtrlFlow, indicates mode dropping (Appendix D.3). Scale-conditioned training removes most of this failure, yet AGD-MultiScale still trails CtrlFlow at every tested configuration, by up to 4.14 FID at (25,8), and matches CFG in 20 of 25 grid configurations against 24 of 25 (Appendix D.2). CtrlFlow also improves over CFG at (8,4) (10.98 versus 11.72) and reaches 19.28 and 48.95 at s=8 with half the forward evaluations. Class adherence survives the damping: CtrlFlow’s top-1 accuracy stays within 2 points of CFG’s at every tested configuration (75.9% versus 77.8% at (4,8)), while AGD-MultiScale falls to 57.3% (Appendix D.5). Against the released GFT checkpoint at matched NFE, CtrlFlow is 0.27 FID worse at s≈1 and 0.11 to 2.12 FID better for s≈2 to 8, with a frozen backbone instead of full fine-tuning (Appendix D.16).

Among two-pass methods, APG gives the best high-s FID through orthogonal projection, but it retains 2N cost and does not provide a single-pass base-flow/guidance interface. Among CFG-style methods, CtrlFlow reaches within 1.05 FID of CFG + Interval at (25,8) with half the forward evaluations while retaining the decomposition interface.

Figure 2 extends this comparison across the full guidance-scale range at N=25. The fixed-scale AGD curve climbs sharply beyond its training scale of s=2, whereas CtrlFlow tracks CFG with half the forward evaluations. Appendix Figure 10 plots FID against NFE at s=4 and shows the same compute-quality pattern.

Across the full 25-configuration grid (Appendix D.1), CtrlFlow achieves 96% CFG-match accuracy (24 of 25 within δ) and a 1.93× wall-clock speedup at N=25. This match count is stable across three generation seeds (Appendix D.6), and all 20 configurations never used for tuning match except (2,8). Beyond the training range of s≤8, CtrlFlow remains competitive, outperforming CFG at s=10 and trailing by 3.1 FID at s=12 (Appendix D.14), and qualitative samples appear in Appendix D.21.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Contribution Isolation. Table 3 separates the value of the explicit decomposition from the benefits of multi-scale training by building up from the core architecture. CtrlFlow-Core uses only the dual-adapter decomposition with unified distillation, omitting modulation and warping. As a controlled comparison, AGD-MultiScale trains a single opaque adapter that receives s as an input, with the same multi-scale curriculum and matched parameter budget (rank 128, 34M parameters). At moderate scales the two are close: AGD-MultiScale reaches FID 11.94 versus CtrlFlow-Core’s 11.48 at (8,4). At the extreme (4,8), however, AGD-MultiScale achieves 52.87 while CtrlFlow-Core reaches only 73.41, so the decomposition constraint alone does not provide a raw optimization advantage. The picture reverses once the interface is exploited, with CtrlFlow-Full reaching 48.95.

Interface versus Transferable Mechanisms. Because windowing, dampening, and warping are not specific to the decomposition, we also give them to the baselines, feeding the opaque student a time-varying scale input s_eff(t)=s w(t) α(s) (Appendix D.12). They improve AGD-MultiScale by 0.7 to 2.3 FID, yet CtrlFlow-Full stays 1.3 to 2.1 FID lower at all four tested configurations, including two never used for tuning, and removing only the alignment gate, the one mechanism that needs v₀ and g, costs 0.6 to 2.4 FID. The decomposition’s value is therefore the interface it opens, not a raw quality gap.

Further Ablations. Four additional studies (Appendices D.8 to D.11) confirm that the mechanisms contribute independently and that the three-phase curriculum is important for stable high-scale performance. Unified distillation produces the largest single effect (FID degrades by 19.5 at (4,8) when removed). The three modulation sub-components are complementary, with each pair outperforming both of its components, and rank 64 sits at the knee of the cost-quality curve. A conditional-field anchor, v_cond+(s-1) g, matches Core within noise but trails Full by 1.1 to 2.6 FID (Appendix D.20). Dead-zone analysis and modulation/warping visualizations appear in Appendices D.13, D.24, and D.25.

4.4 Decomposition Fidelity and Interpretability

The explicit decomposition into v₀ and g enables direct inspection of what guidance changes, a capability unavailable to opaque single-pass methods that predict only the composed guided velocity. Before using this channel for visualization, we verify that the learned components are faithful to the teacher decomposition in two ways. Cosine similarity to the teacher-generated ground truth exceeds 0.83 across all timesteps and peaks at 0.97 for v̂₀ at t=0.5 (Appendix D.18). We then test functional equivalence: each learned component replaces its teacher counterpart in a standard two-pass CFG pipeline, and we measure whether generation quality is preserved. Table 4 reports the results.

At (25,2), swapping in ĝ raises FID by only 0.10, while swapping in v̂₀ raises it by 0.04. At (25,8), the gaps grow to 0.84 for ĝ and 0.27 for v̂₀ because guidance errors are amplified by s. The full CtrlFlow model reaches 19.28 at (25,8), outperforming both swap variants and CFG itself. This gain reflects the deliberate high-scale departure from CFG (Appendix B.2.5), not a closer CFG approximation. Having verified that the split is both geometrically and functionally meaningful, we next visualize what the two components reveal.

Figure 3 uses this verified decomposition to visualize where and when guidance acts on a representative ImageNet class (golden retriever). The top row shows that guidance is spatially diffuse at high noise but concentrates by later timesteps on class-discriminative regions such as object boundaries, fur texture, and facial features, while background regions receive little signal. The bottom row shows the complementary geometric pattern: alignment between v₀ and g starts near zero and increases toward 1 as the trajectory converges. This progression is not imposed explicitly. It emerges from unified distillation and supplies the signal used by the alignment gate φ(a) in Section 3.4. The same spatial and temporal patterns appear for butterfly and volcano classes in Appendix D.22, suggesting that the learned split is not specific to the representative class shown here. Quantitatively, guidance-norm maps on noised ImageNet validation images point to the annotated object with accuracy 0.81, above Grad-CAM [(Selvaraju et al., 2017)] (0.74) and on par with the two-pass teacher’s maps (0.80) (Appendix D.23).

4.5 Cost and Generalization

The interpretability and stabilization benefits of the decomposition come at modest cost. CtrlFlow adds 34M parameters (5% of DiT-XL/2) and requires 48 GPU-hours of training, but at N=25 it reduces latency from 843 ms per image for CFG to 437 ms, and Appendix Table 29 compares all methods. The speedup is 1.93× rather than 2× because the adapters and modulation add 15.5 ms to the 421.5 ms backbone pass (Appendix E.2). To test transfer beyond DiT-XL/2, we also train CtrlFlow on DiT-L/4 with the same protocol. On DiT-L/4, CtrlFlow stays within 0.19 FID of CFG at (25,2) and outperforms CFG at the tested high-scale settings, with full cross-backbone and decomposition-fidelity tables in Appendix D.15. A Stable Diffusion 2.1 [(Rombach et al., 2022)] text-to-image pilot keeps the ImageNet ordering: at N=25 and s=7.5, CtrlFlow reaches COCO FID-10K 10.41 and CLIPScore 0.304, between two-pass CFG (9.82, 0.309) and a scale-conditioned opaque student (11.37, 0.300) (Appendix D.17).

5 Conclusion

CtrlFlow distills CFG into a single forward pass that preserves the base-flow and guidance-direction interface with two LoRA adapters, keeping s adjustable without retraining. With unified distillation, scale-adaptive modulation, and time-grid warping, it matches CFG in 24 of 25 (N,s) configurations with a 1.93× speedup at N=25 on DiT-XL/2, ahead of a matched scale-conditioned opaque student. Because the same decomposition supports post-hoc scale control, per-step diagnostics, and error-aware stabilization, the results suggest that guidance efficiency and interpretability need not compete.

Limitations. Our main evaluation covers two DiT backbones on class-conditional ImageNet 256×256, text conditioning is covered only by a single-setting Stable Diffusion 2.1 pilot, and video and higher resolutions remain untested. Modulation hyperparameters were selected on the headline configurations, although the 20 untuned ones show the same pattern (Appendix C), and above sₜₕᵣₑₛₕ they make CtrlFlow match CFG quality rather than reproduce CFG samples. Decomposition fidelity rests on cosine similarity, component swaps, and localization scores, while Proposition 1 assumes realizability and global zero loss, so finite-sample recovery remains empirical.

Broader Impacts. The interface provides per-step inspection that could support content-safety pipelines, but making guided generation cheaper inherits the risks of the underlying technology, including deepfake misuse. Guidance-aware safety mechanisms monitoring decomposition signals deserve dedicated investigation.
