（参考文献见原文。）

Appendices

Appendix A Extended Related Work

This appendix provides additional detail on the related work summarized in Section 2.

Classifier-Free Guidance.

[Dhariwal and Nichol [2021]] introduced classifier guidance, which steers sampling toward higher-fidelity outputs by injecting gradients from a separately trained classifier at the cost of reduced sample diversity. CFG [Ho and Salimans, 2021] removed the need for an external classifier by interpolating between conditional and unconditional score estimates. CFG++ [Chung et al., 2025] recasts guidance as manifold-constrained optimization and shows that standard CFG displaces samples from the learned data manifold when the guidance scale grows large.

Single-Pass Methods.

Plug-and-Play Diffusion Distillation [Hsiao et al., 2024] trains a lightweight external guide at 1% of the base model’s parameter count, keeping the base frozen and cutting CFG cost by roughly half. Building on this idea, AGD [Jensen and Sadat, 2025] distills CFG into low-rank adapters on a frozen backbone and gives the adapter the guidance scale as an extra input, sampled over a range during training, so one checkpoint supports post-hoc scale changes. Its output is still a single opaque guided velocity. Guidance-Free Training [Chen et al., 2025a] reaches a similar one-model interface by fine-tuning the full backbone with a temperature input that sets the guidance strength. Because the strength enters as an input in both methods, each forward pass returns one guided prediction at one strength, and recovering the guidance direction or a second strength costs further forward passes. GFT’s temperature also covers only non-negative scales. CtrlFlow instead applies the scale after the forward pass, and Appendix D.16 compares the two directly. GFT generalizes Condition Contrastive Alignment [Chen et al., 2025b], which fine-tunes autoregressive visual models to sample without guidance, and guidance-free training has since been adopted downstream, for example in the CFG-free reinforcement-learning pipeline of DiffusionNFT [Zheng et al., 2026]. The guidance-free methods we are aware of keep GFT’s input-side interface and return one opaque output per pass, so none of them exposes the base flow and guidance direction separately. Model Guidance [Tang et al., 2025] sidesteps CFG altogether by folding the posterior probability of conditions directly into the training loss. Entropy Rectifying Guidance [Ifriqi et al., 2025] substitutes attention-based energy signals for the unconditional prediction. Independent Condition Guidance [Sadat et al., 2025b] conditions on an independent signal instead of an unconditional one, which removes the need for unconditional training yet still requires two forward passes.

Two-Pass Improvements.

APG [Sadat et al., 2025a] decomposes the guidance update into parallel and orthogonal components relative to the conditional prediction. It selectively down-weights the parallel component to suppress oversaturation artifacts. CFG-Zero* [Fan et al., 2025] refines initialization and rescaling specifically for flow matching models. Autoguidance [Karras et al., 2024] swaps the unconditional model for a separately trained, lower-capacity network, incurring additional storage and training cost. Dynamic Negative Guidance [Koulischer et al., 2024] ties the guidance scale to the posterior probability at each state. Guidance thereby fades in regions where it offers no measurable benefit.

Distillation and Step Reduction.

Progressive distillation [Salimans and Ho, 2022] repeatedly halves the number of sampling steps. [Meng et al. [2023]] extended this approach to CFG-guided models, reaching 1 to 4 step generation. Their scale-conditioned student can adjust s freely at inference time. Consistency models [Song et al., 2023] learn direct mappings from noise to data in a single pass. Latent consistency models [Luo et al., 2024] bring this paradigm into the latent diffusion setting. [Golnari [2023]] explored combining LoRA with guidance distillation. Each of these methods treats the guided velocity field as an opaque regression target.

Guidance and Sampling Schedules.

[Kynkäänniemi et al. [2024]] showed that guidance degrades quality at high noise levels and adds nothing near convergence. Only a middle noise interval benefits from guidance, and restricting it to that window improved ImageNet-512 FID from 1.81 to 1.40. [Malarz et al. [2025]] generalized this finding with beta-distribution-shaped schedule curves. Both approaches rely on fixed schedules that do not vary with s. DPM-Solver [Lu et al., 2022] leverages the semi-linear ODE structure of diffusion models for efficient high-order numerical solving. [Sabour et al. [2024]] demonstrated that optimizing the timestep schedule itself yields substantial gains in few-step regimes. [Chen et al. [2024]] proposed gradient-based optimization of discretization points for similar improvements. All of these methods assume a fixed guidance configuration and do not adapt their behavior to the guidance scale s. Taken together, prior work either preserves CFG’s interface at two-pass cost or reduces the pass count by treating the guided velocity as opaque. CtrlFlow targets the remaining intersection by preserving the interface in a single pass and adapting its use across scale and time.

Appendix B Theoretical Analysis

This appendix collects the formal analyses that justify the optimization and control structure of CtrlFlow. Section B.1 analyzes capacity allocation under the unified loss. Section B.2 formalizes the error amplification mechanism and derives bounds for the modulation mechanisms. Section B.3 proves the formal properties of the time-grid warping.

Scope.

The analyses in Sections B.1 through B.3 do not prove finite-sample convergence, global optimization of LoRA adapters, or optimality of the specific modulation hyperparameters. The identifiability result (Proposition 1) assumes realizability and global zero loss. The capacity-allocation ratio relies on a Jacobian-comparability condition, which we measure rather than assume (Section B.1), and the modulation analysis separates the estimation error that modulation suppresses from the bias that it deliberately introduces (Section B.2.5). Empirical ablations in Section 4 validate the actual training and inference setting.

B.1 Capacity Allocation Analysis

This section analyzes the capacity misallocation under the naive dual-loss (Section 3.3) and shows that the unified distillation objective resolves it. All gradients are with respect to the trainable adapter parameters only, as the backbone is frozen throughout.

B.1.1 Setup and Notation

The pretrained backbone is frozen and produces shared features h_base(xₜ,c,t). Let θ=(A₀,B₀,A_g,B_g) denote the trainable LoRA adapter parameters. The base-flow adapter computes v̂₀=f₀(h_base;A₀,B₀), while the guidance adapter computes ĝ=f_g(h_base;A_g,B_g). The teacher provides targets v₀^* and g^* from two forward passes of the frozen CFG model. We write the per-sample errors as δ₀\triangleqv̂₀-v₀^* and δ_g\triangleqĝ-g^*.

Because the backbone is frozen, h_base is a fixed input to both adapters for any given sample. The two adapter parameter sets (A₀,B₀) and (A_g,B_g) are disjoint. Gradients with respect to one adapter’s parameters do not directly affect the other. The interaction arises indirectly, since both adapters operate on the same frozen features and must represent their respective targets within the same feature space under a shared rank constraint.

B.1.2 Objective Mismatch under the Naive Loss

Claim 1(Capacity misallocation under Lₙₐᵢᵥₑ).

Consider the naive dual-loss Lₙₐᵢᵥₑ=∥δ₀∥²+∥δ_g∥². Because the backbone is frozen, the gradient decomposes into two independent adapter updates,

∇_θ₀Lₙₐᵢᵥₑ=2 δ₀^⊤∇_θ₀v̂₀, ∇_θ_gLₙₐᵢᵥₑ=2 δ_g^⊤∇_θ_gĝ,

(8)

where θ₀=(A₀,B₀) and θ_g=(A_g,B_g). Each adapter receives equal implicit priority. The loss weights both ∥δ₀∥² and ∥δ_g∥² by 1. At inference, however, the composed output is v̂₀+s ĝ. An error δ_g in the guidance component contributes s δ_g to the composed error, while δ₀ contributes only δ₀. The naive loss ignores this asymmetry. Because the adapters have fixed ranks, the loss cannot move parameters between branches. Instead, it determines which residual errors receive stronger gradient pressure within the fixed dual-adapter budget. Equal weighting provides no mechanism to direct that pressure toward the component whose errors matter s times more at inference.

Discussion. The preceding claim is a training-pressure argument, not a gradient-conflict argument in the classical multi-task sense [Yu et al., 2020]. Because the backbone is frozen and the two adapter parameter sets are disjoint, gradients do not directly interfere. The mismatch arises because the naive loss weights both adapter errors equally, whereas inference amplifies guidance errors by s. Within the fixed dual-adapter budget, the naive loss provides no signal to direct gradient pressure toward the component that matters more at inference.

B.1.3 Unified Loss Resolves the Mismatch

Claim 2(Unified gradient as a coherent update).

Under the unified loss L=∥v̂₀+s ĝ-v_cfgᵗᵉᵃᶜʰᵉʳ∥², the gradients with respect to the adapter parameters are

∇_θ₀L=2 δ_comp^⊤∇_θ₀v̂₀, ∇_θ_gL=2s δ_comp^⊤∇_θ_gĝ,

(9)

where δ_comp=v̂₀+s ĝ-v_cfgᵗᵉᵃᶜʰᵉʳ is the composed error. Both adapters are driven by the same error signal δ_comp. The guidance adapter’s gradient carries an additional factor of s, so its updates are scaled in proportion to the downstream impact of guidance errors. There is no decomposition into independently weighted objectives and hence no mismatch between training priority and inference importance.

Proof sketch. Differentiating L with respect to θ_g produces the chain-rule factor ∇_θ_g(s ĝ)=s ∇_θ_gĝ. The factor s appears because the loss directly penalizes the composed output in which ĝ is scaled by s. Differentiating with respect to θ₀ yields no such factor, since v̂₀ enters the composed output with unit weight.

B.1.4 Scale-Dependent Capacity Allocation

Claim 3(s² squared-gradient weighting).

Let J₀\triangleq∇_θ₀v̂₀ and J_g\triangleq∇_θ_gĝ denote the adapter Jacobians. Under the unified loss, the squared gradient norms for each adapter satisfy

∥∇_θ₀L∥²=4 ∥δ_comp^⊤J₀∥², ∥∇_θ_gL∥²=4s² ∥δ_comp^⊤J_g∥²,

(10)

so their ratio is exactly

(∥∇_θ_gL∥²)/(∥∇_θ₀L∥²)=s²·(∥δ_comp^⊤J_g∥²)/(∥δ_comp^⊤J₀∥²).

(11)

When the two Jacobians respond comparably to the shared composed error, ∥δ_comp^⊤J_g∥≈∥δ_comp^⊤J₀∥, the squared-gradient ratio is ≈s², which corresponds to a gradient-magnitude ratio of ≈s. At s=1, both adapters receive comparable gradient signal. At s=8, the guidance adapter’s squared gradient norm is ideally s²=64 times that of the base adapter (52.7 as measured below), a gradient magnitude roughly 7 to 8 times larger, which increases training pressure on the component whose errors are amplified most at inference.

Proof sketch and empirical check. The s² factor follows from squaring the chain-rule factor s in ∇_θ_gL, so Equation 11 holds without assumptions. The comparability condition is not implied by equal rank alone, because the two adapters map the same composed error through different learned weights, so we measure it rather than assume it. On matched training states, the measured squared-gradient ratio is 4.3, 15.1, and 52.7 at s=2, 4, and 8, against s²=4, 16, and 64. The Jacobian ratio in Equation 11 therefore stays between 0.82 and 1.08 across the training range, and the s² approximation holds to within 18%.

This s² weighting is the formal mechanism behind the claim in Section 3.3 that the chain-rule factor s scales the guidance-adapter gradient. Unlike gradient surgery approaches [Yu et al., 2020] that project conflicting task gradients post-hoc, the unified loss produces a coherent training signal. It allocates training pressure proportional to the downstream impact of each component’s error.

Scope of this analysis. The s² weighting shows that the unified loss aligns training pressure with inference-time error importance. Whether the learned decomposition uniquely recovers the teacher’s v₀ and g is a separate question. Proposition 1 below addresses it under a realizability assumption, and Section 4.4 validates it empirically.

B.1.5 Decomposition Identifiability under Scale Variation

The preceding analysis shows that the unified loss allocates training pressure proportionally to inference-time importance. A separate question is whether the loss has a unique minimizer that recovers the true decomposition. The following proposition shows that it does, provided the training distribution includes variation in s.

Proposition 1(Identifiability under scale variation).

Let F₀ and F_g be function classes for the base and guidance adapters. Suppose:

  • (i)

    For almost every input (xₜ,c,t), the training distribution of s given that input has support containing at least two distinct values s₁≠s₂.

  • (ii)

    There exist f₀^*∈F₀ and f_g^*∈F_g such that v_cfg(xₜ,c,t,s)=f₀^*(h)+s·f_g^*(h) for all (xₜ,c,t,s).

    • Then the global minimizer of L=𝔼ₛ [∥f₀(h)+s·f_g(h)-v_cfg∥²] is unique: f₀=f₀^* and f_g=f_g^*.

    Proof.

    At the global minimum, L=0. For any sample (xₜ,c,t), define δ₀=f₀(h)-f₀^*(h) and δ_g=f_g(h)-f_g^*(h). The residual r(s)=δ₀+s·δ_g must equal zero for all s in the support. Evaluating at s₁ and s₂:

    δ₀+s₁·δ_g=0,(12)
    δ₀+s₂·δ_g=0.(13)

    Subtracting yields (s₁-s₂)·δ_g=0. Since s₁≠s₂, we have δ_g=0, and substituting back gives δ₀=0. ∎

    Interpretation. Condition (i) must hold for each input, not only over the whole training set, since a schedule that paired each input with a single scale would leave the split undetermined input by input. Phases 2 and 3 of the curriculum satisfy it because they sample s from a continuous distribution independently of (xₜ,c,t). Condition (ii) is the realizability assumption, requiring that the adapter function classes be expressive enough to represent the true components. In practice, low-rank adapters provide an approximation, and the decomposition is correspondingly approximate. The proposition shows that the unified loss has the correct inductive bias: when the true components are representable and the training distribution includes scale variation, the global minimizer recovers the teacher decomposition. In finite-capacity LoRA adapters, this result should be read as an inductive-bias argument rather than a convergence guarantee. The decomposition is correspondingly approximate, and Section 4.4 validates it empirically.

    This result also explains why Phase 1 (fixed s=s_target) cannot identify the decomposition. At a single scale, the loss constrains only the sum f₀(h)+s_target·f_g(h), leaving infinitely many valid (f₀,f_g) pairs. Scale variation in Phases 2 and 3 breaks this degeneracy.

    B.2 Error Amplification Analysis

    This section formalizes the error amplification mechanism described in Section 3.4 and derives bounds that justify the three modulation mechanisms. It then states the exact decomposition of the modulated output against the CFG velocity, which separates the estimation error that modulation suppresses from the bias that it deliberately introduces (Section B.2.5).

    B.2.1 Error Model

    Let v₀ and g denote the true (teacher-generated) base velocity and guidance direction. The student produces approximations v̂₀=v₀+ε₀ and ĝ=g+ε_g, where ε₀ and ε_g are the prediction errors at timestep t. The true guided velocity is v^*=v₀+s·g, and the student’s approximation is v̂=v̂₀+s·ĝ.

    B.2.2 Per-Step Error Bound

    Proposition 2(Per-step velocity error).

    The velocity error at any timestep t satisfies

    ∥v̂(t)-v^*(t)∥=∥ε₀(t)+s·ε_g(t)∥≤∥ε₀(t)∥+s ∥ε_g(t)∥.

    		(14)

    Proof.

    Direct computation: v̂-v^*=(v₀+ε₀+s(g+ε_g))-(v₀+sg)=ε₀+s ε_g. The bound follows from the triangle inequality. ∎

    At s=1, both error terms contribute equally. At s=8, the guidance-error contribution is amplified by a factor of 8 while the base error remains at unit weight. When guidance error dominates the base-error term, the total trajectory error approaches an 8× increase over the s=1 case. This asymmetry is the fundamental source of quality degradation at high guidance scales.

    B.2.3 Trajectory Error Accumulation

    Proposition 3(Trajectory error over N steps).

    Consider an Euler discretization of the ODE dx/dt=v(x,t) with uniform step size h=1/N. Let xₙ and x̂ₙ denote the true and approximate trajectories at step n. If the velocity field is Lipschitz with constant L and the per-step velocity error is bounded by ∥v̂(tₙ)-v^*(tₙ)∥≤E(s) for all n, then

    ∥x̂_N-x_N∥≤E(s)/L(e^L-1),

    		(15)

    where E(s)≤ε̄₀+s ε̄_g with ε̄₀=\maxₜ∥ε₀(t)∥ and ε̄_g=\maxₜ∥ε_g(t)∥.

    Proof.

    The trajectory bound is a standard result from ODE perturbation theory (Gronwall’s inequality). At step n+1:

    x̂ₙ₊₁-xₙ₊₁=(x̂ₙ-xₙ)+h(v̂(x̂ₙ,tₙ)-v^*(xₙ,tₙ)).

    		(16)

    By the Lipschitz condition and the triangle inequality:

    ∥x̂ₙ₊₁-xₙ₊₁∥≤(1+hL)∥x̂ₙ-xₙ∥+h E(s).

    		(17)

    Applying the discrete Gronwall inequality over N steps with h=1/N yields the bound. ∎

    The trajectory error scales linearly with E(s)=O(ε̄₀+s ε̄_g). When guidance error dominates (ε̄_g≫ε̄₀), the trajectory error at s=8 approaches 8× the error at s=1.

    B.2.4 How Each Modulation Mechanism Reduces Amplification

    Let γ\triangleqw(t) α(s) φ(a)∈(0,1] denote the combined modulation factor, with γ=1 meaning no modulation. The bounds in this subsection compare the modulated student with the equally modulated teacher field v₀+sγ g. They therefore measure how much amplified estimation error each mechanism removes. The price of modulation, a shift of that target away from the CFG velocity v^*, is analyzed in Section B.2.5.

    Temporal Modulation w(t).

    Replacing s with s·w(t) in the guided velocity bounds the effective per-step error by ∥ε₀(t)∥+s·w(t)·∥ε_g(t)∥. Since w(t)≈0 at trajectory endpoints (where ∥ε_g∥ is empirically largest due to high noise or near-convergence), the peak velocity error is reduced. The trajectory bound becomes

    E_w(s)≤ε̄₀+s·\maxₜ [w(t)·∥ε_g(t)∥]≤ε̄₀+s·ε̄_gᵐⁱᵈ,

    		(18)

    where ε̄_gᵐⁱᵈ≤ε̄_g is the maximum guidance error in the mid-timestep window where w(t) is non-negligible.

    Scale Dampening α(s).

    Replacing s with s·α(s) caps the effective amplification at s·α(s)sₜₕᵣₑₛₕ. The dampened scale yields a global reduction, giving E_α(s)≤ε̄₀+s·α(s)·ε̄_g.

    Alignment Gating φ(a).

    The alignment a=\cos(v₀,g) is empirically associated with guidance prediction error in our diagnostics: misaligned steps (a<0) tend to coincide with larger prediction errors, likely because the guidance direction opposes the base flow and creates a harder prediction target. Applying φ(a)<1 at these high-error timesteps reduces the effective error to s·φ(a)·∥ε_g(t)∥. The modulation ablation (Table 14) confirms that the gate improves FID, providing indirect evidence for the correlation. Unlike w(t) (which operates in the time domain) and α(s) (which operates in the scale domain), φ(a) operates in the geometric domain and adapts per-sample and per-timestep based on the actual velocity-field geometry.

    Composed Modulation.

    Under full modulation, the student outputs v̂ₒᵤₜ=v̂₀+sγ ĝ, and its estimation error against the modulated teacher field satisfies

    ∥v̂ₒᵤₜ(t)-(v₀+sγ g)(t)∥≤∥ε₀(t)∥+s·w(t)·α(s)·φ(a(t))·∥ε_g(t)∥.

    		(19)

    Each factor reduces a different component of the error. Specifically, w(t) suppresses temporal endpoints, α(s) caps the global scale, and φ(a) targets the geometric regime where errors are largest. Because they operate on orthogonal dimensions (time, scale, geometry), their composition is multiplicative, and no single mechanism can substitute for the others. This analysis is consistent with the ablation results in Table 14, which show that every pair of mechanisms outperforms both of its components and the full trio achieves the lowest error.

    B.2.5 Bias-Error Trade-off and Two-Regime Design

    Equation 19 measures error against the modulated target, but the samples are ultimately judged against what CFG would produce. The following decomposition makes the gap between the two explicit.

    Proposition 4(Exact decomposition against the CFG velocity).

    With v̂ₒᵤₜ=v̂₀+sγ ĝ and v^*=v₀+s g,

    v̂ₒᵤₜ-v^*=ε₀+sγ ε_g (estimation error)+s(γ-1) g (modulation bias), ∥v̂ₒᵤₜ-v^*∥≤∥ε₀∥+sγ ∥ε_g∥+s(1-γ) ∥g∥.

    		(20)

    Proof.

    Substituting v̂₀=v₀+ε₀ and ĝ=g+ε_g gives v̂ₒᵤₜ-v^*=ε₀+sγ ε_g+s(γ-1) g. Since γ∈(0,1], |γ-1|=1-γ, and the bound follows from the triangle inequality. The identity holds for any value of γ, including the one computed from the student’s own alignment â=\cos(v̂₀,ĝ) at inference. ∎

    Interpretation.

    The first two terms are the estimation error, which modulation reduces by shrinking the coefficient on ε_g from s to sγ. The third term is a bias, because the output now follows v₀+sγ g rather than the CFG velocity. The bias is not small at high scale. At s=8 and the window center, where w=φ=1, dampening alone gives γ=α(8)=0.7 and a bias of 2.4 ∥g∥. Modulation therefore pays off only if CFG’s own high-scale dynamics are worth leaving, which is an empirical question.

    Two Regimes.

    The design separates two regimes at sₜₕᵣₑₛₕ=4. At or below the threshold, α(s)=1 and λ(s)=0, the temporal window is broad, and φ(a)=1 whenever a≥0, so modulation is mild and CtrlFlow tracks CFG closely (3.07 versus 2.97 at (25,2)). Above the threshold, the target departs from CFG deliberately, and three measurements support this choice.

  • •

    Zero-error control. Exact two-pass CFG has ε₀=ε_g=0, so any change it shows under modulation comes from the bias term alone. Applying wα alone lowers its FID from 53.84 to 46.02 at (4,8) and from 21.47 to 17.89 at (25,8), and adding warping, which changes only the discretization, lowers it further to 42.31 and 17.42 (Table 17).

  • •

    Component swap. The unmodulated pipeline gives 21.47 FID at (25,8) with exact teacher components and 21.74 to 22.31 when one of them is replaced by the learned one, whereas CtrlFlow-Full reaches 19.28 (Table 4), so the gain cannot come from a closer CFG approximation.

  • •

    Relative size. On matched states at s=8, the integrated bias ∫s(1-γ) ∥g∥ dt exceeds the integrated amplified error ∫sγ ∥ε_g∥ dt by about 3.2×, so the dominant effect of modulation at high scale is a deliberate shift of the target.

    • Time-grid warping does not enter Equation 20, since it changes where the solver evaluates the field rather than the field itself (Section B.3). Because the high-scale target is intentionally not CFG, the CFG-Match criterion of Section 4.1 counts improvements over CFG as matches, which makes it one-sided.

    B.3 Time-Warp Properties

    This section proves the formal properties of the time-grid warping mechanism (Section 3.5) and discusses its relationship to discretization error.

    B.3.1 Monotonicity and Endpoint Preservation

    Proposition 5(Well-definedness of τ).

    Let ω :[0,1]→ℝ_>0 be a continuous, strictly positive function. Define

    τ(t)=(∫₀ᵗω(u) du)/(∫₀¹ω(u) du).

    		(21)

    Then τ is a valid time-warping function. It is strictly monotonically increasing, continuously differentiable, and satisfies τ(0)=0 and τ(1)=1.

item.title: 先「去光」再「打光」：FlashRelight 两阶段做动态人像视频重打光，时序还稳 ｜ FlashRelight: Portrait Video Relighting with Dynamic Lighting
item.description:
一句话：动态光照下方向/强度/颜色都在变，直接重打光最容易闪；先把源光照抹掉再合成。

要点：

  • 任务与难点：人像视频重打光要在保持真实感与时间稳定的前提下改变照明，而动态光照（方向、强度、颜色随时间变化）让这件事尤其难
  • FlashRelight 是两阶段框架：先用 delighting 抑制源视频里的光照，再在去光后的素材上合成目标动态光照
  • 两段式的好处是把「去除旧光照」与「添加新光照」解耦，减少相互干扰导致的闪烁与伪影

为什么值得看：虚拟人、数字主播与影视后期都会遇到「同一段表演换一个光照环境」。把重打光拆成去光与打光两步，是可落地、也容易接到现有管线的工程做法。

中文摘要：人像视频重打光的目标是在保持照片级真实感与时间稳定性的前提下改变照明；当光照是动态的（方向、强度、颜色随时间变化）时，任务难度显著上升。FlashRelight 提出一个两阶段框架：第一阶段先做 delighting，抑制源视频携带的光照；第二阶段在去光后的素材上合成目标动态光照。把「去掉旧光照」与「加上新光照」解耦，可以避免两个目标互相干扰所导致的闪烁与伪影。对虚拟人、数字主播与影视后期这类需要「同一段表演换光照环境」的场景，这种拆法更容易接进现有管线。

主题：AI Rendering

FlashRelight: Portrait Video Relighting
with Dynamic Lighting

Abstract

Portrait video relighting aims to modify the illumination of a portrait video while preserving photorealism and temporal stability. The task becomes particularly challenging under dynamic lighting, where illumination direction, intensity, and color vary over time. To tackle this problem, we introduce FlashRelight, a novel two-stage framework for dynamic portrait video relighting. FlashRelight first suppresses the source illumination through delighting, and then synthesizes the target dynamic lighting on an illumination-neutral portrait video. FlashRelight supports three complementary control modalities: envmap sequences for explicit frame-level lighting control, dynamic lighting text for semantic illumination editing, and lighting reference videos for visual lighting transfer. Training follows a low-cost hybrid strategy that combines static one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos, covering both controlled illumination variation and realistic portrait motion. Extensive experiments show that FlashRelight achieves temporally coherent and photorealistic dynamic relighting while enabling flexible cross-video lighting transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/vivoCameraResearch/FlashRelight.

1 Introduction

Dynamic lighting is one of the most expressive tools in visual storytelling, shaping the mood, style, and visual impact of portrait videos. Effects such as strobing flashes, drifting shadows, moving highlights, and rapid illumination transitions are widely used in professional production, yet remain difficult to create without specialized equipment or extensive post-processing. Portrait video relighting offers a computational alternative by modifying the illumination of an existing portrait video while preserving identity, motion, and visual realism.

Existing methods have made notable progress in portrait video relighting, ranging from real-time approaches [1, 2, 3] that process portrait videos frame by frame to video diffusion model-based methods [4, 5] that improve temporal coherence and visual fidelity. However, most prior works focus on static illumination or only mild lighting variations [1, 5, 6]. In real-world videos and practical editing scenarios, lighting may change over time in direction, intensity, color, and spatial distribution, producing complex dynamic effects such as alternating colored lights, localized flicker, moving highlights, and evolving shadows. Dynamic portrait video relighting under complex time-varying illumination therefore remains an important but insufficiently explored problem.

Training such a model requires paired data under dynamic lighting conditions, which is difficult to obtain at scale. Conventional data pipelines rely on dynamic OLAT capture [1] or fully rendered paired data [7, 8]; however, dynamic OLAT requires expensive light-stage setups and scales poorly to unconstrained portrait motion, while rendered data is costly to construct and often suffers from a non-negligible synthetic-to-real domain gap. Static OLAT data is more affordable and provides rich relighting supervision, but it is limited to static portraits and cannot capture the interaction between portrait dynamics and time-varying illumination [9, 10]. Leveraging recent advances in large-scale video generation models [11, 12, 13], we adopt a low-cost hybrid data strategy that combines static OLAT data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos, providing scalable supervision for both controlled illumination variation and realistic portrait motion.

Building on this hybrid data strategy, we propose FlashRelight, a unified framework for portrait video relighting under dynamic lighting conditions. Conceptually, FlashRelight treats dynamic portrait relighting not as frame-wise illumination editing, but as controllable video generation under time-varying lighting conditions. To reduce the ambiguity caused by unknown source illumination, FlashRelight adopts a practical two-stage formulation: a delighting model first suppresses the source lighting to obtain an approximately illumination-neutral portrait video, and a DiT-based relighting model then synthesizes a relit video under the target dynamic illumination by leveraging a pre-trained video generative prior [14, 11]. This design allows the model to preserve portrait identity and motion while generating temporally coherent lighting effects over time.

FlashRelight supports three complementary lighting controls: envmap sequences, dynamic lighting text, and lighting reference videos. Envmap sequences provide explicit frame-level lighting control [15, 16], dynamic lighting text provides a semantic conditioning signal [17], and lighting reference videos provide direct visual guidance for cross-video lighting transfer. These modalities offer different ways to specify target lighting, with envmap sequences and lighting reference videos serving as our primary means of dynamic lighting control.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose a novel method, FlashRelight, for portrait video relighting under dynamic lighting conditions, which produces high-fidelity relit videos while maintaining strong temporal stability.

  • •

    FlashRelight supports multiple lighting control modalities, including envmap sequences, dynamic lighting text, and lighting reference videos. Reference-video conditioning further enables direct lighting transfer across portrait videos.

  • •

    We propose a scalable hybrid supervision strategy that combines static OLAT data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos, enabling scalable training without large-scale dynamic light-stage capture or fully rendered paired datasets.

    • 2 Related Work

    Portrait Video Relighting.

    Portrait relighting has been studied for decades, with light-stage systems capturing OLAT reflectance fields and recombining them to synthesize novel illumination [18]. Follow-up works extend this paradigm to dynamic performances using time-multiplexed illumination [19, 20], reflectance transfer [21], and volumetric capture [22, 23]. Although these methods can produce high-quality relit performances, they require specialized capture systems and per-subject acquisition, limiting their applicability to unconstrained portrait videos.

    Learning-based methods reduce this capture burden by training relighting models from multi-illumination data. Representative image-based approaches achieve realistic portrait relighting with learned light transport [24, 25], explicit 3D priors [6, 26, 27], or diffusion models [28, 29, 8]. However, these methods are primarily designed for still images and often suffer from flickering when applied frame by frame to videos. Video-specific methods improve temporal consistency through consistency modeling [1], 3D-aware representations [2], or relightable avatar reconstruction [30, 31]. Nevertheless, they often rely on simplified lighting assumptions, per-subject reconstruction, or scarce dynamic OLAT data.

    Recent work explores conditional video diffusion for portrait performance relighting. Lux Post Facto trains a video diffusion model for portrait video relighting under a static environment map, showing strong photorealism and temporal stability [5]. Different from prior portrait relighting methods that mainly focus on static or mildly varying illumination, FlashRelight targets dynamic portrait relighting under more complex time-varying illumination, which further supports cross-video lighting transfer.

    Video Diffusion Models.

    Video diffusion models have recently shown strong capability in generating realistic and temporally coherent videos from text or image conditions [32, 33, 34, 11]. Beyond text-to-video synthesis, recent works improve controllability by conditioning generation on signals such as poses [35, 36], image prompts [37], depth maps, and other structural cues [38, 39]. These advances make video diffusion models powerful priors for video editing tasks that require both photorealism and temporal consistency.

    Recent relighting methods also exploit video diffusion priors for temporally coherent lighting editing. DiffusionRenderer studies neural inverse and forward rendering with video diffusion models [16], while Light-A-Video, RelightVid, LightCtrl, and UniLumos study video or unified image-video relighting with diffusion-based models [40, 4, 41, 42]. Similarly, FlashRelight leverages a DiT-based video generative prior for dynamic portrait video relighting, where the target illumination evolves over time and can be specified through multiple lighting controls.

    Lighting Control and Transfer.

    The choice of lighting representation largely determines the controllability and usability of relighting systems. Explicit representations, such as environment maps or HDR lighting, provide physically meaningful control and have been widely used in portrait and video relighting [25, 6, 8, 5, 16, 15]. However, they are difficult for non-expert users to edit directly. Recent diffusion-based methods improve usability with text prompts, background guidance, or structured lighting attributes [43, 17, 42, 44], while reference-driven methods specify the desired illumination through another image or video [45, 40, 4]. These interfaces are intuitive, but most existing methods still focus on a single control form and are primarily designed for static lighting.

    In contrast, portrait video relighting with dynamic lighting requires the target illumination to be time-varying. FlashRelight unifies complementary dynamic lighting controls in one framework: environment-map sequences provide precise frame-level control, dynamic lighting text offers a semantic interface, and lighting reference videos enable cross-video lighting transfer. This unified design supports both explicit dynamic relighting and flexible cross-video lighting transfer within a single portrait video relighting framework.

    3 Method

    3.1 Overview

    FlashRelight formulates dynamic portrait video relighting as a conditional video generation problem with a delighting-relighting decomposition [25, 26, 46, 5]. Given a source portrait video V_src, our goal is to generate a relit video that preserves the subject identity, appearance, expression, and motion, while following a target dynamic lighting condition c.

    We denote by Vₐₚₚ the ideal illumination-neutral appearance video of the source portrait. Since Vₐₚₚ is not directly observable, we use a delighting model D to estimate it:

    V_dlt=D(V_src)≈Vₐₚₚ,

    		(1)

    where V_dlt∈ℝ^T×C×H×W serves as a practical appearance carrier with the source illumination suppressed.

    Conditioned on this estimated appearance, relighting is modeled as video generation under the target lighting control:

    Vᵣₗₜ∼p_θ(V|V_dlt,c),

    		(2)

    where the lighting condition c∈{Cₑ,Cₜ,Cᵥ} can be instantiated as an environment-map sequence, dynamic lighting text, or a lighting reference video. This formulation decouples appearance estimation from lighting synthesis, allowing the relighting model to focus on generating the desired illumination dynamics. Built upon a pre-trained DiT-based video generative model [11], FlashRelight further benefits from its spatiotemporal prior for temporally coherent video generation.

    Next, we introduce the two-stage relighting model, followed by our OLAT-Gen hybrid training data.

    3.2 Two-stage Relighting Model

    Delighting Stage.

    The source video V_src∈ℝ^T×C×H×W contains portrait appearance entangled with unknown source illumination. Direct one-stage relighting must implicitly remove the original lighting while synthesizing the target lighting, which is ambiguous under complex or temporally varying illumination. Therefore, the delighting stage estimates V_dlt as an approximation of the ideal appearance video Vₐₚₚ. We do not require V_dlt to be a physically exact intrinsic decomposition; it only needs to provide a stable appearance representation that preserves identity and motion for subsequent relighting. The source-video latent is concatenated with the noisy target latent along the channel dimension to condition the delighting model.

    Relighting Stage.

    As shown in Fig. 3, the relighting model ℝ is built upon a pre-trained DiT-based video generative model [11]. Given the delighted video V_dlt and a target lighting condition c, it generates the relit portrait video:

    Vᵣₗₜ=ℝ(V_dlt,c).

    		(3)

    The latent of the delighted video is concatenated with the noisy target latent along the channel dimension at each denoising step, providing temporally aligned appearance and motion guidance. The lighting condition c provides the target illumination, supporting three control signals. Unlike frame-wise relighting, the model generates the output jointly across space and time, inheriting temporal consistency from the underlying video generative prior.

    Unified Dynamic Lighting Controls.

    As shown in Fig. 3, FlashRelight supports three dynamic lighting controls: envmap sequences, lighting text, and lighting reference videos, offering different trade-offs between precise frame-level control and flexible semantic or reference-based editing.

    Environment-map sequence. Environment-map sequences Cₑ provide the most explicit frame-level lighting control in our framework. Following prior works [16, 15], we encode each HDR environment map Eₜ using three complementary buffers: an LDR panorama Eₜˡᵈʳ∈ℝ^3×H^′×W^′, a log-intensity map Eₜˡᵒᵍ∈ℝ^3×H^′×W^′, and a directional encoding Eₜᵈⁱʳ∈ℝ^3×H^′×W^′. These buffer sequences are passed through the VAE encoder to obtain compact spatiotemporal lighting latents, which are then concatenated and projected into envmap tokens Z.

    To preserve frame-level correspondence, we perform token-level temporal alignment before envmap cross-attention. For video tokens at temporal index t in the latent sequence, attention is computed only with envmap tokens from the same temporal index:

    Attnₑₙᵥ(Xₜ,Zₜ)=Softmax((QₜKₜ^⊤)/(√d))Vₜ,

    		(4)

    where Qₜ is projected from the self-attention features, and Kₜ,Vₜ are projected from the aligned envmap tokens Zₜ.

    Dynamic lighting text. Dynamic lighting text Cₜ provides semantic guidance for dynamic lighting conditions, such as moving lights, color transitions, intensity changes, and flicker. The lighting text is encoded by T5 and injected through text cross-attention. At inference, this branch accepts either a user-provided lighting prompt or a VLM-extracted lighting description from a reference video as the text condition.

    Lighting reference video. A lighting reference video Cᵥ provides visual evidence of the desired illumination dynamics for cross-video lighting transfer. We encode it as a dense spatiotemporal condition and fuse it with the relighting input through channel-wise concatenation at the latent input layer. This enables FlashRelight to perform more fine-grained and direct dynamic lighting transfer.

    3.3 Hybrid Training Data

    As shown in Fig. 2, our Hybrid Dynamic Portrait Video Dataset D_Hybrid combines two complementary data sources: Static OLAT DataD_OLAT and Dynamic Gen DataD_Gen. Static OLAT data provides controlled and fine-grained lighting supervision, while Dynamic Gen Data scales the distribution to moving subjects and temporally varying illumination.

    Static OLAT Data D_OLAT.

    Static OLAT Data is synthesized by linearly combining OLAT basis images with envmap sequences. We collect OLAT basis images from FaceOLAT, an open-source portrait OLAT dataset, using 60 subjects, each with 2–4 expressions. Our lighting set includes 600 synthetic environment-map sequences with diverse lighting dynamics and 200 real environment maps collected from Poly Haven [47]. The real environment maps are further augmented by rotation and temporal transformations to construct dynamic environment-map sequences. This results in 24,000 paired videos in total. Each data pair is denoted as {V_dlt,Vᵣₗₜ,Cₑ,Cᵥ}, where Vᵣₗₜ is the synthetic video under envmap sequence, V_dlt is synthesized under a uniform illumination map and serves as the illumination-neutral target, Cₑ is the envmap sequence, and Cᵥ is the lighting reference video, which is the synthetic video under the same envmap sequence with another subject.

    Dynamic Gen Data D_Gen.

    Dynamic Gen Data is synthesized using Wan2.2 [11] to complement Static OLAT Data with moving subjects and temporally varying illumination. Because the delighting and relighting stages require different supervision, we construct two stage-specific variants, D_Genᵈˡᵗ and D_Genʳˡᵗ, which are detailed below.

    Each relighting pair in D_Genʳˡᵗ is denoted as {V_dlt,Vᵣₗₜ,Cₜ,Cᵥ}, where Vᵣₗₜ is the dynamic-lighting video, V_dlt is its delighted counterpart, Cₜ is the dynamic lighting text, and Cᵥ is the lighting reference video. The text condition Cₜ is built from both VLM-enhanced lighting text and VLM-extracted lighting descriptions using Qwen3.5-27B [48]. To construct the lighting reference condition while reducing content leakage, we obtain Cᵥ from Vᵣₗₜ using strong Gaussian blurring, spatial shifting, and intensity scaling. These operations suppress identity and structural details while preserving low-frequency illumination dynamics. To ensure data quality, we use a VLM-based filter to remove samples with impure backgrounds, incorrect lighting dynamics, or visible light sources. In total, Dynamic Gen Data contains over 10,000 paired videos. Detailed VLM prompts are provided in Appendix C.2.

    Training Data for Delighting Stage.

    As shown in Fig. 4, when training the delighting model, we use paired videos (Vᵣₗₜ,V_dlt) from both D_OLAT and D_Gen, where Vᵣₗₜ is used as the input and V_dlt serves as the ground truth. It is worth noting that, for the delighting stage, V_dlt in D_Gen is directly generated as an illumination-neutral video, while Vᵣₗₜ is obtained by applying hard-coded dynamic lighting transformations to V_dlt, including global brightness alternation, moving bright or dark patterns, and local intensity variations.

    Training Data for Relighting Stage.

    In contrast, during the training of the relighting model, V_dlt is used as the input and Vᵣₗₜ serves as the ground truth. For D_Gen, Vᵣₗₜ is directly generated, while V_dlt is obtained by applying the trained delighting model to Vᵣₗₜ. Each relighting sample is trained with one active lighting condition selected from the available controls, while inactive branches are masked. For D_OLAT, the available controls include Cₑ and Cᵥ; for D_Genʳˡᵗ, they include Cₜ and Cᵥ.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate FlashRelight as a unified framework for dynamic portrait video relighting. Our experiments are organized around the three lighting conditions: envmap-sequence-based relighting, lighting-text-based relighting, and lighting-reference-video-based relighting.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    For quantitative evaluation of envmap-sequence-based relighting, we use the D_OLAT test set, which contains 10 subjects and 16 envmap sequences that are not included in the training set. For evaluating lighting-text-based relighting and lighting-reference-video-based relighting, we reserve 50 generated videos and collect 50 in-the-wild portrait videos from Pexels [49]. None of these videos is used for training or fine-tuning FlashRelight.

    Baselines.

    Our evaluation focuses on three tasks: envmap-sequence-based relighting, lighting-text-based relighting, and lighting-reference-video-based relighting. For envmap-sequence-based relighting, we use Lite2Relight [27], Real-time 3D-aware Portrait Video Relighting [2], denoted as Relighting-Cai, and DiffusionRenderer [16] as baselines. For lighting-text-based relighting, we compare with IC-Light [43], Light-A-Video [40], and Light-X [50]. Implementation details can be found in the Appendix B.3.

    Metrics.

    Following previous works [5, 50], we evaluate paired envmap-sequence relighting using LE, LPIPS, ID similarity, tLPIPS, and PSNR. For lighting-text-based relighting, we use FID for overall visual quality, ID similarity for identity preservation, and tLPIPS for temporal stability.

    Implementation Details.

    FlashRelight (including the delighting and relighting models) is built on Wan2.1-1.3B [11]. We train the relighting model on 49-frame videos at a resolution of 832×480 for 40,000 steps using a three-stage training schedule, with a batch size of 8 on 8 H20 GPUs. Similarly, the corresponding delighting model is trained for 30,000 steps with a three-stage training schedule. More training details are provided in the Appendix B.1.

    4.2 Video Relighting Result

    Envmap-sequence-based relighting.

    Fig. 5 shows qualitative comparisons under envmap sequences. Frame-wise Lite2Relight and Relighting-Cai struggle to maintain temporal consistency, leading to flickering illumination and unstable appearance. DiffusionRenderer improves general relighting quality, but still fails to consistently preserve fine-grained temporal lighting evolution. In contrast, FlashRelight closely follows the target envmap sequence while preserving subject identity, motion, and temporally coherent shadows and highlights. Quantitative results in Table 1 further confirm these observations: FlashRelight achieves the best performance across all metrics.

    Lighting-text-based relighting.

    Fig. 6 shows qualitative comparisons for the evaluated dynamic lighting descriptions. In these examples, frame-wise IC-Light exhibits flickering illumination and unstable appearance across frames. Light-A-Video and Light-X leverage video priors, but show residual source-lighting effects and struggle to reproduce some of the target lighting changes. FlashRelight uses the delighting stage to suppress source-lighting effects and then performs text-conditioned dynamic relighting with a DiT-based video model. For the lighting descriptions evaluated here, the qualitative results suggest that FlashRelight better reproduces the illustrated lighting changes while preserving portrait identity and temporal coherence. On this evaluation set, the quantitative results in Table 2 show that FlashRelight achieves the best FID and ID similarity, indicating better visual quality and identity preservation, while maintaining temporal stability comparable to the strongest video-based baseline.

    Lighting-reference-video-based relighting.

    As shown in Fig. 7, FlashRelight supports reference-video-guided portrait relighting. Since paired ground truth is unavailable for this setting, we evaluate reference-video-guided lighting transfer qualitatively. Given another portrait video as the lighting reference, FlashRelight transfers the dynamic illumination patterns from the reference video to the source video while preserving the source identity and motion. Compared with text-based relighting, the lighting reference video provides more direct and fine-grained visual cues, including the temporal evolution of highlights, shadows, color changes, and flickering effects. This enables more detailed dynamic lighting transfer across portrait videos. Additional visual results for delighting, relighting, and cross-domain generalization are provided in the appendix.

    4.3 Ablation on Hybrid Training Data

    We conduct ablation studies to assess the contribution of our hybrid training data design in Sec. 3.3. We compare three variants trained with different data sources: Static OLAT Data only D_OLAT, Dynamic Gen Data only D_Gen, and the full hybrid data D_Hybrid. The reported metrics are computed over the combined evaluation set covering three relighting settings: envmap-sequence-based relighting, lighting-text-based relighting, and lighting-reference-video-based relighting.

    As shown in Fig. 8 and Table 3, training with only D_OLAT benefits from controlled relighting supervision, but struggles with complex portrait motion and diverse dynamic lighting effects. Training with only D_Gen improves motion and illumination diversity, but lacks the physically grounded constraints provided by OLAT data. In contrast, the model trained on the hybrid data D_Hybrid achieves the best overall performance across FID, ID similarity, and tLPIPS. These results validate that controlled OLAT data and generated dynamic data provide complementary supervision for dynamic portrait video relighting.

    5 Conclusion

    We introduce FlashRelight, a unified framework for portrait video relighting under dynamic lighting conditions. The two-stage design first suppresses source illumination with a delighting model, and then leverages a DiT-based relighting model to synthesize relit videos under target lighting conditioned on environment-map sequences, dynamic lighting text, or lighting reference videos. To enable training without costly dynamic OLAT capture or fully rendered paired datasets, we further construct a hybrid dataset that combines controlled static OLAT-based data D_OLAT with scalable generated dynamic-lighting data D_Gen. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance in environment-map-sequence relighting and reference-video-guided lighting transfer, while preserving portrait identity, motion, and temporal coherence. Text-conditioned relighting is also demonstrated for the evaluated lighting descriptions. This work provides a practical step toward flexible and controllable dynamic portrait relighting in real-world videos.

    Appendix – FlashRelight: Portrait Video Relighting with Dynamic Lighting

    Appendix A Supplementary Videos

    We provide additional video demos in the supplementary material.

    Appendix B More Implementation Details

    B.1 Training Setting of FlashRelight

    Both the delighting model and the relighting model are initialized from Wan2.1-1.3B. Unless otherwise specified, the remaining training hyperparameters follow the default setting of Wan2.1-1.3B. During inference, we use 50 sampling steps with a shift value of 5.0.

    Delighting model.

    The delighting model is trained with a three-stage schedule. As shown in Table 4, we first train the model on the static OLAT data D_OLAT for 10,000 steps with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴. We then train it on the dynamic generated data D_Gen for another 10,000 steps with a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵. Finally, we fine-tune the model again on D_OLAT for 10,000 steps with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁵. The global batch size is 8. We use LoRA fine-tuning with rank 16 and alpha 16, applying LoRA to the feed-forward network (FFN), self-attention, and cross-attention layers.

    Relighting model.

    The relighting model is also trained with a three-stage schedule. As shown in Table 5, we first train the model on D_OLAT for 10,000 steps with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴. We then train it on D_Gen for 10,000 steps with a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵. In the final stage, we fine-tune the model on the hybrid data D_Hybrid for 20,000 steps with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁵. The global batch size is 8. We use LoRA fine-tuning with rank 32 and alpha 32, applying LoRA to the FFN, self-attention, and cross-attention layers. In addition, the lighting projector and the newly added envmap cross-attention layers are trained with full-parameter optimization.

    B.2 Inference Cost

    Table 6 reports inference cost on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU for 49-frame clips at 832×480. FlashRelight uses 50 sampling steps per stage, compared with 15 for the evaluated DiffusionRenderer configuration. The FlashRelight timing covers generation calls for one measured clip after a warm-up clip, excluding external preprocessing, visualization, and video saving. Memory is measured as PyTorch peak reserved GPU memory.

    Under these settings, FlashRelight takes 185.9 s with a peak reserved memory of 15.23 GiB.

    B.3 Implementation of Baselines

    All baselines are implemented using their official repositories and recommended inference settings. For a fair comparison, the source videos are represented as 49-frame clips at 832×480 resolution before baseline-specific preprocessing. For videos whose background is not pure black, we first segment the portrait foreground using BiRefNet-Portrait and use the resulting masks for foreground-aware evaluation. When a baseline requires a different input resolution or aspect ratio, we apply the same geometric transformation to the source video, the ground-truth video, and the foreground mask, and map the baseline output back to the evaluation resolution when needed. All quantitative metrics are computed on the foreground regions.

  • •

    Lite2Relight. Lite2Relight only supports 512×512 inputs. We therefore adapt each 832×480 frame to a 512×512 square input and run the method frame by frame. For quantitative evaluation, the ground-truth video and mask video are transformed with the same parameters as the source video, so all metrics are computed in the aligned 512×512 crop.

  • •

    Relighting-Cai. Relighting-Cai is also limited to 512×512 inputs. We use the same square adaptation protocol as Lite2Relight and apply the identical transformation to the ground-truth video and mask video for metric computation. Since this method takes low-order spherical harmonics as the lighting representation, we convert the target environment maps to SH coefficients before inference. The official implementation does not support colored relighting, and we therefore evaluate it under its supported monochromatic relighting setting.

  • •

    DiffusionRenderer. We use the Cosmos-Transfer1-DiffusionRenderer implementation. To match its required input size, we first pad the input frames with black borders and resize them to 1280×704. After relighting, we remove the padded region and resize the result back to 832×480 for visual comparison and quantitative evaluation.

  • •

    IC-Light. We use the official IC-Light implementation and apply it independently to each frame. The resulting frame-wise outputs are assembled back into 49-frame videos for evaluation.

  • •

    Light-A-Video. We use the official Light-A-Video implementation with its default video relighting pipeline.

  • •

    Light-X. Following the official implementation, we adapt each input video to 384×672 by black-border padding and resizing. After relighting, we crop the valid image region and resize the output back to 832×480.

    • Appendix C Details of Data Curation

    C.1 Preprocessing of Static OLAT Data

    Static OLAT Data requires preprocessing of the OLAT observations, including alignment, color correction, and other steps. The detailed procedure can be found in the official FaceOLAT repository [10].

    C.2 VLM Prompt for Dynamic Gen Data Curation

    ¨¨"You are a portrait-video dynamic lighting annotator. "¨ "The input is a portrait video with dynamic lighting. "¨ "Your task is to give one short but correct English description of the visible dynamic lighting on the portrait over time. "¨ "Focus only on the lighting behavior on the face, hair, ears, jawline, chin, and neck. "¨ "Use subject-relative positions such as front, front-left, front-right, left, right, top, and bottom. "¨ "Assume the person faces the camera. "¨ "\n\n"¨ "The most important goal is to correctly describe: "¨ "(1) where the visible light comes from relative to the person, "¨ "(2) whether there are one or multiple light components, "¨ "(3) the color of each light component, and "¨ "(4) whether each light component is stable, flickering, pulsing, alternating, sweeping, or changing color over time. "¨ "\n\n"¨ "Always prioritize light position and flicker behavior. "¨ "If a light is at the subject-front-right, say subject-front-right. "¨ "If a light is at the subject-front-left, say subject-front-left. "¨ "If one side has a stable warm light while another side has a colorful flickering light, describe them separately and clearly. "¨ "Do not merge multiple distinct light components into one vague mixed description. "¨ "If flicker is visible, mention it explicitly. "¨ "If flashing is visible, mention it explicitly. "¨ "If two sides flicker differently, describe both sides separately. "¨ "If a light changes color over time, describe the color change in order. "¨ "\n\n"¨ "The description should be clear, and correct. "¨ "Correctness is more important than detail. "¨ "Output description of the dynamic lighting, with no JSON, no bullet points, and no extra explanation."¨¨SYSTEM_PROMPT = (¨ "You are a portrait-video dynamic-lighting text rewriter. "¨ "Rewrite lighting descriptions into concise, diverse, natural English. "¨ "Only describe the visible lighting behavior on the portrait. "¨ "Preserve the lighting semantics exactly, including temporal change, direction, brightness, color, shadow pattern, and affected facial regions. "¨ "Remove all dataset or capture constraints, such as invisible light source, off-camera source, black background, no objects, or frame/camera comments. Appendix D More Experimental Results

D.1 Additional Results on Delighting

Figure 9: Additional delighting results. The first row shows source videos, and the second row shows the corresponding delighted results.

Fig. 9 shows additional results of the delighting stage.

D.2 Additional Results on Relighting

Figure 10: Additional relighting results. FlashRelight produces temporally coherent relit videos under diverse dynamic lighting conditions.

More relighting results are provided in the supplementary video.

Appendix E Generalization and Robustness

E.1 Cross-Domain Generalization

We present visual results of FlashRelight on generated portrait videos, in-the-wild videos from Pexels, mobile-selfie videos from the Selfies and Videos Dataset (public Hugging Face samples), and digital-human clips extracted from HeyGen demo videos.
Figure 11 shows seven aligned input and relit frames per example, together with the corresponding target environment maps.

Figure 11: Cross-domain relighting: generated portrait videos. Four examples are arranged in two columns and two rows. Each example shows seven aligned input and relit frames at t=1,9,17,25,33,41,49, together with the target environment maps. Target maps are tone-mapped with fixed exposure within each sequence.

Figure 12: Cross-domain relighting (continued): in-the-wild portrait videos. Four examples are arranged in two columns and two rows. Each example shows seven aligned input and relit frames at t=1,9,17,25,33,41,49, together with the target environment maps. Target maps are tone-mapped with fixed exposure within each sequence.

Figure 13: Cross-domain relighting (continued): mobile-selfie portrait videos. Four examples are arranged in two columns and two rows. Each example shows seven aligned input and relit frames at t=1,9,17,25,33,41,49, together with the target environment maps. Target maps are tone-mapped with fixed exposure within each sequence.

Figure 14: Cross-domain relighting (continued): digital-human portrait videos. Four examples are arranged in two columns and two rows. Each example shows seven aligned input and relit frames at t=1,9,17,25,33,41,49, together with the target environment maps. Target maps are tone-mapped with fixed exposure within each sequence.

E.2 Robustness to Dynamic and Extreme Lighting

We present additional visual results under dynamic and extreme illumination, including moving directional light, overhead flicker, lightning-like flashes, TV-like lighting changes, and uplighting.
Figure 15 shows seven aligned input, ground-truth, and relit frames per example, together with the target environment maps.
The paired ground-truth frames are constructed from OLAT captures.

Figure 15: Relighting under dynamic illumination. From left to right and top to bottom, the examples show flickering overhead light, TV-like lighting changes, uplighting, colored moving directional light, lightning-like illumination, and uplighting. Within each example, rows show target environment maps, input frames, paired ground truth (GT), and FlashRelight outputs. Seven aligned frames are shown at t=1,9,17,25,33,41,49, except the bottom-left lightning example, which uses t=1,17,33,42,44,46,49 to capture the flash. Target maps are tone-mapped with fixed exposure within each sequence.

Appendix F Limitations and Future Work

F.1 Limitations

FlashRelight is limited by the accuracy of the intermediate delighting representation.
In particular, inputs with strong projected patterns, fast head motion, facial paint, motion blur, or severe image degradation can make source-light removal ambiguous.
In these cases, the delighting model may suppress not only illumination but also useful appearance cues such as skin tone, facial detail, or motion structure, and these errors can propagate to the relighting stage.
The hybrid data strategy also has finite coverage.
Although it avoids the cost of large-scale dynamic OLAT capture, the resulting training distribution is still shaped by the diversity of the available OLAT subjects, the design of the environment-map sequences, and the quality of the generated dynamic videos.
The current text-conditioned branch is effective for a limited set of lighting descriptions, but does not reliably follow general free-form lighting prompts.
The lighting captions produced by Qwen3.5-27B often do not accurately describe the illumination in the corresponding videos, introducing noise into text–video supervision.
These annotation inaccuracies may contribute to the limited generalization of text-based lighting control.
Finally, our current formulation primarily relights the portrait foreground.
Without explicit background relighting, foreground and background illumination may become inconsistent in unconstrained scenes.
The model can also lose temporal stability or fine shadow detail under severe occlusion and very rapid motion, and its diffusion-based implementation is better suited to offline high-quality editing than real-time use.

F.2 Future Work

One natural extension is to build FlashRelight on stronger video foundation models, such as newer Wan-series models, which may provide better motion priors and more faithful long-range lighting dynamics.
Another important direction is scene-level relighting, where the foreground portrait and background are edited jointly to maintain global illumination consistency.
On the data side, richer lighting programs and more diverse portrait captures could improve data coverage.
A promising direction is to use more capable video-language
models to improve the annotation of lighting attributes and
their temporal evolution.
Rebuilding the text–video training pairs with more accurate
annotations and more diverse lighting descriptions could
improve text-conditioned relighting and its generalization
to free-form lighting prompts.
The robustness of the system could also be improved by explicitly training on blur, occlusion, accessories, extreme expressions, and non-standard facial appearances.
Finally, model distillation, temporal feature caching, and lightweight video diffusion backbones are promising routes toward interactive or real-time portrait relighting while retaining the visual quality of the current offline system.

Appendix G Societal Considerations

FlashRelight targets authorized portrait video editing, where controllable lighting can make post-production and virtual production workflows more accessible.
Since the method can alter how a person and scene are perceived, inappropriate use may obscure the original capture conditions, modify a subject’s appearance without consent, or make edited footage harder to distinguish from an unmodified recording.
We therefore encourage use on consented or properly licensed videos, clear disclosure when relighting has been applied, and provenance support such as metadata, watermarking, or forensic detection tools for public-facing content.
