一句话：辅助损失会改变优化目标、还得和光度拟合配平；改成限制优化空间就绕开了这个问题。

要点：

  • 逆渲染要把外观分解成材质与光照，这本身是病态问题，学到的材质预测能提供有用的先验
  • 现有做法大多把先验作为辅助正则损失加进去，代价是会改变优化目标，还要与光度拟合项做权重平衡
  • 本文提出「先验引导的材质重参数化」：用预测特征之间的关系直接限制优化空间，而不是额外加一项损失

为什么值得看：逆渲染落地时，调损失权重常比建模更费时间。把先验变成参数空间的结构约束，等于把「调参」换成「改坐标」——对做材质扫描转资产的团队是实打实的工程收益。

中文摘要：基于物理的逆渲染要把外观分解成材质与光照，这是一个本质病态的问题，而学习方法预测的材质可以充当有用的先验。现有做法大多把这些先验以辅助正则项的形式加进损失，代价是会改变优化目标本身，还要在光度拟合与先验之间平衡权重。这篇提出「先验引导的材质重参数化」：利用预测特征之间的关系去直接限制优化空间，而不是额外增加损失项。对材质扫描转资产这类工作，这意味着少了一组需要反复调的超参，把调参问题变成坐标选择问题。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-07

本期推送：2026-11-09

Integrating Learned Priors through Prior-Space Reparameterization
for Physically Based Inverse Rendering

Abstract

Physically based inverse rendering decomposes appearance into materials and illumination, an ambiguous problem for which learned material predictions provide useful prior information. Most existing methods incorporate these cues through auxiliary regularization losses, which alter the optimization objective and require balancing their influence against photometric fitting. We propose a prior-guided material reparameterization that uses the predicted feature relationships to restrict the optimization space while leaving the objective unchanged. We fuse multi-view material predictions onto a mesh and construct a permutohedral lattice in the resulting prior feature space. Surface points with similar predictions share material variables, which are optimized jointly with geometry and illumination using a purely photometric objective. Experiments with two learned predictors on three synthetic benchmarks and Stanford-ORB demonstrate improved material decomposition and relighting. Our method improves relighting PSNR by 1.5–2.5 dB over the strongest evaluated mesh-based baseline on Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR-Synthetic, and outperforms a regularization loss using the same prior in controlled comparisons. We further show that our reparameterization pools noisy photometric gradients, producing updates that are more consistent across sampled views. This consistency enables a shortened joint optimization schedule that takes less than a minute while retaining relighting quality above all evaluated baselines on TensoIR-Synthetic.

1 Introduction

Physically based inverse rendering recovers the geometry, materials and illumination of a scene from photographs, enabling relighting, editing and novel-view rendering. The task is inherently ambiguous in that different combinations of materials and illumination can explain the same observations. When materials are optimized independently at each surface point, this ambiguity can cause shadows and highlights to be absorbed into the recovered reflectance.

Learned material predictors provide useful cues for resolving this ambiguity. Although their predictions may contain errors, they often reliably reveal which surfaces have similar materials [41, 19, 25, 39]. Recent inverse rendering methods incorporate these cues through auxiliary losses that anchor materials to predicted values [45], distill a material diffusion model [29], or encourage points with similar predictions to have similar materials [28]. Such regularization losses can help guide the decomposition, but they also alter the objective and shift the resulting solution. The strength of the regularization loss must therefore be balanced against the primary photometric loss, and choosing this balance is itself non-trivial. This motivates an alternative: using learned prior predictions to reduce the degrees of freedom and restrict the optimization space. Specifically, we use relationships between vertices inferred from these predictions to define how material variables are linked, leaving the optimization objective unchanged.

In this work, we propose a prior-guided material reparameterization for physically based inverse rendering. We fuse multi-view material predictions of learned models onto a mesh and construct a permutohedral lattice [1] in the resulting prior feature space. Surface materials are represented by shared lattice variables, coupling points with similar predictions even when they are spatially distant. We optimize the lattice values jointly with geometry and illumination using a purely photometric objective.

Experiments on Synthetic4Relight, TensoIR-Synthetic, DTC-Synthetic and Stanford-ORB demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach with two different learned predictors. With either predictor, our method improves relighting PSNR by 1.5–2.5 dB over the strongest evaluated mesh-based baseline on Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR-Synthetic and achieves competitive results on real captures.

We also analyze individual vertex updates at a single optimization step across controlled baselines that only differ in how the prior is incorporated. Our novel reparameterization significantly removes noise in the individual gradients and produces updates that are more robust and consistent across sampled views. Exploiting this increased consistency, we also demonstrate that the optimization schedule can be greatly compacted. Relighting quality remains above all evaluated baselines on TensoIR-Synthetic, with less than a minute for the joint optimization stage.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A material reparameterization that incorporates learned prior prediction through a prior-space lattice representation without changing the optimization objective.

  • •

    State-of-the-art relighting among mesh-based inverse rendering methods on synthetic benchmarks, with effective transfer to real captures.

  • •

    Substantially faster optimization for inverse rendering with little loss in quality, enabled by the more consistent material updates induced by our reparameterization.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Inverse Rendering

    Inverse rendering separates the intrinsic properties of an object from its illumination, with common approaches falling into two families. Optimization-based methods treat materials and lighting as free variables and fit them to the observations, on meshes [31, 12, 36, 28], on Gaussian primitives [10, 37, 26, 11, 8, 45], or on hybrids of the two [40, 27]. They explicitly fit the input images, but the many material degrees of freedom can allow shadows and highlights to be absorbed into the material. Learning-based methods train a network on large, mostly synthetic datasets to predict materials directly, usually either with image [41, 17, 35, 14, 19] or video diffusion models [25, 13, 32, 42, 9]. There are also approaches that use multi-view transformers such as MVInverse [39], MVID [7], LIRM [23] or LSRM [24]. They are fast and capture the overall structure, but are not guaranteed to be consistent across views or to faithfully reproduce the observed images.

    2.2 Integrating Priors in Inverse Rendering

    Hand-crafted priors, such as total variation, smoothness of the material maps, or a white-light assumption, have long been added to optimization-based inverse rendering pipelines as regularization losses [36, 10, 11, 26, 31, 12]. Recently, learned priors are increasingly injected the same way. DiffReg-PBIR [28] uses only the structure of the G-buffers predicted by DiffusionRenderer [25]: a joint-bilateral regularizer on a permutohedral lattice encourages points with similar predicted materials to have similar optimized materials. PTIR-GS [45] regularizes the optimized material properties by anchoring the optimization to predictions from RGB↔X [41]. MaterialFusion [29] distills a material diffusion model into the optimized albedo and roughness through a score-distillation loss. All of these methods add an auxiliary term to the photometric objective. MaterialClusterGS [43] instead restricts the degrees of freedom, exploiting the fact that a real scene contains few distinct materials, and softly assigns primitives to a fixed-size material palette. Like DiffReg-PBIR, we use similarities in predicted materials. In our method, these similarities define shared variables rather than being incorporated as an auxiliary loss.

    2.3 Preconditioning and Reparameterization

    Poor conditioning of the loss landscape and noisy gradient estimates can slow the convergence of gradient-based optimization. Adaptive coordinate scaling, as in Adam [18], and spatial smoothing, as with Sobolev gradients [33], modify the updates to improve optimization. A linear change of variables can also couple updates without adding a loss [33, 34]. When the map spans the original variable space, it preserves the set of attainable solutions; a lower-rank map additionally constrains the representation.

    In inverse rendering, Large Steps [34] uses a mesh-based change of variables to couple geometry updates and permit larger steps. Chang et al.[5] further improve this smoothing through a spatiotemporal bilateral filter, by combining cross-bilateral spatial filtering with Adam’s temporal averaging to suppress noise while preserving sharp features.

    In computational photography, bilateral-space methods lift pixels into a grid indexed by position and color, operate on its few vertices, and slice the result back to the pixels. Grouping pixels by position and color supports edge-aware processing, while the compact grid makes filtering and global optimization efficient [6, 1, 21, 2]. For example, Barron et al.[3] optimize stereo for synthetic defocus using this idea: disparity maps are smooth within regions of similar color and sharp across their edges, and the optimization can run on a smaller subspace, with far fewer variables using bilateral grids than with pixels. Our method follows the same principle. We use learned material-prior features to define the optimization space, representing surface materials through shared lattice variables in this space.

    3 Preliminaries

    3.1 Linear Reparameterization

    Let x∈ℝⁿ be the variables of an objective L(x), e.g., per-vertex materials. Instead of x, one can optimize latent variables w∈ℝᵏ through a fixed linear map,

    x=x₀+P w,

    		(1)

    with P∈ℝ^n×k and a constant x₀. The chain rule gives ∂L/∂w=P^⊤∂L/∂x, so a gradient descent step of size η on w moves x by

    Δx=-η PP^⊤(∂L)/(∂x).

    		(2)

    The map determines both the representable values, x₀+range(P), and their update coupling, PP^⊤. A full-row-rank map preserves the attainable solutions, whereas a lower-rank map restricts optimization to this affine subspace. Thus a reparameterization can regularize the representation while also reshaping gradient steps, without introducing an auxiliary loss. Large Steps [34] uses P=(I+λL)⁻¹ on a mesh graph, where L is the graph Laplacian, to couple updates over the surface.

    3.2 The Permutohedral Lattice

    The permutohedral lattice [1] is a data structure designed for fast high-dimensional Gaussian filtering for images. It tessellates feature space ℝᵈ with simplices of d+1 vertices, instead of the 2ᵈ corners of a hypercubic bilateral grid. A point with feature p∈ℝᵈ is assigned to a simplex and represented by barycentric weights on its d+1 vertices, which sum to one. Thus n points touch at most (d+1) n lattice vertices. Collecting these weights for all n points gives a sparse matrix S∈ℝ^M×n over the M occupied lattice vertices.

    Splatting a per-point signal g∈ℝⁿ onto the lattice is the product Sg, which accumulates the barycentrically weighted values of all points sharing a lattice vertex. Slicing a lattice signal c∈ℝ^M back to the points is done by S^⊤c, a barycentric interpolation.

    Two lattice vertices are neighbors if they differ by one step along a lattice direction; these connections define the graph used in Sec.4.3.

    4 Method

    Our pipeline (Fig.2) recovers a triangle mesh with PBR materials and an environment map from multi-view images captured under fixed illumination. A setup stage builds the mesh and a fixed prior-space lattice (Secs.4.2 and 4.3). A joint optimization stage then refines geometry, materials and illumination, with vertex materials reparameterized through the lattice (Secs.4.4 and 4.5).

    4.1 Scene Model and Objective

    We represent the scene as a mesh with vertex positions V∈ℝ^N×3, per-vertex material logits Q∈ℝ^N×4, and an environment map E of 64×128 texels. The per-vertex material logits include albedo RGB and roughness, and are decoded to bounded physical values using sigmoid for rendering. Metallic is fixed to zero in our experiments, but its prediction is retained as a prior feature.

    We render the scene at the training cameras using Mitsuba 3 with automatic differentiation [15]. Our photometric objective L(V,Q,E) uses 0.8 L_L1+0.2 (1-SSIM) on the object [38] and sRGB L1 on observed background pixels, which directly supervise environment radiance [36, 28]. No auxiliary prior loss is added.

    4.2 Setup: Mesh and Material Prior

    Mesh.

    We initialize the mesh using the neural surface reconstruction stage of DiffReg-PBIR [28], guided by normals predicted by the prior. From the training-view images, a dense-grid signed distance field (SDF) is optimized and a triangle mesh is extracted using marching cubes. Botsch remeshing [4] is then applied to improve the mesh quality.

    Material Prior and Refinement.

    A learned prior model predicts sRGB albedo, roughness, and metallic values for all training views. These predictions are often blurry and not perfectly consistent with the input image. Fusing predictions from multiple views onto a single mesh can further smooth out fine details. Since our reparameterization couples vertices with similar prior predictions during optimization, inaccurate priors may couple vertices with different underlying materials, leading to suboptimal material estimates. Before mesh fusion, we therefore refine each albedo prediction to better align its details with the corresponding input image.

    To this end, we apply joint trilateral refinement using input RGB, predicted albedo, and spatial proximity [20, 30]. The input RGB guides fine texture boundaries, while predicted-albedo affinity favors samples with similar predicted colors, reducing the mixing of distinct material colors. This produces albedo predictions that better preserve the fine details of the input images. Implementation details are provided in Sec.S8 of the supplement.

    We then fuse the refined albedo, roughness and metallic predictions onto the mesh using viewing-angle weights, yielding the final per-vertex prior feature pᵢ∈[0,1]⁵ for training-visible vertices. Vertices that have never been observed in any training view are optimized separately.

    4.3 Building the Prior-Space Lattice

    We embed the Nₛ training-visible vertices in a permutohedral lattice [1] using their prior features pᵢ with lattice spacing σₚᵣᵢₒᵣ. We set σₚᵣᵢₒᵣ to the median cross-view standard deviation of the prior features over vertices observed in at least two training views. This gives the splat matrix S∈ℝ^M×Nₛ over the M occupied lattice vertices. This relationship between the mesh and lattice vertices remains fixed throughout the optimization process.

    The features contain no position, so coupling depends on predicted material similarity rather than spatial proximity. Identical features share the same interpolation weights, while nearby features can share lattice vertices even if they lie far apart on the surface. On the occupied lattice vertices, we build an undirected graph with unit-weight edges between lattice neighbors. Its Laplacian is L=D-A, normalized by the mean degree d̄ as L̂=L/d̄. The lattice, graph and vertex assignments remain fixed throughout joint optimization, including when the mesh geometry changes.

    4.4 Changing the Variable to Lattice Vertices

    Instead of directly optimizing the per-vertex material-logit values, we can now optimize material-logit offsets stored at the occupied lattice vertices. The material logits Qₛ at training-visible mesh vertices can then be decoded as their initial logits Q₀ plus a weighted sum of these lattice offsets C∈ℝ^M×4:

    Qₛ=Q₀+S^⊤C,

    		(3)

    Here, the initial material logits are identical across vertices, and C is initialized to zero. The slice operator S^⊤ interpolates the lattice offsets back to each mesh vertex using weights determined by its prior feature. This realizes the linear map in Eq.1 with P=S^⊤. Unobserved vertices use free per-vertex offsets, also initialized to zero.

    The lattice representation regularizes materials by sharing variables across points with similar prior predictions. Compared to directly optimizing per-vertex materials, which results in a high-dimensional, ill-posed optimization problem with many degrees of freedom, changing the optimization variables to those at the lattice vertices restricts optimization to a much smaller subspace. Vertices with similar prior predictions must have similar optimized materials. Rather than relying on similar material estimates to emerge from independent per-vertex optimization, we couple vertices with similar prior predictions through shared lattice variables.

    4.5 Material Updates through the Lattice

    Automatic differentiation through the renderer gives the per-vertex gradient G=∂L/∂Qₛ. The splat operator pools these gradients across mesh vertices sharing lattice variables:

    (∂L)/(∂C)=SG.

    		(4)

    We optimize the lattice variables with Adam [18], whose first-moment averaging also attenuates temporal gradient noise. We additionally employ Large Steps preconditioning [34] to smooth updates over neighboring lattice vertices. With L̂ denoting the normalized lattice graph Laplacian, the resulting material update is

    ΔQₛ=-η S^⊤LS (Adam (LS(SG))).

    		(5)

    Here, LS applies the Large Steps preconditioner (I+λL̂)⁻¹ on the lattice graph, and S^⊤ slices the update back to the mesh vertices. More details on the implementation and the effect of Large Steps are provided in Sec.S2 of the supplement.

    Cost.

    Splatting and slicing are sparse matrix products with at most six non-zeros per supported vertex, shared by the optimized attributes. For Large Steps, I+λL̂ is fixed and shared by all material channels. Its factorization is reused where feasible, with sparse conjugate-gradient solves for larger lattices.

    4.6 Geometry and Illumination

    Vertex positions are optimized jointly with materials by Large Steps [34] on the mesh graph with UniformAdam, clipping nonzero per-vertex gradient norms at their 99th percentile. For illumination, we adopt Neural-PBIR’s parameterization [36]: spherical Gaussians followed by a Large Steps environment texture in log-radiance, optimized with Adam. Geometry and illumination are updated jointly with material at every step from the same renderings.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Details

    Datasets.

    We evaluate our method on three synthetic datasets, Synthetic4Relight [44], TensoIR-Synthetic [16] and DTC-Synthetic [28], and a real-world benchmark, Stanford-ORB [22].

    Baselines.

    We primarily compare our approach with mesh-based inverse rendering baselines: Neural-PBIR [36], which does not employ learned priors; MaterialFusion [29], which incorporates learned priors via score distillation; and DiffReg-PBIR [28], which uses learned priors through a joint-bilateral regularization loss.

    Metrics.

    We evaluate novel-view synthesis (NVS) under the captured illumination, relighting under novel illumination, and albedo, roughness and normals where ground truth is available. Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR-Synthetic score all 200 test views using one RGB albedo scale fitted over these views and shared between albedo evaluation and material rescaling for relighting. PSNR uses RGB-mean squared error and is averaged over views.

    Prior and initial mesh.

    For the learned model of Sec.4.2 we use MVInverse [39] and DiffusionRenderer [25], though any per-pixel material predictor could be used. In each configuration the same model also provides the normal maps that guide the surface reconstruction. We run the neural surface reconstruction of DiffReg-PBIR’s second stage [28] for 25k iterations with a normal-loss weight of 10⁻⁶.

    Detailed setup for the joint optimization stage is provided in Sec.S1 of the supplement. Unless stated otherwise, all quantitative results are means of three runs with random seeds. All experiments run on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU.

    5.2 Results on Synthetic Datasets

    Tab.1 summarizes both synthetic benchmarks. Our two prior configurations improve relighting PSNR over the strongest evaluated baseline by 1.47–1.50 dB on Synthetic4Relight and 2.28–2.48 dB on TensoIR-Synthetic. The corresponding albedo PSNR gains are 1.77–1.98 dB and 2.48–2.69 dB, respectively. NVS improves over DiffReg-PBIR by 1.65–1.72 and 5.01–5.12 dB on the two benchmarks, respectively. Fig.3 qualitatively compares novel-view synthesis and relighting.

    Optimization takes 5.9–6.4 minutes per scene, compared with 6.5–7.2 for Neural-PBIR, about 23 for DiffReg-PBIR and two hours for MaterialFusion. Tab.1 also reports total pipeline time; Sec.6.2 evaluates a shortened joint schedule.

    We additionally compare with DiffReg-PBIR on the released seven-scene DTC-Synthetic relighting benchmark, following its public evaluation protocol (Tab.3). Our method improves mean relighting PSNR over DiffReg-PBIR with either prior.

    5.3 Results on Real-World Datasets

    Tab.2 reports the seven scenes of Stanford-ORB’s official light scene split. The advantage in novel-view synthesis carries over to real captures: both configurations of our method achieve a higher HDR PSNR and SSIM than every baseline. Both prior configurations also exceed DiffReg-PBIR in relighting HDR PSNR and SSIM, with DiffusionRenderer giving the strongest results. DiffReg-PBIR retains a higher PSNR on tone-mapped images in both tasks. We examine refinement of the material prior on real data in Sec.6.3.

    6 Analysis

    6.1 Effect of Reparameterization

    To isolate the use of the prior from other architectural choices that differ across baselines, we compare three variants with the same optimization setup (Tab.4): free per-vertex materials without a prior, per-vertex materials with DiffReg-PBIR [28]’s joint-bilateral loss, and our prior-space reparameterization. Compared to the prior-as-a-loss variant, our reparameterization shows better quality on every metric, including NVS, relight, albedo PSNR and roughness for all datasets. This can be attributed to the fact that our parameterization does not alter the overall objective of the optimization.

    We additionally compare adaptations of Large Steps [34] and STAdam [5] in Sec.S3 of the supplement. Large Steps smooths material updates through mesh connectivity, while the STAdam adaptation filters Adam moments using both mesh connectivity and current material values. Although mesh Large Steps achieves higher novel-view PSNR, our prior-space reparameterization yields better relighting and albedo quality than both alternatives.

    We next examine how our reparameterization affects update behavior. Per-vertex updates can vary substantially with the sampled training views and Monte Carlo rendering samples. To measure this variability, we fix the optimization state and compute the update for each of 16 randomly sampled pairs of training views. We separate the energy (squared magnitude) of these updates into a consistent component, which captures the direction that persists across samples, and noise, which captures the variation around that direction. For the prior-loss variant, we further distinguish the photometric and prior-loss contributions to the consistent component. Implementation details are provided in Sec.S1.1 of the supplement.

    As Fig.4 shows, noise accounts for more than 90% of the update energy without a prior. Our reparameterization increases the consistent share from 8% to 54% for albedo and from 2% to 25% for roughness. By sharing variables across vertices with similar prior predictions, it pools their photometric gradients and reduces variability across samples. The prior loss also increases consistency, but most of its consistent energy comes from the added prior term, which accounts for 41% and 75% of the total update energy for albedo and roughness, respectively. Its photometric contribution is smaller than that of the no-prior variant.

    The two uses of the prior therefore stabilize updates differently. The auxiliary loss encourages agreement with the prior’s similarity structure even when this competes with photometric fitting. The prior-space reparameterization instead couples the photometric updates through shared variables. This distinction is consistent with its edge on NVS quality in Tab.4 and motivates the shorter schedule below.

    6.2 Optimization Speedup

    We test a 100-step schedule on TensoIR-Synthetic leveraging the improved update consistency. The albedo, geometry and illumination learning rates decay exponentially from 10× their defaults to 1× and illumination switches from SGs to the environment texture at step 50. We also render two farthest-point views per step with mesh Large Steps λ=5. We apply this schedule to all three MVInverse variants in Tab.4 and to ours with DiffusionRenderer.

    In Tab.5, our update loop takes 34–39 seconds, compared with 5.9–6.4 minutes for the corresponding 1000-step runs and 23.5 minutes for DiffReg-PBIR’s optimization loop. Although relighting differs from the corresponding 1000-step configurations by about -0.70 dB, our 100-step versions still relight better than every evaluated baseline on TensoIR-Synthetic.

    6.3 Effect of Prior Refinement

    We now demonstrate how poor prior predictions, as discussed in Sec.4.2, affect downstream optimization. This issue is particularly apparent in real-world captures containing lettering and fine patterns. Fig.5 shows the effect of prior refinement on Stanford-ORB Curry. Prior refinement restores lettering contrast in the fused albedo, allowing the lattice to better distinguish lettering from the surrounding material. Although refinement enhances local contrast and fine detail, it cannot create contrast from locally constant predictions, and illumination or geometry edges can still misguide selection. Additional examples are provided in Sec.S8 of the supplement.

    6.4 Effect of Subspace Restriction

    Sharing lattice variables restricts the material fields that our method can represent. To quantify the potential loss of albedo detail due to this restriction, we first fuse ground-truth albedo onto the final mesh to obtain a per-vertex oracle. Using our reparameterization, we then solve for the coefficients at the fixed prior-space lattice vertices by least-squares fitting to the oracle vertex albedos. We evaluate both the per-vertex oracle and its lattice approximation using the same albedo protocol as the optimized results. Details and results with both prior models are provided in Sec.S4 of the supplement.

    With MVInverse priors, Tab.6 shows that the lattice oracle is only 1.10 and 0.74 dB below the per-vertex oracle on Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR-Synthetic, respectively. Despite this slight reduction in representational capacity, our optimized albedo PSNR is 3.56 and 2.28 dB higher than that of independent per-vertex optimization, despite the latter’s higher representational ceiling. With DiffusionRenderer priors, our optimized albedo PSNR is likewise 3.17 and 2.35 dB higher on the two datasets, respectively. Our result also comes closer to its own oracle ceiling. Across both prior models, our optimized results still fall 1.94–4.35 dB short of the lattice oracle, leaving substantial room for improvement within the existing representation. These results suggest that subspace restriction is not the dominant bottleneck in albedo recovery on these scenes. Sharing lattice variables instead helps optimization recover more detail than optimizing each vertex independently.

    We also examine the effect of lattice resolution, controlled by spacing, in a controlled 2D texture reconstruction experiment with rapid target-color variation in prior feature space (Sec.S4.1 of the supplement). With sufficient lattice resolution, the restriction introduces little visible degradation in the reconstructed texture.

    7 Conclusion

    We have presented a material reparameterization method that effectively integrates learned priors into optimization-based physically based inverse rendering. A fixed prior-space lattice defines shared material variables, optimized jointly with geometry and illumination from photometric observations. Our representation significantly improves relighting on three synthetic benchmarks and transfers well to real captures. Thanks to our reparameterization, updates are more consistent across sampled views and the joint optimization stage can be shortened to less than a minute while still outperforming all baselines on TensoIR-Synthetic. Our method connects learned material priors with photometric optimization to reconstruct scenes that better explain the input images. We view this as a step toward learned inverse rendering models that achieve such consistency directly in their predictions.

    Acknowledgements

    This work was supported by Institute of Information & communications Technology Planning & Evaluation (IITP) grant funded by the Korea government (MSIT) [NO.RS-2021-II211343, Artificial Intelligence Graduate School Program (Seoul National University)], the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government (MSIT) (No. 2022R1A3B1077720) and the BK21 FOUR program of the Education and Research Program for Future ICT Pioneers, Seoul National University in 2026.

    LLM Usage Statement

    In this work, we used generative AI, including Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, to assist with implementing the methods, executing experiments, and preparing figures and tables presenting the results, under continuous author supervision and interaction. Additionally, we used generative AI to refine the writing of the paper. We have reviewed all AI-generated material and take responsibility for the final content of this work.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    S1 Optimization Setup

    We run 1000 joint steps, each rendering two training views at 800×800 with 32 samples per pixel and a maximum path depth of 4. Materials start from constants (albedo 0.3, roughness 0.6); metallic is fixed to zero and enters only as a prior feature. Variants with learned metallic are evaluated in Sec.S6. The lattice variables and unobserved per-vertex offsets use Adam rates of 0.025 for albedo and 0.075 for roughness. The prior-space Large Steps strength is λ=20. Vertex positions are optimized by Large Steps [34] with λ=19 at a rate of 6×10⁻⁴, and the environment parameters by Adam at a rate of 0.04 with a 10-step warm-up, cosine decay to 2% and gradient-norm clipping at 0.1. Following Neural-PBIR [36], we use 128 spherical Gaussians for the first 250 steps, then switch to a Large Steps environment texture (λ=6). The Gaussians are initialized from the observed background on Synthetic4Relight, DTC-Synthetic and Stanford-ORB, or from a uniform initialization on TensoIR-Synthetic, where the background is unobserved.

    S1.1 Update Consistency Measurement

    We evaluate each variant at its step-100 checkpoint, keeping geometry, materials, illumination and optimizer state fixed. We sample 16 independent pairs of training views, with independent Monte Carlo rendering seeds, and compute the resulting material-logit updates on training-visible vertices. The updates use the checkpoint’s bias-corrected Adam second-moment normalization, without first-moment momentum, to isolate the current gradient variability. The lattice variant retains its material preconditioning and slicing operations. For updates uₖ, let ū be their sample mean and s²=∑ₖ∥uₖ-ū∥²/(K-1) with K=16. We report noise energy s² and consistent energy ∥ū∥²-s²/K, normalized by the total mean update energy. For the prior-loss variant, we separate the photometric and prior-loss contributions through their inner products with the mean combined update, with the same finite-sample covariance correction.

    S2 Material Large Steps Preconditioning

    S2.1 Formulation

    For the lattice values C in Eq.3, we use the Large Steps change of variables [34]

    C=B⁻¹W, B=I+λL̂,

    		(S1)

    where L̂=(D-A)/d̄ is the Laplacian of the unit-weight lattice-neighbor graph, normalized by its mean degree. We initialize W at zero and use λ=20. Since B is symmetric, the gradient in these coordinates is

    (∂L)/(∂W)=B⁻¹SG.

    		(S2)

    Before pooling, we clip the per-vertex material gradient G=∂L/∂Qₛ to limit outliers. Let c be the 99th percentile of the nonzero row norms of G. We define G̃ by replacing each nonzero row gᵢ with g̃ᵢ=gᵢ\min(1,c/∥gᵢ∥), leaving zero rows unchanged. Using this clipped gradient, we update

    W←W-η Adam (B⁻¹SG̃).

    		(S3)

    Slicing ΔC=B⁻¹ΔW back to vertices yields Eq.5. The two solves smooth the pooled gradients and the resulting updates on the prior-space graph. The fixed matrix B is shared by all material channels; its factorization is reused where feasible, with sparse conjugate-gradient solves for larger lattices. Since B is invertible, this preconditioning changes the optimization trajectory without changing the material fields representable by the lattice.

    S2.2 Ablation

    We isolate this preconditioning by comparing λ=0 (B=I) and our default λ=20. Both variants use the same refined predictions and post-refinement spacing σₚᵣᵢₒᵣ, initial scene, optimizer settings and 1000-step joint schedule. We evaluate both MVI-MVI and DR-DR initializations over all 15 scenes, with one seed per scene.

    Tab.S1 reports the effect at a fixed optimization budget. Across the two synthetic datasets and initializations, material Large Steps changes albedo PSNR by +0.19 to +0.83 dB, roughness MAE by -0.022 to -0.005, and novel-view PSNR by -0.22 to -0.05 dB. Relighting changes by +0.03/-0.04 dB with MVI/DR on Synthetic4Relight. Relighting changes by +0.16/-0.07 dB with MVI/DR on TensoIR-Synthetic. On Stanford-ORB the relighting changes are +0.29/+0.07 dB, respectively. We adopt the Large Steps preconditioner mainly for the consistent positive effect on albedo.

    S3 Alternative Material Smoothing

    We compare our prior-space reparameterization with two controls that smooth per-vertex material updates without using a material prior: mesh Large Steps [34] and a mesh adaptation of STAdam [5]. Both controls start from the no-prior variant and retain its uniform material initialization, learning rates, gradient clipping, geometry and illumination settings, and optimization schedule. All variants share the refined MVInverse inputs used to initialize the scene. We evaluate the 1000-step schedule on all 15 scenes and the 100-step schedule on the four TensoIR-Synthetic scenes.

    Large Steps.

    We parameterize the material logits as Q=Q₀+B⁻¹U, where B=I+20Lₘₑₛₕ/d̄ and d̄ is the mean mesh degree. Adam updates U, initialized at zero. This uses the mesh connectivity to smooth material updates, whereas ours pools and smooths updates on the fixed prior-space lattice.

    STAdam.

    We adapt STAdam’s texture optimizer to per-vertex materials by filtering the bias-corrected first and second Adam moments before forming the update. The filter follows mesh edges and is guided by the current albedo RGB or roughness values, with edge weights wᵢⱼ=\exp(-∥mᵢ-mⱼ∥/0.02). Since the original texture-grid filter does not directly apply to a mesh, we replace it with bilateral diffusion, W=(I+20L_w/d̄)⁻¹, where L_w is the weighted mesh Laplacian. The moments are stored unfiltered; the material update uses Wm̂/(√Wv̂+ε). The diffusion systems are solved by Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients with relative tolerance 10⁻⁵. Thus this control evaluates our adaptation of STAdam.

    Results.

    Mesh Large Steps improves on the no-prior variant in novel-view and relighting PSNR on all three datasets at 1000 steps, and achieves the highest novel-view PSNR among the five variants (). Our method nevertheless achieves higher relighting PSNR by 0.62, 0.50 and 0.81 dB on Synthetic4Relight, TensoIR-Synthetic and Stanford-ORB, respectively, along with higher synthetic albedo PSNR and lower roughness MAE. The STAdam adaptation remains close to the no-prior variant in image PSNR. At 100 steps, mesh Large Steps has slightly higher novel-view PSNR and lower roughness MAE than ours, while ours retains higher relighting and albedo PSNR (Tab.S3). These results show that smoothing through mesh connectivity helps optimization, but does not recover the relighting and albedo quality obtained by sharing updates through the material prior.

    S4 Albedo Oracle Fits

    We assess the albedo capacity of the fixed learned-prior lattice used in Sec.6.4. For each of the four Synthetic4Relight and four TensoIR-Synthetic scenes and both prior models, we use the final mesh and the lattice of the 1000-step run with a single seed. Both oracle variants use this same mesh. The lattice coordinates and assignments are built from the run’s learned prior features.

    Ground-truth fusion.

    We replace the per-view predicted albedo with ground-truth albedo and apply the same visibility tests, mask erosion and viewing-angle weighting as in prior fusion. TensoIR-Synthetic supplies training-view albedo ground truth. Since Synthetic4Relight does not supply training-view albedo ground truth, its oracle uses all 200 test-view albedo maps. The fused per-vertex albedo defines the vertex oracle. Vertices without a GT observation retain the optimized albedo.

    Lattice fitting.

    Let a_GT denote the fused linear albedo and Q₀ the initial material logits. For each channel, we solve

    C^*=\arg\min_C∥S^⊤C-(logit(a_GT)-Q₀)∥²,

    		(S4)

    using only lattice-supported vertices with a GT observation. Albedo is clamped to [10⁻³,1-10⁻³] before taking logits. The resulting lattice oracle is sigmoid(Q₀+S^⊤C^*). Vertices outside the lattice use the same GT values as the vertex oracle where available, matching the free offsets of our representation. We use LSQR with absolute and relative tolerances of 10⁻¹⁰ and at most 20000 iterations per channel. We additionally fit in linear albedo space and clip the sliced values to [0,1].

    Evaluation and comparison.

    We render all 200 test views and use the paper’s scene-level RGB scale alignment and gamma-2.2 albedo PSNR. Tab.6 compares both MVInverse and DiffusionRenderer runs using the same three optimization seeds for the per-vertex control and ours; each optimized result retains its own jointly optimized geometry. The DiffusionRenderer per-vertex control averages 29.91 and 26.37 dB on Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR-Synthetic, respectively, compared with 33.08 and 28.72 dB for ours. The two oracle fits are evaluated on the final mesh of ours to isolate the material representation, so the vertex oracle is a common representational reference rather than a separately fitted oracle on the control’s final mesh. Tab.S4 reports both predictors and both fitting spaces. The logit-space oracle loses 0.74–1.26 dB relative to the vertex oracle, while the optimized lattice albedo remains 1.94–4.35 dB below the logit-space oracle. Thus the remaining error is not exhausted by the lattice’s representational restriction in these experiments.

    S4.1 Controlled 2D Texture Reconstruction

    We complement the learned-prior oracle experiment with a controlled texture reconstruction task. Rapid changes in target color over short distances in prior feature space can be difficult for a coarse lattice to represent. We construct a nonlinear synthetic prior to examine how lattice resolution affects this approximation error, using a 614×768 RGB photograph (471552 pixels) as the target.

    Synthetic priors.

    We use either the original target or a bilaterally filtered target with spatial standard deviation 0.5 pixels and RGB range parameter 0.1. For filtered RGB values t, let x=10⁻⁴+(1-2×10⁻⁴)t. We apply the fixed cross-channel color warp

    r=σ (logit(x_R)+s\tanh(x_G-0.45)/(w)),(S5)
    g=σ (logit(x_G)+0.8s\tanh(x_B-0.35)/(w)),(S6)
    b=σ (logit(x_B)-0.9s\tanhr-0.50/w),(S7)

    where σ is the sigmoid, s=0.9 and w=0.08. We then reduce saturation by a factor of 0.8 and mix in 5% white. All warp parameters are fixed in advance. The localized transitions create a nonlinear mapping between prior features and target colors; a global affine correction achieves only about 27 dB.

    Reconstruction.

    We build a fixed RGB-only permutohedral lattice from each synthetic prior. At spacings 0.1 and 0.025, we optimize its RGB values from a uniform gray initialization using full-batch Adam with learning rate 0.03 for 2000 steps. This toy updates texture by t̂=0.5+S^⊤C and an RGB mean squared error loss in the image’s encoded color space. Each occupied lattice point carries three scalar color parameters.

    Results.

    In Fig.S1, reducing the spacing from 0.1 to 0.025 improves reconstruction from 44.50 to 61.98 dB with the unfiltered prior and from 42.83 to 47.86 dB with the filtered prior. The finer lattices use 4602 and 4463 lattice points, respectively, over 100 times fewer than the 471552 target pixels. Thus finer lattice resolution recovers detailed variation under this nonlinear mapping while retaining a substantial reduction in parameter count. The lower score with the filtered prior also illustrates that improved lattice resolution cannot generally undo information lost in the prior.

    S5 Baseline Settings

    TensoIR baselines.

    For a fairer comparison, we run Neural-PBIR and DiffReg-PBIR with the environment hidden from camera rays on TensoIR-Synthetic, whose images have composited backgrounds. We also disable Neural-PBIR’s background-observation loss during distillation.

    S6 Learned Metallic Setting

    We compare fixed-zero metallic with a variant that learns metallic from a uniform value of 0.2, using refined priors and the same scene initializations in both arms. Metallic uses the same fixed prior-space lattice, preconditioning and learning rate as roughness. The prior coordinates, lattice spacing and support, initial albedo and roughness, geometry and illumination settings, and 1000-step budget are unchanged within each pair. We evaluate both predictors on four Synthetic4Relight scenes, four TensoIR-Synthetic scenes, seven DTC-Synthetic scenes and the seven Stanford-ORB light scenes.

    The effect depends on the dataset. On Synthetic4Relight, learning metallic changes relighting by -0.20/-0.22 dB and albedo PSNR by -1.40/-0.64 dB for MVI/DR. On TensoIR-Synthetic, learning metallic changes relighting by +0.35/+0.27 dB and albedo PSNR by -0.31/+0.55 dB for MVI/DR. On Stanford-ORB light, learning metallic reduces relighting HDR PSNR by 0.15/0.07 dB for MVI/DR. On DTC-Synthetic, mean relighting PSNR increases by 0.61/0.87 dB for MVI/DR, with lower LPIPS in both cases (Tab.S7). The added material freedom therefore helps some metrics, without consistently improving material recovery or relighting across benchmarks. The main-paper results and the following qualitative comparisons retain fixed-zero metallic.

    S7 Evaluation Protocol

item.title: 玩家永远在盖房子的世界怎么渲染：Unity SEED 讲清「持续建造」下的性能与内容管线 ｜ How SEED renders a world players never stop building
item.description:
一句话：当世界由玩家持续生成，渲染预算、批次与资源流送都得围绕「不可预知的内容」重新设计。

要点：

  • 设定本身就是难点：世界由玩家不停建造与改动，因此内容无法预先烘焙或静态优化
  • Unity SEED 团队分享的正是这类项目在渲染侧的处理方式——如何在内容持续变化时维持可预期的帧预算
  • 文章属于 Unity 官方的技术复盘，讲的是工程取舍而不是功能介绍

为什么值得看：UGC 世界的渲染问题与静态关卡完全不同：你不能提前知道玩家会造出什么。这类一线复盘比任何特性介绍都更接近「AI 生成内容 + 引擎」将要面对的情况。

中文摘要：Unity 官方博客的一篇技术复盘：在一个玩家永远不会停止建造的世界里，渲染该如何做。难点在于内容无法预先烘焙或静态优化——世界由玩家持续改动，任何静态的资源与批次规划都会失效。SEED 团队分享的正是这类项目在渲染侧的处理方式，重点落在「当内容持续变化时如何维持可预期的帧预算」。对正在做 UGC、沙盒或 AI 生成内容进引擎的团队，这种一线工程取舍比任何功能特性介绍都更贴近真实问题。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：Unity Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-11-06

本期推送：2026-11-09

How SEED renders a world players never stop building

Nov 6, 2026

Adam Axler - Unity

Senior Content Marketing Manager

Platforms and publishingTarget platformsPlatforms and publishingTarget platforms

You can’t predict what players will build. In SEED, that’s the whole point – and the core rendering challenge.

SEED is Klang Games’s persistent MMO sandbox, built with Unity. It’s set on a distant planet where players manage autonomous characters called seedlings, build homes and businesses, trade in a player-driven economy, and organize societies with their own roles and laws. The world keeps running after players log off, and it’s continuously growing. Every new house, shop, tree, and seedling puts more pressure on Unity rendering performance, across hardware ranging from high-end PCs to phones.

The simulation itself runs on Klang Games’s servers. The Unity client’s job is to render whatever state the server streams in, so its workload depends on what players have built, not on what the team planned for.

“Since SEED is a fully server-authoritative game, the client mostly reads and renders the state and forwards player interactions, like clicking or camera movement,” says Artem Dyadichkin, graphics engineer at Klang Games.

We spoke with Dyadichkin and Nikita Fetisov, senior game engineer, about rendering player-built societies with the Universal Render Pipeline (URP), keeping thousands of small objects cheap, and using real player data to find bottlenecks on PC and mobile.

A world built from tiny pieces

SEED’s art style does a lot of the scaling work before any code runs. The game is stylized and low-poly, and instead of relying on textures, it stores most of its surface data in the geometry.

“Most of our color data is actually stored inside the vertex data,” says Dyadichkin. “The vertex data knows which color it is, which material definition it has – is it metal, is it smooth? All those things are baked into the meshes themselves.”

That saves on shading and memory bandwidth, which matters most on mobile.

Buildings take the same approach to an extreme. Instead of treating each structure as a single large mesh, SEED constructs buildings from many small, brick-like modules: walls, floors, roof edges, and corners on a one-meter grid. Players place coarse building blocks (voxels), and the game expands each one into around 15 modules, roughly half forming the building’s exterior and half its interior, which is generated only when a player looks inside. The largest society on one of SEED’s busiest islands has 172 buildings, made up of roughly 12,500 voxels, or 190,000 modules.

“We utilize BatchRendererGroup to render them and batch them together, and we do those batches through jobs,” says Dyadichkin. “Even though there are very many modules we need to render, buildings themselves have never really been a bottleneck in terms of pure rendering performance.”

Those jobs run on the C# Job System, and the team compiles them with the Burst compiler. Dyadichkin says they almost always go hand in hand in SEED’s client code.

SEED | Klang Games

Staying on the default path in URP

SEED uses URP to scale across PC and mobile, and Klang Games deliberately sticks close to Unity’s defaults.

“We try to stick to default solutions from Unity, so we can always be sure that whenever the next update comes, it gets covered,” says Dyadichkin.

That matters because the team upgrades Unity roughly once or twice a year – SEED currently runs on Unity 6.3 – picking up new rendering features as the project grows. Where the game needs something custom, the team extends URP rather than replacing it, using custom renderer features for game-specific effects and interactions.

Their use of Shader Graph follows the same principle. Nature assets use the default Lit shader, while characters and objects use Unlit shaders with a custom lighting pass. Either way, the team doesn’t have to worry about breaking URP’s performance features.

“You can be sure that if you create a shader graph, it won’t break SRP [Scriptable Render Pipeline] batching, and it won’t break GPU Resident Drawer,” Dyadichkin says. “Being certain that all the URP core features are still supported, while you still have space to customize whatever you want in a shader, is very powerful.”

That safety net matters in a world where players, not designers, decide how much the client has to draw.

Maximize performance across platformsExplore Universal Render Pipeline

Interacting with thousands of objects

The denser players build, the harder it gets to render a society – and to let them click on any part of it.

When players are zoomed in, SEED uses pixel-perfect picking. A custom renderer feature draws objects into a separate render target, an off-screen texture the GPU renders into instead of the screen. Each object is encoded with a unique ID that both the CPU and GPU can read. The client reads the pixel under the cursor to find exactly which object the player is hovering over.

On mobile, a fingertip is far less precise than a cursor, so the client also checks the pixels surrounding each tap. If it detects more than one object nearby, it shows the player a list to choose from, making smaller objects easier to select in densely built areas.

When players zoom out, the client switches back to physics raycasts, since GPU picking is harder to scale across a wide view.

Behind those raycasts sits a huge number of colliders. SEED uses Unity Physics not for simulation, but to bootstrap them quickly and query them.

“Every tree has a collider, every object and potentially every building brick can have one, and characters and seedlings do as well,” says Dyadichkin. “We can bootstrap this huge amount of colliders very quickly and then do queries against them for placement checks and other interactions.”

Once a player opens a building, its interior appears, and the client has more to track as they move between floors and inspect individual rooms. A continuously running job determines whether each object is inside or outside a building and which room and floor it occupies.

“That allows us to do all sorts of things – disable or enable GameObjects, or set the correct rendering layers to control the lighting situation,” Dyadichkin explains.

SEED | Klang Games

Profiling the world players actually built

The hardest part of optimizing for player-built worlds is getting realistic data. Klang Games gets it from the live game.

The team keeps server snapshots for disaster recovery, and once players have built large enough societies, those snapshots become test cases.

“We can restore what players have actually built and use that for performance testing and testing features at scale,” Fetisov says. “We can work with these built-out societies instead of starting from scratch or trying to simulate the data ourselves.”

Loading a snapshot of a large city locally exposed an unexpected CPU rendering bottleneck on PC.

“Our game is not GPU bottlenecked most of the time, but rather CPU bottlenecked,” says Dyadichkin. “It’s a very stylized, low-poly game with almost no textures.”

Using the Unity Profiler, Dyadichkin found the render thread spending more time than expected submitting draw calls. The team uses GPU Resident Drawer, so Dyadichkin expected it to instance those objects. The Frame Debugger showed otherwise.

SEED | Klang Games

“We were still defaulting to SRP batching rather than hybrid batching,” Dyadichkin says. “It turned out GPU Resident Drawer wasn’t capturing all these objects because almost all of our Prefabs have LOD Groups.”

The difference matters at SEED’s scale. The SRP Batcher reduces the CPU cost of setting up each draw call, but still submits one per object. GPU Resident Drawer goes further, grouping objects that share a mesh and material into instanced draws, which the Frame Debugger labels as hybrid batches. With thousands of small objects, that’s the difference between many lightweight draw calls and a few large ones.

The culprit behind the missed objects was animated LOD cross-fading. The effect looked better, but it kept the objects off the GPU Resident Drawer path.

“We disabled the animation portion. We still have cross-fading, but now with manually set transitions,” he says. “Now the draw calls are instanced again, which eased the load on our CPU render thread.”

SEED | Klang Games

Rendering a mature society within mobile memory

On mobile, SEED’s rendering hit a different constraint. “On the mobile side, we’re not CPU bound – we’re memory bound,” Fetisov says. “That is the main bane of our project.”

A mature society can contain enormous numbers of buildings, outdoor objects, characters, and meshes. Every mesh and material the client renders has to fit in memory first. Klang Games relies heavily on the Memory Profiler and memory snapshot comparisons to track down where that memory goes. The team found textures stored three times because of a broken reference, Addressables dependencies that duplicated the same material, and C# collections far larger than they needed to be.

“A lot came up where, on desktop, it was fine and people didn’t really notice it, but on mobile it was a big issue,” says Fetisov. “We relied on the Unity Memory Profiler quite a lot, especially [memory] snapshot diffs.”

Even without textures, geometry adds up.

“Some of the meshes were pretty chunky, especially the trees,” Fetisov says. “If you load all the LODs, a single tree can take megabytes of memory, and we have many tree variations.”

Because the team builds Addressables per platform, it can ship simplified trees to mobile without changing any game code. “The same code that loads the chair on desktop loads the chair on mobile,” Fetisov explains. “But the Addressables themselves can be assets optimized for mobile.”

The bigger shift was replacing LOD Groups on mobile altogether. Classic LODs meant storing multiple meshes per object type in memory – the same cost Fetisov describes with the trees. Mesh LOD, introduced in Unity 6.2, instead stores every level of detail inside a single mesh, and SEED’s mobile variants now use it exclusively. It also reduced the workload for Klang Games’s small art team.

“Switching from LODs to Mesh LOD was a crucial step in making it possible to render the game world on mobile devices,” says Fetisov.

SEED | Klang Games

Designing for what players build next

SEED’s core rendering challenge isn’t going away: Players decide what the client has to draw, and they never stop building. “It’s a constant balance between the visual fidelity we envision for these player-created worlds and stable frame rates on low-end devices,” Dyadichkin says.

Klang Games can’t predict what players will build next – but it can test against what they’ve already built.

“Design, build, and test for your target scale from day one,” Fetisov says. “Profile against realistic loads early and keep doing it.”

SEEDis available in early access. Check out more stories from Unity developers on the Unity Blog and Resource Hub.

The simulation itself runs on Klang Games’s servers. The Unity client’s job is to render whatever state the server streams in, so its workload depends on what players have built, not on what the team planned for.

“Since SEED is a fully server-authoritative game, the client mostly reads and renders the state and forwards player interactions, like clicking or camera movement,” says Artem Dyadichkin, graphics engineer at Klang Games.

We spoke with Dyadichkin and Nikita Fetisov, senior game engineer, about rendering player-built societies with the Universal Render Pipeline (URP), keeping thousands of small objects cheap, and using real player data to find bottlenecks on PC and mobile.

A world built from tiny pieces

SEED’s art style does a lot of the scaling work before any code runs. The game is stylized and low-poly, and instead of relying on textures, it stores most of its surface data in the geometry.

“Most of our color data is actually stored inside the vertex data,” says Dyadichkin. “The vertex data knows which color it is, which material definition it has – is it metal, is it smooth? All those things are baked into the meshes themselves.”

That saves on shading and memory bandwidth, which matters most on mobile.

Buildings take the same approach to an extreme. Instead of treating each structure as a single large mesh, SEED constructs buildings from many small, brick-like modules: walls, floors, roof edges, and corners on a one-meter grid. Players place coarse building blocks (voxels), and the game expands each one into around 15 modules, roughly half forming the building’s exterior and half its interior, which is generated only when a player looks inside. The largest society on one of SEED’s busiest islands has 172 buildings, made up of roughly 12,500 voxels, or 190,000 modules.

“We utilize BatchRendererGroup to render them and batch them together, and we do those batches through jobs,” says Dyadichkin. “Even though there are very many modules we need to render, buildings themselves have never really been a bottleneck in terms of pure rendering performance.”

Those jobs run on the C# Job System, and the team compiles them with the Burst compiler. Dyadichkin says they almost always go hand in hand in SEED’s client code.

SEED | Klang Games

Staying on the default path in URP

SEED uses URP to scale across PC and mobile, and Klang Games deliberately sticks close to Unity’s defaults.

“We try to stick to default solutions from Unity, so we can always be sure that whenever the next update comes, it gets covered,” says Dyadichkin.

That matters because the team upgrades Unity roughly once or twice a year – SEED currently runs on Unity 6.3 – picking up new rendering features as the project grows. Where the game needs something custom, the team extends URP rather than replacing it, using custom renderer features for game-specific effects and interactions.

Their use of Shader Graph follows the same principle. Nature assets use the default Lit shader, while characters and objects use Unlit shaders with a custom lighting pass. Either way, the team doesn’t have to worry about breaking URP’s performance features.

“You can be sure that if you create a shader graph, it won’t break SRP [Scriptable Render Pipeline] batching, and it won’t break GPU Resident Drawer,” Dyadichkin says. “Being certain that all the URP core features are still supported, while you still have space to customize whatever you want in a shader, is very powerful.”

That safety net matters in a world where players, not designers, decide how much the client has to draw.

Maximize performance across platformsExplore Universal Render Pipeline

Interacting with thousands of objects

The denser players build, the harder it gets to render a society – and to let them click on any part of it.

When players are zoomed in, SEED uses pixel-perfect picking. A custom renderer feature draws objects into a separate render target, an off-screen texture the GPU renders into instead of the screen. Each object is encoded with a unique ID that both the CPU and GPU can read. The client reads the pixel under the cursor to find exactly which object the player is hovering over.

On mobile, a fingertip is far less precise than a cursor, so the client also checks the pixels surrounding each tap. If it detects more than one object nearby, it shows the player a list to choose from, making smaller objects easier to select in densely built areas.

When players zoom out, the client switches back to physics raycasts, since GPU picking is harder to scale across a wide view.

Behind those raycasts sits a huge number of colliders. SEED uses Unity Physics not for simulation, but to bootstrap them quickly and query them.

“Every tree has a collider, every object and potentially every building brick can have one, and characters and seedlings do as well,” says Dyadichkin. “We can bootstrap this huge amount of colliders very quickly and then do queries against them for placement checks and other interactions.”

Once a player opens a building, its interior appears, and the client has more to track as they move between floors and inspect individual rooms. A continuously running job determines whether each object is inside or outside a building and which room and floor it occupies.

“That allows us to do all sorts of things – disable or enable GameObjects, or set the correct rendering layers to control the lighting situation,” Dyadichkin explains.

SEED | Klang Games

Profiling the world players actually built

The hardest part of optimizing for player-built worlds is getting realistic data. Klang Games gets it from the live game.

The team keeps server snapshots for disaster recovery, and once players have built large enough societies, those snapshots become test cases.

“We can restore what players have actually built and use that for performance testing and testing features at scale,” Fetisov says. “We can work with these built-out societies instead of starting from scratch or trying to simulate the data ourselves.”

Loading a snapshot of a large city locally exposed an unexpected CPU rendering bottleneck on PC.

“Our game is not GPU bottlenecked most of the time, but rather CPU bottlenecked,” says Dyadichkin. “It’s a very stylized, low-poly game with almost no textures.”

Using the Unity Profiler, Dyadichkin found the render thread spending more time than expected submitting draw calls. The team uses GPU Resident Drawer, so Dyadichkin expected it to instance those objects. The Frame Debugger showed otherwise.

SEED | Klang Games

“We were still defaulting to SRP batching rather than hybrid batching,” Dyadichkin says. “It turned out GPU Resident Drawer wasn’t capturing all these objects because almost all of our Prefabs have LOD Groups.”

The difference matters at SEED’s scale. The SRP Batcher reduces the CPU cost of setting up each draw call, but still submits one per object. GPU Resident Drawer goes further, grouping objects that share a mesh and material into instanced draws, which the Frame Debugger labels as hybrid batches. With thousands of small objects, that’s the difference between many lightweight draw calls and a few large ones.

The culprit behind the missed objects was animated LOD cross-fading. The effect looked better, but it kept the objects off the GPU Resident Drawer path.

“We disabled the animation portion. We still have cross-fading, but now with manually set transitions,” he says. “Now the draw calls are instanced again, which eased the load on our CPU render thread.”

SEED | Klang Games

Rendering a mature society within mobile memory

On mobile, SEED’s rendering hit a different constraint. “On the mobile side, we’re not CPU bound – we’re memory bound,” Fetisov says. “That is the main bane of our project.”

A mature society can contain enormous numbers of buildings, outdoor objects, characters, and meshes. Every mesh and material the client renders has to fit in memory first. Klang Games relies heavily on the Memory Profiler and memory snapshot comparisons to track down where that memory goes. The team found textures stored three times because of a broken reference, Addressables dependencies that duplicated the same material, and C# collections far larger than they needed to be.

“A lot came up where, on desktop, it was fine and people didn’t really notice it, but on mobile it was a big issue,” says Fetisov. “We relied on the Unity Memory Profiler quite a lot, especially [memory] snapshot diffs.”

Even without textures, geometry adds up.

“Some of the meshes were pretty chunky, especially the trees,” Fetisov says. “If you load all the LODs, a single tree can take megabytes of memory, and we have many tree variations.”

Because the team builds Addressables per platform, it can ship simplified trees to mobile without changing any game code. “The same code that loads the chair on desktop loads the chair on mobile,” Fetisov explains. “But the Addressables themselves can be assets optimized for mobile.”

The bigger shift was replacing LOD Groups on mobile altogether. Classic LODs meant storing multiple meshes per object type in memory – the same cost Fetisov describes with the trees. Mesh LOD, introduced in Unity 6.2, instead stores every level of detail inside a single mesh, and SEED’s mobile variants now use it exclusively. It also reduced the workload for Klang Games’s small art team.

“Switching from LODs to Mesh LOD was a crucial step in making it possible to render the game world on mobile devices,” says Fetisov.

SEED | Klang Games

Designing for what players build next

SEED’s core rendering challenge isn’t going away: Players decide what the client has to draw, and they never stop building. “It’s a constant balance between the visual fidelity we envision for these player-created worlds and stable frame rates on low-end devices,” Dyadichkin says.

Klang Games can’t predict what players will build next – but it can test against what they’ve already built.

“Design, build, and test for your target scale from day one,” Fetisov says. “Profile against realistic loads early and keep doing it.”

SEEDis available in early access. Check out more stories from Unity developers on the Unity Blog and Resource Hub.

item.title: 更便宜、片段更长的视频模型：Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash 把「成本」当成主要卖点 ｜ Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
item.description:
一句话：长片段的成本曲线比画质更影响能不能进生产管线。

要点：

  • DeepMind 发布 Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash，主打速度与成本效率，同时支持更长的片段
  • 对生成式内容管线而言，「更长片段 × 更低单位成本」直接决定了它能否被用在预演、素材扩充等高频场景
  • 官方博客给出了能力定位与使用口径，适合与既有视频模型做成本对照

为什么值得看：做 AI 原生内容管线时，真正卡住生产的是成本与时长，而不是峰值画质。这条给了新的成本基线，值得拿来重算「生成一分钟画面」的账。

中文摘要：DeepMind 发布 Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash，定位是「快且成本友好」，同时把单次生成的片段长度拉长。对生成式内容的生产管线来说，这组指标（更长片段 × 更低单位成本）比峰值画质更直接地决定它能否用于预演、素材扩充这类高频场景。博客给出了能力范围与使用口径，适合与现有视频模型做一次成本对照。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：DeepMind Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-11-05

本期推送：2026-11-09

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings 15-second clips, stronger consistency, and faster, more cost-effective generation.

Anish Nangia

Product Manager, Google DeepMind

Listen to article [[duration]] minutesThis content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

We’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, which offers native 15-second video creation, improved reference adherence, and multi-turn conversational editing. This update lowers costs by 30% and provides better consistency for your professional projects. You can start using these capabilities today across the Gemini API, Google Vids, and Gemini for business to produce high-quality video content at scale.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.
  • We are launching Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with support for fifteen-second videos and improved reference adherence.
  • You can now edit clips through multi-turn conversations, which allows for faster adjustments without starting over.
  • We reduced the price by 30% to help you produce high-quality video content at a lower cost.
  • This model is generally available on the Gemini API and Google Cloud for your production needs.
    • Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

    Explore other styles:

    Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.

    Here’s an overview of what’s new:

    Fast and cost-effective at scale

    Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.

    Longer clips up to 15 seconds

    You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.

    Better reference adherence

    You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.

    Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.

    More consistent results

    You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.

    Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.

    Easier editing in conversation

    You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.

    Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.

    More natural speech

    You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow, creating video explainers in Gemini for business, or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids.

    Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.

    More controllable, cinematic look

    You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.

    Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.

    Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency

    Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.

    15 second long clips: Turns one style frame into a 4-shot, 15-second macro science explainer with accurately spelled, motion-tracked callouts.

    Multi-turn motion transfer: Generates a rippling octopus in Turn 1, then replaces it in Turn 2 with a dancer whose gown mirrors the exact fluid motion.

    First-to-last frame consistency (1.1 vs. 1.2): Connects an exterior start frame and interior end frame in one continuous camera push in 1.2 Flash. You can see subtle differences like the cats on the roof, the soup ladle turning into chopsticks, and some other minor changes.

    Unbroken crash zoom-out: Pulls continuously from a tight shoreline close-up to an aerial island vista in one 10-second shot with natural scale and zero cuts.

    Real-world results, from creatives to global brands

    Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

    Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash

    While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:

  • For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio, explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing.
  • For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console, and build enterprise solutions with the API.
  • For everyone using Google apps: Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in Flow, generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the Gemini app (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in Google Ads.
    • Posted in:
